# PREFACE.

->BIBLE-LOVING READER!<-

When I published my Latin *Treatise on the Fundamental Principles and Rules of Symbolic, Typical, Allegorical, and Prophetic Theology* <note>original: "Verhandeling over de Grond-beginzzelen, en Stok-regelen der Zinne-beeldige, Voorbeel-dige, Leen-ſpreukige, en Prophetiſche God-geleerdheid"</note> last year, my Reader could easily infer—and in some places clearly read—that I intended to publish several portions of God's Holy Word explained according to those fundamental rules. These were pieces that I had already prepared in draft form <note>literally "in the rough"</note> some years ago, and which required a further polishing to be made ready for the printing press, in order to see the light of day in either the Dutch <note>original: "duitſche," referring here to the local vernacular Dutch</note> or Latin language, just as they had been drafted by me. I therefore now give to **You**, good-

# P R E F A C E.

willing Reader, a treatise on all the Miracles of Jesus, composed according to those rules <note>original: "Regel-wetten"</note> that I had prescribed for myself in my *Diatribe* <note>A "Diatribe" here refers to a formal scholarly discourse or preliminary treatise</note>, and have repeated in the Introduction to this Work. I do not wish for these interpretations of mine to be viewed as mathematical demonstrations: nor do I presume that I have hit the mark in every instance: I only think that I have provided a closer occasion to track down the hidden sense, which I firmly believe lurks beneath the literal shell <note>The "literal shell" refers to the surface-level meaning of the biblical text, beneath which lies a deeper spiritual truth</note>, and which must be extracted according to fixed rules by which I am guided. To show that such treatises provide rich material for truly spiritual and pious contemplations, I have everywhere added a Sketch *of common Truths* at the end; these, due to their brevity and pertinence, cannot bore my Reader, and can be used by young Teachers <note>Referring to student ministers or young clergy</note> who wish to make use of our Work by expanding upon them for further application. I have also added the Parable-
*discourse of the Wise and Foolish Virgins*, and worked it out in that manner, in order to [show] those who presume that such treatments of God's Holy Word are meager and thin,

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's preface, likely following an introduction of the work's theological purpose. The author is discussing the rapid production of the book following his career advancement.</meta>

# -> P R E F A C E. <-

and to refute by deed itself those things which give little nourishment to truly godly reflections. This work is also a specimen <note>original: "Proefstuk"</note> of parabolic explanations <note>Interpretations of biblical parables</note>, a great portion of which I would have published shortly hereafter, had my changed circumstances not hindered it.

If ever an author had reason to request some excuse for his work—should any errors, overlooked through inattention, be found here or there—I certainly have such reason. This work had just gone to the press, with only about three sheets printed, when I was called to the *Professorship of Theology* <note>original: "Theologiſche Profeſſie"</note>. The printer, well understanding that if I departed and became occupied with new work before this entire piece was printed, this "paper-child" would remain long in the birth, made such haste—sometimes printing five, sometimes six sheets in a week—that the work was brought to an end within the time of three months. Now, I had indeed composed these treatises eight years ago in my first congregation, at EISDEN, yet with no intention of handing them over to the press. There was much to be polished, changed, added, removed, and rearranged, etc.

<summary>The author explains that this work serves as a sample of his parabolic interpretations and apologizes for potential errors caused by the printing process being rushed after his appointment as a Professor of Theology.</summary>
<keywords>preface, parables, theology professor, Eisden, printing process, biblical interpretation</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>The catchword 'LYST' (List) from the previous page suggests this preface follows a table of contents or list of subscribers. The author is concluding their introductory remarks.</meta>

# P R E F A C E .

I could have done everything much more conveniently, and intended to do so while the work was being printed, if only a normal pace had been maintained. But since everything proceeded so rapidly, one can easily understand that I—besides my usual service-work <note>The author likely refers to his official duties as a clergyman or professor</note> and other occupations—did not have sufficient space to work everything out as accurately as I wished; nor do I now have the time to revise it anew. Therefore, may the reader please look upon these or other circumstances with a favorable eye. And I would not bring this work into the world without hesitation, did I not think that it was nevertheless suited—however it may be—to lead the inquisitive reader, who does not cavil at trifles, into scriptural knowledge <note>original: "Schriftuur-kennis"</note>; and toward that end, I believe, its essential content is directed. Farewell, and love Truth and Virtue!

->Groningen, this 28th<-
->of June, 1717.<-

# Introduction to the Treatise

## §. II. Concerning now in particular the **Miracles** of **Jesus**, these were irreproachable and undeniable proofs of his true **Messianic Office**, **Divinity**, and **Heavenly** mission.

A. These were performed by a single command of his will, without any outward apparatus or artifice; "I will, be thou clean": "**Little daughter**, arise": and similar is often the language of the **Savior**; so spoke no **Moses**, no **Elijah**, no **Elisha**; or if **Jesus** employed something external, it appeared clearly that such an external act was not the working or instrumental cause of the **Miracle**. <note>The author argues that unlike Old Testament prophets who used staves or prayers, Jesus's power was innate.</note>
B. **Miracles** that had never occurred before, and which exceeded the powers of secondary causes: "Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind," John 9:32.
C. **Miracles** that were foretold by the **Divine Prophets** as being performed by the **Messiah**: See Isaiah 35:5, 6 and Matthew 11:5.
D. That which adds a demonstrative power to the **Miracles** of **Jesus**, for the **Lord God** would by no means have permitted an **Impostor** to perform those signs and **Miracles** which, according to the **Prophecies**, are unique to the **Messiah**, and especially at that time when, according to the **Oracles of God**, the **Messiah** was expected. Furthermore, **Jesus's Miracles** were accompanied by a godly life, or a perfectly holy conduct.
E. Surpassing the **Miraculous Deeds** of **Satan**, indeed that **Prince of Hell** must always yield in his workings to **Jesus**, whose name is **WONDER**. <note>original: "WONDER" - likely a reference to Isaiah 9:6.</note> We see this clearly in the **Holy Gospels**, that **Satan** at that time possessed men and mistreated them in a miserable fashion, thus effecting miraculous **Workings**, yet each time having to depart at the command of **Jesus**, from which it appeared that **Jesus** could have no agreement with that **Prince** of darkness. That **Satan**, in the aforementioned manner through a **Holy** permission from **God**, abused the bodies of many men at the time of the **Savior**, is so clearly to be read in the **Holy Historical Scriptures** that it would be an unbearable boldness to wish to [deny] so many clear, infallible testimonies...

The **Doctrine** of truth is sufficiently confirmed by **miracles**, and since the **Lord God** no longer performs outward miracles through His **Servants**, the question would be whether it is probable that in later times **Satan** or the instruments of **Satan** would have a privilege above the **Servants of God**? When the **Lord God** under the **Old Testament** and especially at the time of the **Savior**, and indeed shortly after His **Ascension**, permitted the **Devil** and his **Servants** to carry out wondrous things, He performed greater things through His **Ministers**, so that the great distinction between those in whom the **Spirit of God** works and those in whom the **Spirit** of this world works might be seen. Yet we make no determination here; nevertheless, we believe nothing except that which either sound **Reason** or a **Divine** testimony [confirms]...

So also the passage <term>Isaiah 35 v. 5, 6.</term> Which / as the context points out / primarily refers to spiritual miraculous deeds / is applied by Christ to his physical works / <term>Matthew 11 v. 5.</term> Here then the aforementioned reason applies again.

# Of Miracles.

c. The **Christ** generally teaches that beneath those astonishing works of his, another secret lies hidden. On the occasion of the multiplied loaves, he desires that one shall think of him as the bread of life, and that food which does not perish, **John 6, verse 27.** By that outward fishing catch, [he points] to the spiritual one, **Luke 5, verse 10.** On the occasion of the restored sight of one born blind, he wishes to be regarded as the light of the world. See **John 9, verses 5, and 39, 40, 41.**

d. A powerful proof is the correspondence between those bodily and spiritual miraculous deeds; between the restoring of the sight of a blind man and the opening of the eyes of the understanding; between the healing of a deaf and mute person and the giving of spiritual observation and eloquence to recount **Jehovah's** <note>The author uses the tetragrammaton/divine name to emphasize the continuity between the Old Testament God and Christ's works.</note> works, ways, praise, etc.; between the restoring of the lame and making the wayward walk upon the paths of salvation and life. The raised dead—how fittingly do they sketch the quickening of sinners dead in sins and trespasses.

And how wonderfully shall this conception commend the Power and Wisdom of **Jesus**; if those outward Masterpieces are but a prelude to those more glorious deeds in the **Kingdom of Heaven**, in the conversion, confirmation, adornment, and perfection of his favored ones; in the raising, founding, defending, and completion of his **Church**? Thus shall these Miraculous Deeds, as we have already said, be like a demonstrative Doctrine, hiding such truths under those signs to which—when placed in the clear daylight—certainty cannot fail to give its consent.

e. And who would suppose that **Jesus'** Miracles would be of less figurative significance than those of **Moses** and **Elijah**?

H. However, the Miracles of the **Savior** are teaching-pictures <note>original: "leer-schilderyen" — a vivid Dutch term for allegorical or pedagogical illustrations.</note> not only of that work of Grace which the **Lord God** exercises in every one of the Elect; but also of those deeds, ways, and actions which he maintains in his entire Sanctuary, in the visible **Church**. Thus that over-abundant, rare catch of fish, the torn net, the preservation of the fish, **Luke Chapter 5, verse 3, etc.**; the Ship in the Sea tossed by storm-winds and waves, the unbelief of the disciples, **Christ** rebuking the Sea and Winds, the stilled storm, the people in amazement;

He compares these allegorical meanings to the miracles of Moses and Elijah, suggesting the outward acts are preludes to greater spiritual realities.</summary>

...recognizing Jesus's **Miraculous Power** <note>original: "Wonder-magt"</note> / Matthew 8, §. 24. etc. undoubtedly signify something that would be seen not merely in an individual believer, but in the visible **Body of the Church**.

I. We also maintain that not only the Body, or the essential substance of the **Miracles**, but also all the surrounding circumstances possess a significant power; and who shall deny this, when it can be demonstrated:

a. That they signify something that corresponds with **God’s wisdom** and the nature of the matter being depicted.
b. That they serve further to glorify God’s wisdom.
c. That they find their precise truth in the **antitype** <note>The "antitype" is the New Testament fulfillment of an Old Testament "type" or symbol.</note>.
d. That they guide and steer the understanding of the researcher in applying the Miracle to that specific Church event being intended; whereas the "Body" of the Miracle is often a more general portrait, applicable to almost all times. Thus, the raising of the dead, the cleansing of a leper, the healing of a paralytic, giving gait to the lame, or restoring sight to the blind, is a general portrait that has its fulfillment in the Church at all times; however, what Jesus specifically intended to sketch through this or that particular **Miraculous Deed**, and at what time such would be seen in the fulfillment—concerning this, the circumstances must provide the guidance.
e. And truly, it is not without a wise reason that Jesus performed Miracles not only in general, but precisely upon these specific occasions and in specific circumstances, all of which Divine wisdom has ordained and governed.
f. And if it is true of the words of God that they signify everything they can possibly signify when viewed in all their context and relation, shall not the signs of God—as they are also a form of instruction—signify everything they can in their connection, provided they yield a sense worthy of God and harmoniously agree with the analogy of faith, the divine oracles, and historical accounts?

§ IV. We will explain the literal sense only briefly, though sufficiently, as we assume readers who are not entirely unpracticed in these matters, and who can find the literal explanation more broadly elsewhere if they so desire. Nevertheless, we will clarify the literal events enough so that one can form a sufficiently vivid imagination of the literal account, which must serve as the foundation for the spiritual application.

§ V. We treat the truth of the histories and the proofs for Jesus's Divinity and Messiahship <note>original: "Messiaschap"</note> briefly, since this subject has been fully established in detail by others.

§ VI. Our primary effort is to extract the spiritual sense, transferring all the pieces and parts of the miraculous deeds—as much as is possible for us—and placing them in a spiritual light. We attempt to pinpoint the specific time and subject in which one must seek the antitype <note>term: "Antitype" (tegenbeeld) - The historical fulfillment of a prophetic symbol or "type."</note>, according to proven fundamental rules, by marking the indicators of time and person. This is done in the same manner as one brings a Divine prophecy to its own era by virtue of the internal connection or the chaining together of events. And we demonstrate by trial that Jesus usually provides us with the key to open the secret, either:
a. Immediately before the performed miracle.
b. Or shortly after the performed miracle.
c. Or during the performance of the miracles.
d. Or through the miraculous deed itself, which is a specific "painting" <note>The author views each miracle as a visual allegory or "schilderye" composed by God.</note> that cannot be applied to various different things, so that one can always proceed with certainty in limiting the time and the subject.

§ VII. Our applications are therefore not general, but specific. I do not say: such instructional images have their fulfillment first in Judaism <note>original: "Joodendom"</note>, then in Heathenism <note>original: "Heidendom"</note>, and afterwards in Popery <note>original: "Papendom" - a common 18th-century Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church</note>, etc. But I endeavor to keep an eye on all the specific features and the joining together of matters, which cause me, and with me the reader, to cast our eyes upon specific subjects and times.

# Water changed into Wine.

Nevertheless, he does not entirely reject her request. *My hour*, the most fitting moment to glorify myself through miracles, *is not yet come.* <note>original: "Mijne uure... is nog niet gekomen"</note> As soon as that time has arrived, I shall reveal my miraculous arm.

Mary, listening to this with a respectful humility, commands the servants to listen to this Lord and to pay heed to his commands and signals.

*Whatever he shall say unto you, do that,* <note>John 2:5</note> who then were immediately ordered to fill with water six stone water-jars, placed there according to the purification rites of the Jews, each holding two or three measures <term>metreeten: an ancient liquid measure, roughly 10 gallons or 40 liters</term>. Just as they then immediately—though ignorant of what was to happen—nevertheless followed the Savior's will with an obedient readiness and filled them to the brim. These water-jars were used either for those who had made themselves unclean according to the Law by touching a dead body to wash therein, or to cleanse the hands and cups of the guests; the Jews were set upon this outward cleanliness in a superstitious manner. A *Metreet* is a measure of liquid things, containing as much as the *Ephah*, which is a measure of dry goods. Indeed, it appears that these vessels were of a sufficiently large capacity.

<margin>B.</margin>
Jesus, through his miraculous power, **CHANGED** this **WATER INTO WINE**, and indeed into the most fragrant kind; thus transforming the water-particles into wine-particles through his Divine Omnipotence. He commands the servants to draw it out and carry it to the Master of the Feast <term>Hofmeester: the steward or toastmaster overseeing the banquet</term>, who had oversight of the food and its arrangement. Upon receiving this wine to taste and savoring its fragrance—being ignorant of the miracle—he showed himself extremely wondered and surprised that the Bridegroom had not given the best wine first and the lesser wine later, according to the custom which dictates that the most flavorful and potent wines be served earlier, and the less-good later, when the tasting-senses <note>original: "proef-leeden"</note> are dulled and not as sharp.

Meanwhile, Jesus' Disciples, perceiving their Master's hand in this and seeing his Glory revealed through this sign, believe in him, being persuaded that he is the true God-man, the Messiah, the long-awaited salvation of the Fathers. They had indeed already followed him—two upon the preaching of John, the others called to him—nevertheless, they did not yet have that conviction which they received upon this miracle.

# Water changed into Wine.

B. **OMNIPOTENCE** <note>original: "AL-VERMOGEN"</note>—to change the nature of things in such a way is solely the work of Him who calls the things which are not as if they were, and does so through a simple act of will, through a single word.

### III.
But the brilliant rays of these Divine perfections will shine even more powerfully in our eyes when we draw into the light the miraculous mystery hidden beneath this outer husk.

<margin>The spiritual sense traced.</margin>
A. There are theologians who consider that the exchange of the Old Dispensation <note>The "Old Huishouding" refers to the era of the Mosaic Law.</note>—when the distribution of Grace was more meager—with the New—which delivers a more spacious and richer enjoyment of grace—is to be read here in this miraculous image. Let us compose the painting according to this supposition, so that we may see which features then appear and which are lacking.

The lack of wine shall signify that deficient dispensation of the Law. See Hebrews 8:7. The believers of the Old Testament did not yet possess such an abundant measure of knowledge, holiness, and soul-rejoicing; they did not dare to approach their Father so boldly, being held as minor children, even servants under a heart-pressing yoke of the Law, enslaved to the first principles of the world, or of the worldly Sanctuary. See Galatians 4:3. The Mother of Christ, being sensitive to this lack, would then be a portrait of the Jewish Church—I mean the true believers among them, those with longing expectations who hoped for the consolations of Israel; they are the Mother of Christ, that Woman who gave birth to that male Son. Revelation 12:5.

The anticipatory desire of these believers was all too hasty; that lack could not be filled before Jesus' hour had come, before He had fulfilled all obedience to the Law and had brought about the purification of sins. First, He had to awake from His sleep of death before He could make the weary souls drunk <note>In this context, "dronken maken" refers to being filled to overflowing with spiritual joy or the Holy Spirit.</note> and fill all sorrowful souls. Jeremiah 31:26. And He had to, therefore, speak to them in His word, through His messengers, yes, through the Spirit of bondage peculiar to the Old Testament, thus: *What is to me and to You?* <note>original: "Wat is my en U"</note>—for so the words actually lie in the original language <note>Referring to the Greek phrase "Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί," often translated as "Woman, what does this have to do with me?"</note>—that is to say: indeed, that close relationship is not yet between me and you; the handwriting of sins is not yet broken; the spiritual Marriage-Covenant is not yet consecrated in my sacrificial blood; and therefore, what relationship is between me and you, that I should fulfill all your lack? My hour has not yet come. When that hour shall have come—that is, when the Christ, exalted by the right hand of Jehovah, shall have received gifts to distribute among men—then He shall send down His Spirit...

### Wedding Feast. Matthew 22, where the King prepares a Wedding Feast for his Son.

This Wedding was celebrated on the third day. The Dispensations <note>original: "Huishoudingen," referring to the theological concept of God's different eras of dealing with humanity</note> of Grace can be called days; thus the end of the Ministry of the Law is a "last of the days." Isaiah 2:2. The first day is the time of the Promise, the second of the Law, the third that joyful dawn of the better Covenant. See then, how on a spiritual third day this feast was held.

The place is Cana in Galilee; thus the Oracles <note>prophetic scriptures</note> foretell that in Galilee the Savior would first seek his Bride. Isaiah 8:23, Matthew 4:17. It is a true proverb flowing from the mouth of the dying Jacob: Naphtali (located in Galilee) is a hind let loose of him who speaks good words; so those words can be translated. Naphtali would follow the Savior, revealed in the flesh, because grace is poured out over his lips. Psalm 45: his palate being nothing but sweetness. Song of Solomon 5:16. He gave good words. Cana comes from a Hebrew word *qanah* <note>original: קנָה</note> which means to obtain or to buy; this Wedding is celebrated in the place where Jesus has his ransomed, redeemed host of salvation: Indeed, Cana is written with a *qoph* <note>original: ק</note> in Joshua 19:28.

If seven days were spent with Wedding-joy and stately solemnity among the Jews; and if that Time was also given to this Wedding, this will also align well with the hidden meaning. Thus the course of time of the New Testament is divided into seven days, successions, or time-series in the sacred Books of Mystery <note>likely referring to the Book of Revelation</note>. During this heptad of times this feast shall be held, but on the last Church-day most solemnly of all, when so many shall come from East and West, and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 8:11. When the Bride, the Wife of the Lamb, in shining fine Linen, in the Adornments of the Sanctuary, shall be brought to her Bridegroom in the most stately manner. Revelation 19:8.

# The Son of the Royal Official

Having returned alone, he passes by Nazareth—the place of his upbringing, and therefore called his Fatherland—turning instead toward the northern regions, and arrives at Cana. There he is received with affection, as the Galileans had seen his signs at the Feast. Here, the opportunity for this miracle is presented to him.

<margin>
The literal sense explained.
</margin>

I. The literal meaning of this miracle is not complex, and therefore requires no lengthy clarification.

Jesus, having returned from Judea through Samaria into Galilee, came again to Cana in Galilee (a place we described in the explanation of the first miracle) where he had turned the water into wine. And there was a certain royal official <note>original: "Koninklijke hoveling"; likely a courtier or officer of the crown</note> (undoubtedly a servant of Herod; whether he was Chuza, Herod’s steward, whose wife Joanna was among those who followed and served Jesus—Luke chapter 8, verse 3—is uncertain). His son was sick at Capernaum (his illness being a fever, see verse 52). We also mention the city of Capernaum in connection with other miracles, particularly on the occasion of that extraordinary catch of fish. It was a city of Galilee (Luke 4:31) on the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:13), and specifically a seaside city located by the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:17), where there was a synagogue (John 6:59). Christ lived in this city (Mark 2:1 and Matthew 4:13), which is why it is called "his own city" (Matthew 9:1). It was a flourishing city, situated lower than Cana and Nazareth, which is why one is said to "go down" to Capernaum (John 2:12 and 4:46; Luke 4:31). Its exact location is unknown today, which perhaps lies in the fulfillment of the threat in Matthew 11:23. <note>See Reland, *Palestine*, page 683.</note>

This official, having heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death. He must have heard of the first miracle performed at Cana; also, Jesus’s stay in Judea and his signs seen by the Galileans at the Passover Feast in Jerusalem had made him very famous, so that his return to Galilee immediately caused a great stir, as appears from the previous account of our Evangelist. And perhaps Jesus, immediately upon his return, spread the fragrance of his teaching in those regions. This official gave a clear sign of his faith regarding Jesus’s miracle-working power, yet at the same time revealed his ignorance and unbelief by prescribing to Jesus the method of healing—as if Jesus, being absent, could not have performed that healing by a spoken word. It seems he did not yet know him as that God

*Jesus*, who was otherwise so inclined and ready to lay his healing and miraculous hands upon *Sufferers* when requested, had reasons to address this *Courtier* <note>original: "Hoveling," referring to the royal official in John 4</note> in a stern and authoritative tone, and even more so to rebuke the *Jewish People* in this man's *Person*. The teaching of *Jesus* was demonstrative, of a soul-winning content, drawn from *Moses* and the *Prophets*, agreeing with them in every respect, and therefore possessed an irrefutable credibility even without the Miracles. Therefore, the *Jews* should have been more eager for the Teaching of *Jesus*, to listen to it with reverent attention, than to behold *Jesus's* Miracles. By this speech of rebuke and exhortation, the *Savior* intended neither to make the *Jewish People* disregard the Signs and Wonders to be performed by the *Messiah* as manifest proofs of his mission from the *Father* into the world, nor to reject this courtier, but to bring to his mind what he ought to be more eager for than the Miracles.

At the repeated plea of this man—who accepted this grieving word from *Jesus* with reverent humility and persisted with confidence in *Jesus's* power and goodness, asking that *Jesus* would please come down before his child died—the *Savior* said: Go your way, your *Son* lives. And the man believed the word that *Jesus* said to him and went his way, becoming convinced during his persistent requests that *Jesus*, through his all-commanding will (for he had placed him in his faithful conception above the rank of all *Creatures*), could restore his *Son* from his illness while absent. However, it seems this faith only first progressed to a soul-saving faith when he, informed of the miraculous healing, believed with his whole household; see verse 53.

The description, the appearance, and the plea of this Courtier;

<margin>A.</margin> Regarding the words of the **Savior**, they point us immediately to the **Jews**, who even after **Christ's** Ascension were still charged with demanding a sign, 1 Corinthians 1:22. But before we speak more of that, let us first consider the ailment of this sufferer, of which he could be a symbolic image.

I speak of that astonishing pulse, the burning of the body, the flushing of the face, brown lips with a coated tongue, a deathly countenance, and more other symptoms which are the signs of this disease—what a vivid painting they are of a spiritless and comfortless doctrine and state, especially when one considers how corrupted the doctrine of faith and morals had become under **Judaism**.
    The **Jewish People** had entirely departed from the doctrine of faith and morals of the ancient believers. The Key of Knowledge was lost. Of that tender and as necessary as it is comforting Mystery of God—the doctrine of the adorable **Trinity**, the only foundation of a God-worthy and, for the sinner, a soul-saving redemption—the bulk of the people in **Israel** were ignorant. To expect a **Messiah** who was both **God** and **Man** was to them a paradox: therefore, within that external Church-body, there was as little right understanding as among the Heathens of how **God** reconciles and how He could become the **God** of a sinner. Must this not cause a spiritual fever? If their conscience awoke, if it set before their eyes the vileness of their sins and the holiness and justice of **God**, and they did not then know that **Savior** in whom the previous believers delighted and in whom all salvation rested, what an inflammation of spiritual thirst and burning, what a restless tossing that takes away all comfort and joy! What a state of terror when one cannot behold **Jehovah** <note>The Hebrew name for God, often used in Reformed theology to emphasize His covenant faithfulness.</note> in that joyful relationship as the **God** of the sinner, who can become the salvation of a mortal guilty of death and damnation; what a dismal deathly countenance must such people show? The lips are brown, the tongue coated; all their words, even their prayer to **God**, are unclean when they do not approach Him through the **Mediator**. Now, it would also be the merciful and wondrous way of **Jehovah God** concerning that people, or those among them who are a remnant according to the election of grace: when He wishes to heal them, He gives them a vivid sight and the most painful feeling of that state of theirs.

# The Son of the Royal Courtier,

servant or official of Herod. The father of this child must be considered in two respects: either *a.* as a courtier, or *b.* as the initiating cause for the healing of the sufferer. In the first respect, he will once again sketch for us the state of the Jewish people, as those preoccupied with an earthly prince, gaping at outward glory, while the luster and radiance of the true glory of the Prince of Peace—of him upon whose shoulders the government would rest <note>A reference to Isaiah 9:6.</note>—had slipped from their eyes and hearts. In the second respect, he will be an image of those whom the Lord initially prepares and sets in motion to go to the true Physician for the restoration of the plague of their people. Thus, many among the Jews indeed believed that Jesus Christ, through death and suffering, could and would perfectly heal this spiritual ailment; yet out of weakness, they imagined that they still had to keep Jesus with and among them in an outward manner for that purpose. That is, they felt they had to add the Law and the shadows of the Law (outward signs of the Savior's presence) to the Gospel. This was as much as if they had said, *Who shall bring Jesus down to us from Heaven?*—the kind of language that must not be heard under the New Testament. Romans 10:6. For that shadowy presence of Jesus was a token under the Old Testament that Jesus still had to be fetched from Heaven to make satisfaction; but now, having fulfilled the requirement of the law, that outward presence had to cease. Therefore, to still wish to cling to the shadows is to say one still wants to have Jesus with them in such an outward manner, and to want to fetch him down as if from Heaven, or to make Jesus descend to perform that healing; folly! Jesus now sits at his Father's right hand, and from that place of his glorious dwelling, he will sufficiently manifest his strength. Yet that reverence for those solemn religious rites remained so deeply impressed upon many of the professors of the Gospel that they did not entirely renounce them, nor did they perfectly believe in the completed Savior until they saw signs and wonders—that is, the remarkable conversion of the Gentiles and the overturning of the City and Temple. It was then that, looking away from all those externalities and eyeing only Christ Jesus, the Apostle of their confession, they perceived in earnest the healing wonder-power of him, even though he was absent.

<margin>D.</margin> The Miracle itself lies in a sudden departure of the fever at the very moment when Jesus spoke those words: *Your son lives.*

# Healing from the Fever

The disturbances in the blood cease once it is restored to its former moderation: the fluidity of the blood, the movement of the Spirits <note>In 18th-century medicine, "animal spirits" were thought to be fluids that carried nerve impulses.</note>, the opening of the pathways, and the arrangement of a well-tempered mixture of the humors <note>Referring to the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> are immediately brought about anew. How meaningful an image is all of this of the comforting grace and Doctrine of Life, when rightly known, faithfully accepted, holily embraced, and joyfully practiced and experienced! Through this, the lively, joyful, and fruitful works of God's Children are steadily set in motion, guided, and promoted, displaying outwardly a healthy spiritual moderation. If one knows the Triune Covenant God, that only Mediator between God and men, and that work of Atonement and Redemption worthy of God—if one goes to the Father through the Son—that hot burning and thirst is quenched; that sensation ceases, and a quiet calm arrives. *Being justified by faith, we have peace with God* <note>original: "door den geloove geregtveerdigt zijnde, heeft men vreede by God"</note>, Romans 5:1, which passes all understanding; they receive the joy of God's salvation, and the *free spirit upholds them* <note>original: "vrijmoedige geest ondersteunt hun"</note>, Psalm 51:12 <note>The text cites Psalm 51:14 following the Dutch Statenvertaling numbering.</note>. That grim vision of death is turned into a lively appearance; those brown lips and coated tongue are turned into a sanctified capacity to recount Jehovah's righteousness, ways, and wonders, and to praise Him with joyfully singing lips.

D. The circumstances of this miracle are that the servants proclaim it, first to the Father—whose faith climbed by degrees—and finally the whole House of this Nobleman <term>Hoveling: a court official or royal attendant</term> became believers. Thus, that spiritual healing was also immediately proclaimed, and shall finally have the result that the whole House of Israel shall be saved.

Rightly might Jesus—now beginning and continuing His teaching in earnest in Galilee—depict this for the Jews (who were more desirous of wonders and signs than of that demonstrative Doctrine) through this instructional image.

### IV.
<margin>Sketch of the common truths.</margin>
Should anyone wish to represent to themselves the common truths contained in this miracle, let them note:

A. Depicted by this symbol: a spiritless and comfortless Doctrine and condition.
B. By the healing: the opposite.
C. The folly of wanting to prescribe means and methods to the Lord Jesus.
D. The Spiritual presence of Jesus portrayed.
E. The folly of men, and even the weakness of God's Children, who also frequently desire to experience something too sensory or external.
F. The obligation to adhere to the demonstrative Doctrine with reverence, etc., without regard for the circumstances with which that Doctrine is clothed.

<margin>Literal sense I. opened.</margin>
Because the literal sense of these miraculous cases does not require much clarification, we shall present the histories only in a brief sketch.

Here he continues his Teaching on the Sabbath. **Mark**: and they entered into Capernaum, and immediately having entered into the Synagogue on the Sabbath day, he taught, and they were astonished at his Teaching: for he taught them as one having power, and not as the Scribes. **Luke**: and they were astonished at his Teaching: for his word was with power. *Jesus* spoke with demonstration to the conscience, persuading from innate principles and from the Scriptures of *Moses* and the *Prophets*: he spoke through the eye into the heart: with authority as the Son of God, who is above all, bending and inclining the minds of the listeners according to his pleasure: how the insipid and lowly boasting of the Scribes must have paled beside such Heavenly language! This Teaching he confirms through many miracles, among which are these.

## XI. And when they had brought their ships to land, they left everything and followed him.

<note>The woodcut initial 'O' depicts a peaceful landscape within the letter, symbolizing perhaps the transition from worldly labor to spiritual reflection.</note> To indicate the connection and to determine the correct timing of this miracle, one would certainly need to know whether we should simply follow the single thread of *Luke's* narrative here, or whether the accounts of *Matthew* and *Mark*—regarding the calling of *Jesus'* disciples, soon to be mentioned—should be placed simultaneously with this miraculous catch of fish. Indeed, some add here what *Matthew* Chapter IV, verses 18–23 and *Mark* I, verses 16–21 mention concerning the calling of the disciples of *Jesus*—*Peter*, *Andrew*, *James*, and *John*—as being one and the same history. For although *Luke* mentions several things about which *Matthew* and *Mark* remain silent, it seems that *Luke* indicates the circumstances omitted by the others somewhat more accurately, because in all three Evangelists the words of the calling are the same: <note>original: "Ik zal u viſſchers der menſchen maken: Gy zult menſchen vangen"</note> *I will make you fishers of men: You shall catch men*; likewise, they, leaving everything, followed him. Furthermore, *Matthew* and *Mark* testify that *Peter* and *Andrew* cast the nets into the sea. *Luke* would then only explain more closely how this came to pass. Then again, *Matthew* and *Mark* testify that *James* and *John* were found mending their nets. *Luke* would then give to understand where these were broken. It also seems to have its difficulties if the calling of the disciples mentioned by *Matthew* and *Mark* must be placed earlier than this history recorded by *Luke*; for then the aforementioned disciples would have returned to their profession or fishing nets after having previously left Christ. The place is also the same: the Sea of *Galilee*. Yet on the other hand, if one sets these events simultaneously, this history recorded by *Luke* must be placed earlier than the miracles occurring in *Capernaum*, of which *Luke* speaks in the previous chapter and which we have already explained. For when *Jesus* performed those (settling his residence in *Capernaum*), the disciples had already been called. This is stated by the clear words of *Mark*, who, having recounted the calling of *Peter*, *Andrew*, *James*, and *John*, immediately follows with: *and they entered into Capernaum*, verse 21. Namely, *Jesus* and those named disciples.

Nevertheless, the entire thread of Luke’s narrative seems to imply that this miraculous catch of fish occurred after those performed wonders took place at Capernaum, and after Christ had departed from Capernaum to proclaim the Gospel to other cities as well. *See Chapter IV, verses 42 and 43.* If it were a certain proposition (concerning which we cannot yet make a final judgment) that Saint Luke strictly follows the chronological order everywhere, it is as clear as day that these two histories must be distinguished from one another; and that here, it is merely a sealing of the previous calling, and that the disciples, having been called previously, yet having returned to their profession for a while with Jesus' permission, follow him anew, leaving everything behind. <margin>Literal sense opened.</margin> I. First, we shall clarify the literal sense through a brief opening of the words, noting: 1. Jesus’s teaching-discourse. 2. The miracle. 3. The consequence thereof.

A. And it came to pass that he stood by the Lake of Gennesaret. The Lake of Gennesaret is also called the Sea of Galilee, the Lake of Tiberias, and in *Numbers 34, verse 11,* the Sea of Chinnereth. <note>original: "Cinnereth"</note> Chinnereth was a region in Galilee, famous for its princely gardens, providing the most pleasant fruits; the city of Chinnereth, situated in this region, is named among the fortified cities in *Joshua Chapter 19, verse 35.* Some maintain that it is the same city as Tiberias. Others think that they were distinct cities. *See Reland’s Palestine, Page 161.* <note>Refers to Adriaan Reland (1676–1718), a famous Dutch orientalist and cartographer.</note> However, the geographers may decide this dispute.

# The Miraculous Catch of Fish

Go into the deep, and cast out your nets to catch; and Simon answered and said to him: Master, we have labored throughout the entire night and caught nothing, yet at Your word <note>trusting in it</note> I shall cast out the net. Peter had already seen proofs of Jesus’s miraculous power at Cana—and if that event occurred earlier in time, which is most likely, at Capernaum—having also encountered it in the case of his own mother-in-law; therefore, despite having spent the entire night fruitlessly, he nevertheless trusts in Jesus’s word. And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, and their net tore. Some believe that the net did not actually tear, and that such a reading would contradict the literal truth because otherwise the fish would have escaped from the torn net; they argue it should be understood that the net *would* have torn if the fish had not been immediately transferred into the ships, or that it *began* to tear. However, the words are too emphatic: <note>original Greek: διερρήγνυτο δὲ τὸ δίκτυον</note> "the net was breaking" or "tore." This certainly indicates that the net was already somewhat torn; yet, through Jesus’s miraculous power, the fish remained in that torn net, which was preserved from further tearing.

This abundant catch of fish differs from the one mentioned in John Chapter 21 in that there the net did not tear, while here the net tears, etc. The casting-net was a tool which every Israelite was permitted to use for fishing, but the Jewish laws did not allow for weirs or hurdles <note>fixed traps or fences in the water</note> because they obstructed the flowing water <term>Baar-water: navigable or flowing water</term> and were a hindrance to ships. Matthew Chapter 4 and Mark Chapter 1 use the word <note>original Greek: ἀμφίβληστρον</note> *amphiblestron*, which signifies a type of net that is cast out from both sides, pulled, and finally gathered together so that the fish are enclosed within it; here the word is <note>original Greek: δίκτυον</note> *diktyon*, which is of a more general meaning.

And they beckoned to their partners—namely John and James—who had likewise gone out with them to fish, so that they might have a share in the catch. That they should come and help them; and they came and filled both the ships, so that they sank from the burden of the fish—that is, they sat deeper in the water.

<margin>Hidden symbolic meaning.</margin>
III. But oh! if only that miraculous Savior would truly open the eyes of our understanding, so that we might rightly comprehend the spiritual significance, how we would behold the wisdom of the Savior glorified here! A greater amazement and wonder ought then to carry us away, even as Simon Peter was so powerfully driven out of himself by those rare deeds.

Indeed, that this miracle has its hidden meaning is taught by Christ himself, when he assures his disciples through this miraculous work that he will make them <term>fishers of men</term> <note>A reference to Matthew 4:19 and Luke 5:10, signifying the transition from catching fish to winning souls for the Kingdom of God</note>.

Ah! adorable Savior, be not here as a God who keeps himself hidden; grant us to penetrate into the inner chamber of this miraculous wisdom, to follow you from the land to the sea, and to see your footsteps upon the great waters, and thus to be more and more vividly convinced that you are that great Angel who has one foot on the earth and the other on the sea <note>A reference to Revelation 10:2, symbolizing Christ's universal authority over both the stable (land) and the chaotic (sea)</note>.

We shall trace all the circumstances in order to be firm in determining the spiritual meaning.

We note: *a.* The time of this miracle; *b.* The place; *c.* The circumstances; *d.* The persons; *e.* All the matters involved.

A. The place where the Lord Jesus teaches is now not the Synagogue, but he teaches outside the Synagogue, on the shore of the sea, still standing on the land; yet immediately thereafter the place of instruction is the sea, and a ship in the sea, though not launched far from land. Thus we see the Church of the New Testament <note>original: "N. T." (Nieuwe Testament)</note> in its tender beginnings. It would not remain long under Judaism, but would stretch out toward the prize of the high calling from above, forgetting those things which are behind and reaching forth unto those things which are before—I mean the beautiful inheritance of the hosts of the Gentiles <note>original: "Heidenen"</note>. Let us then behold the Church in a ship, a set-apart society; the ship being frequently a symbolic image of the Church, which like a ship has its governors, and indeed a ship where Jesus is present through his Spirit and word, floating upon the sea (a symbol of the raging and barren Heathen world, with its waves constantly clashing against the ship of the Church), yet not far from land, still being close by...

# The Miraculous Draught of Fishes

Adhering to *Judaism*; for the Church in her first efforts—before the judgment of hardening came upon *Judaism* and they had made themselves altogether unworthy of eternal life—did not yet depart so far from the earth, from that shadowy *Canaan* <note>The author refers to the Old Testament Promised Land as a "shadow" or precursor to spiritual realities.</note>; yet immediately thereafter, at *Jesus'* command, she would put out deeper into the Sea, and then have that rare catch of fish.

From all this we learn that by this amazing catch of fish is portrayed the conversion of the Heathen <note>original: "Heidenen," referring to non-Jewish nations or Gentiles.</note>, especially (for the Sea is a symbol of Heathendom) that which would occur when the Church, having gone out from the Jewish *Synagogue*, and having separated herself from the Jewish People into a spiritual ship, would constitute a distinct society.

<margin>B.</margin> *Christ* explained a portion of this miracle to *Peter*; namely, that they were to become fishers of men.

<margin>C.</margin> It is certain that a portion of this "teaching-picture" <note>original: "Leer-schildery," a metaphorical term for a parable or illustrative miracle.</note> must have its fulfillment in *Peter* and his companions. However, it will appear that this instructional image was not for those early times alone, but that the spiritual fishing, having then begun, would be seen more closely in the sequel, with all those circumstances mentioned here; therefore it will not be absurd that, just as *Peter* and his companions represent themselves with respect to the first period, they may, in the course of time, well represent other spiritual fishers. Thus the entire spiritual meaning—namely, of the tearing of the nets, the transferring of the fish into two ships, the mending of the nets (if that also pertains to it), the voluntary following of the fishers at the word of the *Savior* with the abandonment of all—was not fully disclosed to them. This, as will presently appear, relates to later times; only that which would actually come true in those disciples was explained by the *Savior*; the rest, which would only first have its truth in following times, is left to the godly investigation of the Church, which would live to see the fulfillment.

*Peter*, then, and the other disciples of *Jesus* would become fishers of men; the word "fishing" often has a bad sense in the *Holy Scriptures* <note>original: "H. # The Miraculous Draught of Fishes

When the crowds rushed into the forecourt of the Church, and that entire multitude could not be given the necessary instruction, how miserably was that firm bond of interconnected truths broken and torn! Indeed, when outward riches, honor, and ambition—the churchgoers having become wealthy under an all-too-favorable fate and the sudden influx of fish into this net—had twisted and entangled them in the nets of Satan, how miserably was the outward bond of Brotherhood, the fishing net, torn between the Eastern and the Western Church? 

Let us clarify this tear somewhat from the Church Memoirs <note>The author refers to historical ecclesiastical records and chronicles.</note>. When Constantine the Great moved the seat of the Empire from Rome to Constantinople, there was a constant rivalry between the Bishop of Rome and the Bishop of Constantinople; the one would recognize no one above him, the other would recognize no equal. Therefore, the Church Fathers in their solemn assemblies—first at Nicaea, thereafter at Constantinople, and very emphatically in the Council of Chalcedon—restrained the bold defiance and pride of the Bishop of Rome by granting equal honor and authority to the Bishop of old and new Rome (Constantinople was called the New Rome). 

This has always embittered the Roman Bishop against the one of Constantinople and the Eastern Church. Afterward followed the disputes between the Western and Eastern Churches over Iconoclasm <note>original: "Beeldendienst" - the worship or use of religious images</note>, the proceeding of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son <note>A reference to the "Filioque" controversy regarding the Nicene Creed</note>, the Marriage of Priests, and other differences concerning ecclesiastical ceremonies. Finally, the minds of men having been embittered against one another from time to time, the net was completely torn; the solemn Excommunication <note>original: "Kerkban"</note> of the Western against the Eastern, and of the latter again against the Western, was pronounced in the year 1054 <note>The author uses the Roman numeral CIOLIV for 1054, marking the Great Schism.</note>. And however often men have wished to repair this broken net in various Church assemblies—and lastly in that of Florence—it has never succeeded. The Lord had broken the staff of the "Binders." <note>A biblical allusion to Zechariah 11:14, symbolizing the breaking of brotherhood.</note>

But yet another and sadder tear in this net has been seen even in the West. Dear God! How has that chain of Heavenly truths been unlinked, how has the Confession of Faith been violated, and this spiritual net torn by all those erroneous opinions arising from the abyss of hell: the invocation of Saints, Iconoclasm, Purgatory, the merit of works, the Sacrifice of the Mass, and that idol, Free Will! And these monstrous doctrines piled up most violently after—under Charlemagne—so many and innumerable nations, previously ignorant of the Christian name and religion, were [forced] by weapons...

E. The marks or signs of whether one is restored are these: let one ask oneself whether the reconciliation brought about by the Savior has been applied to the soul in the aforementioned manner? One should then subsequently portray
F. The happiness of those who are cleansed.
1. They are no longer barred from the Sanctuary, but dwell within it.
2. No longer wearing torn clothes, but clothed with the garments of Salvation. <note>In biblical times, lepers were required to wear torn clothes as a sign of mourning and social exclusion.</note>
3. Their lip is no longer covered, but they joyfully praise Jehovah's Righteousness. <note>Lepers had to cover their upper lip and cry out "Unclean!" to warn others; here, the restriction is replaced by worship.</note>
4. Having now an elegant headdress.
5. An inalienable share in the Blood and the Spirit of Christ.
    They are obligated to wash themselves more and more, and to make a continually repeated application of the Savior's sacrificial blood.

# The Paralytic Restored.

After Jesus had traveled through the land of Galilee, having filled the same with his teaching and wonders, he returned again to his place of residence and dwelling, Capernaum. He was teaching in a house, to which there was the greatest influx of people; among Jesus's listeners were also Pharisees and Scribes, who had come from every village of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem (some possibly sent by the Jewish Council to spy upon the Savior’s teaching and conduct) and the power of God was there to heal.

However, from those manifold miraculous healings, the Holy Gospel-writers will pick out but one miracle, which is particularly suited to confirm and clarify Jesus's teaching, and to depict spiritual things. They record for us the healing of that paralytic. 1. We shall clarify the literal sense. 2. We shall assert the truth of the history. 3. We shall show that this performed miracle is a proof that Jesus is that God of Israel, who forgives iniquities and heals infirmities. 4. We shall endeavor to discover the spiritual sense.

<margin>Literal sense opened.</margin>
I. And behold, they brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed, who was carried by four. See Mark. The plague of this sufferer is the palsy, or stroke; in the Greek he is called <term>paralytikos <note>original: "παραλυτικός"</note></term>, that is, the "unbound one," which expresses his ailment very well, since <term>paralysis <note>original: "παραλυσις"</note></term> is a loosening or relaxation of the nerves, which, being without sufficient power of tension, makes the person limp-limbed; the body, or that part of the body where the nerves are as if unbound, is left without strength or firmness, and previously causes trembling and shaking. The pathways through which the animal spirits flow are blocked in the nerves and muscles, so that their free radiation being hindered, the person cannot have the proper natural use of his limbs. Or also, this limpness is caused by cold and sharp humors. When the palsy spreads through the entire body, such a person, being completely deprived of his firmness and steadiness, cannot stand up, move, or perform anything; and then the physicians call this disease <term>apoplexia <note>original: "ἀποπληξία"</note></term>, apoplexy; there are also those who maintain that our sufferer was such a case, see <term>Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), an eminent Lutheran theologian.</note></term>, yet this is contradicted by <term>Bartholinus <note>Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), a famous Danish physician and anatomist.</note></term>. At any rate, he was very severely afflicted, for which reason he was carried on a bed, which was an ancient custom, that either the dead, or also...

# The Paralytic Restored.

Certainly, when the Savior—simultaneously with that outward address—caused his inward voice of love and life to be heard in the heart of this Sufferer, how appropriately and with total wisdom did he then answer the sighing and desire of this miserable man! This was so even though the surrounding crowd might have thought that he did not satisfy the request, since a commanding word of healing did not immediately proceed from his mouth.

Oh! This Sufferer could think: if my sins are forgiven me, then my ailment is an ailment no longer. The sting and prickle <note>The author uses "angel en prikkel," referring to the biblical concept of the "sting of death" or sin.</note> of that evil has been taken away regarding me. And even if the Lord God wished to be glorified in my illness for even longer, oh! that is now only a matter of joy for me, because I know that this too must work together for my salvation. This ailment is now no longer a reproach of sin, or a sign of Jehovah’s hidden wrath over me. Or otherwise, should His wisdom find it advisable to also relieve me of this painful bodily evil, He will surely not lack in His loving-kindness; He who has granted me the greatest thing (the forgiveness of sins) will not refuse me the lesser, if it only serves His honor and my salvation. But as inwardly content and satisfied as the heart of this Sufferer was—filled with inward joy and the exaltations of God—so too did the hearts of the Pharisees and Scribes boil with such bitter hatred and displeasure over these words of the Savior.

They said within themselves:
> This man blasphemes God; who can forgive sins but God alone?

They did not find it advisable to attack the Savior with biting words; they feared the Crowd, among whom Jesus had made too much progress through his Heavenly Teaching and works; yet bitter folly remained bound in their hearts. *This man*, they think, *blasphemes God*. It is true: no one can forgive sin but God alone; he who is not God cannot forgive sin. And yet, this language from Jesus was no blasphemy, which the gentle Savior points out to them.

And Jesus, seeing their thoughts—His eye could wander through the hiding places of their hearts and see their thoughts from afar, for nothing is hidden from His eyes—Said,
> Why do you think evil in your hearts?

Here we learn from Jesus that he is gentle; as that great Prophet <note>original: "Propheet"</note>, whom one must hear in all things without contradiction, he could have used harsher language:
> You blind and blinded leaders <note>original: "Leidlieden"</note>, how are your conceptions so wild and strayed from the true Doctrine of reconciliation <note>original: "verzoeninge"</note> or the forgiveness of sins?

—or he could have used even sharper and more cutting expressions...

he use; but no, his appropriate and friendly answer is: *Why do you think evil in your hearts?* It was then an evil conception that Jesus would not be able to forgive sin; it was a sign of deep ignorance regarding the righteousness of God. The Jews believed that God alone, and indeed as a single being (without acknowledging the three adorable Heavenly Witnesses <note>A reference to the Trinity, likely alluding to the "Johannine Comma" in 1 John 5:7</note>), could forgive sin. And this is certainly preeminently evil to think in one's heart; this is an absolute denial of the entire work of grace, of God's eternal counsel of love, and the revelation of the same in time, upon which the entire doctrine of expectation is grounded. Yes, it is a denial of all God's virtues and perfections. It is true, God alone forgives sin, but the Triune God, by virtue of a sufficient satisfaction provided by the Surety <term>Surety: A theological term for Christ acting as a legal guarantee or substitute for humanity's debt</term>, who is also God. How can God be understood to forgive sins without satisfaction to His justice? And who can perfectly obey the Law of God for the sinner, and bear infinite punishments, and offer his soul as a worthy ransom, who is not himself God? And how can the Lord God be at once the claimant of the debt and the payer of the debt, if He is not Triune—indeed, if there were but one Divine Person? Well then, the Son of God, being also God, and standing ready to shortly pay the last penny for the sinner, can He not say: *your sins are forgiven you*? Is He not that God who would bear the iniquity of sins? See Psalm 32, verse 5. That Angel who had power to forgive or retain the sins of Israel, Exodus 23, verse 21. Why then, you Jews, do you think evil in your hearts? *For which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven you, or to say: rise up and walk?* We shall not transcribe the thoughts of the Commentators on these words; they mostly conclude that it is surely no lesser, if not a greater proof of Christ's Divine authority, to say to the paralytic, *rise up and walk*, and by that word to command his healing and bring it to pass, than to say, *your sins are forgiven you*; so that it would be easier, or at least not harder, to say *your sins are forgiven you* than to say *rise up and walk*. <margin>Proof for *Jesus’s* Divinity</margin>
II. This history has all the marks of an undeniable certainty. The paralytic was—beyond doubt—a well-known Sufferer; his healing happened in everyone’s presence / in *Capernaum* / in the house where *Jesus* taught / in the presence of the *Pharisees* / *Jesus’s* defeated enemies / publicly he carried his bed. Everyone could inquire about this event; how would it be possible to invent such a thing / and to recount it in that time (when it could be investigated). The evidence of *Jesus’s* omniscience / which discovered the most hidden thoughts of the *Pharisees* / is of no less certainty. Had the Savior accused them of a different reflection / than what they felt welling up in their bosoms / how quickly they would have accused the Savior of lying / now they stand ashamed and speechless / by no means daring to deny / that they pondered in their hearts / that which *Jesus* charged them with.

Well / does the Savior not give evidence here / that he is the one / who can perceive the fear of the Lord / and who also knows the evil deliberations of men as the omniscient one? Does he also not clearly give to understand through that miraculous healing and authoritative forgiveness of sins / that he is that righteous servant / who through his knowledge makes many righteous, *Isaiah 53* verse 11. I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins, *Isaiah 43* verse 25. Namely / that *God* / who speaks in the very preceding [verse] / you have made me serve because of your sins, you have wearied me with your iniquities.

It appears then clearly / that *Jesus* is that *God* of *Israel*, who made known his ways to *Moses*, and his deeds to *Israel*, who forgives all iniquities / who heals all diseases: *Psalm 103* verse 3. # The thirty-eight-year illness cured

Here Jesus [healed] this man on the Sabbath. Just as that woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years (Luke 13), also the man with dropsy (Chapter 14), and the man born blind (John 9); all on a Sabbath, in order to impress upon the Jews on those occasions that the <term>antitype</term> <note>The spiritual reality that fulfills a symbolic "type" or shadow from the Old Testament.</note> of that shadowy rest was a Holy activity in God, for which He, as the great Physician-Lord in Israel, would give fresh powers and spiritual strength to His own.

But still, the foolish Jews did not understand the things that are of the Spirit of God. The Jews said to the one who was healed: "It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed." Thus, malicious bitterness is accustomed—when it dares not try its sharp teeth against a matter itself—to attack one or another circumstance of a matter. Just as here with the Jews: the miracle was too illustrious, too rare, and it had awakened too high an esteem for its <term>Master-Worker</term> <note>referring to Jesus as the divine craftsman of the miracle</note> in the hearts of the bystanders to find fault with it; and therefore, the circumstance must be criticized here: "It is Sabbath," etc.

He answered them: "He who made me well, He said to me, 'Take up your bed and walk.'" The healed man did not yet know the Savior well; he did not know that it was Jesus who had healed him (see verse 13). Nevertheless, he understood this: that his wonderful <term>Healer-Master</term> must be a distinguished Heavenly Messenger, a Prophet mighty in words and in works; how else could He have performed such a rare healing through a single word? Also, he likely knew—or perhaps Jesus, when He healed him, instilled this knowledge in him (so that he could better justify his actions against the Jews)—that the commandment of that shadowy rest was not eternally binding, but only until a "time of reformation." Indeed, the ancient Jews knew well enough that during the days of the Messiah, it would always be Sabbath. Therefore, this healed man could easily surmise that such a high-worthy Heavenly Messenger could certainly make some determination regarding that solemn commandment, or (since that outward resting was not essential holiness, nor was the carrying of the bed on such a day an inner unholiness) that he, at the command of such an illustrious Heavenly Teacher, might well do it and say: "He who made me well, said to me," etc.

They then asked him: "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?" Whether it be that they did not know it was Jesus, or—which is more probable—that they did know...

Proof for Jesus' Divinity

II. The truth of this history is evident, indeed of a persuasive certainty; all circumstances are reported. The time: it was a Feast, and a Sabbath. The place: it was the Bath-water <note>The Pool of Bethesda</note>. The Person: it was a sick man who had lain with his ailment for thirty-eight years. When the day of our true God is announced to stubborn Judaism by the Prophet Malachi, Chapter IV, verse 2, we simultaneously hear that joyful promise of salvation to the converts among that people:

> But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth. <note>Quoting Malachi 4:2. The author uses this to link the physical healing at Bethesda to spiritual healing through Christ.</note>

God’s name represents His divine virtues and perfections, displayed in their full luster through the Christ (see Psalm XXII, verse 23; John XVII, verse 26); or it refers to the Christ himself, in whose midst the name of Jehovah dwelt. He is the self-existent God, in whom and through whom the Father named Himself a God of the sinner. Through the Christ, He spells out and expresses all His promises and prophecies for mankind as if in legible letters—writing them through their fulfillment—proving that He, Jehovah, is the fulfiller of promises. To fear this name means to celebrate it with such reverent awe that one acknowledges the Savior as the Supreme Lawgiver and High Teacher, depending on His lips alone. It means not enslaving oneself to human doctrines or commandments, and recognizing no other name under Heaven by which one can be saved but the name of Jesus. Therefore, looking away from all merit of works and self-righteousness, and seeking righteousness and strength in Jehovah the Savior alone, the Sun of Righteousness shall rise upon such people. Here the Savior appears under the symbol of the Sun, because He is that Great Light (Isaiah IX, verse 1), as much more glorious than all the Prophets and Heavenly messengers as the light of the Sun surpasses and extinguishes that of the stars. The Sun is of the purest substance; it sets everything around it in motion; it is the cause of freshness, joy, and fertility.

Christ is essential purity itself, who brings everything within the spiritual Heavenly circle into a truly vivid motion; He is the cause of all light, joy, life, and fertility for the Believers. And indeed, He is a Sun of Righteousness. Orpheus calls the Sun <term>ὄμμα δικαιοσύνης</term> <note>original Greek: "omma dikaiosynes" — the eye of justice</note>, the eye of justice; so too did the Heathens in their idolatry call it Sadocum and <term>σωτήρα</term> <note>original Greek: "sotera" — savior or preserver</note>, the righteous one and the Savior or preserver. This title applies with full emphasis only to the Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, because He has brought about eternal righteousness. This doctrine of the justification of a sinner before God is the foundation of all life, delight, joy, and fruitful activities of the People of the Covenant. # The Literal and Spiritual Sabbath.

In the guidance of our thoughts, we propose this order: I. We shall open the Letter of the Commandment. II. Then we shall examine what the nature of this Commandment is. III. Where we must seek its origin: in Paradise, or in the Wilderness during the raining of the Manna. IV. Then we shall appropriately explain the letter, and also the Spirit of this Commandment. V. And we shall assert that our sentiment leads most of all to a tender holiness. VI. Indicating that the prominent Church Reformers agree with our opinion. VII. Although it shall appear that some who, differing from us, do not understand the way of God modestly enough in this matter, we shall settle the disputes, placing their weight in a rightful balance. VIII. In a short sketch, we shall show how to treat the common truths.

<margin>The literal sense opened.</margin>
I. In the Opening of the Commandment, we pay attention to (1) The command **remember the Sabbath**. (2) The motivating reasons, for the seventh day is the Sabbath etc. verse 10. For in six days the Lord made etc. verse 11.

A. The matter with which this Commandment is concerned is the Sabbath day. <term>Shabbat <note>original Hebrew: שבת</note></term> signifies Resting, the ceasing of work. The Sabbath day is such a day on which one does no work; we do not mention the Sabbaths of the Years or of the Months at this time, as the subject of our negotiation is the weekly Sabbath. This is further defined as the seventh day, and indeed with a finger-pointing: *that* seventh day. Thus, here, not just any day out of seven is set apart for Rest in a general sense, but the specific seventh day of the week. In imitation of God, who Rested on the seventh day of the first week, Israel was also bound—in the Wilderness—to celebrate precisely that day which followed the sixth day when the Manna rained doubly. Furthermore, the Jews, as such precise observers of the letter, hold fast strictly to the specific seventh day of the week.

B. The Lawgiver charges them to remember the Sabbath day. To remember means to recall a matter that has gone before, and also to occupy oneself with a singular observation regarding a matter; in this latter sense it is used in Ecclesiastes 12:1, **Remember your Creator**.

To remember the Sabbath day, then, means to bring to mind that which was previously mentioned concerning the Sabbath, and to pay attention with a singular observation regarding this matter, which is of a higher significance.

To sanctify it. To sanctify means to recognize the holiness of a matter; to this I relate the expression "to sanctify the Lord in one's heart"; also to set a matter apart for a holy use.

# The Literal and Spiritual Sabbath

Israel, hearing mention of "sanctifying" or "making holy," could, according to that dispensation <note>The "dispensation" refers to the specific period of Biblical history and the religious system of the Old Testament</note>, form a twofold understanding: either of a substantial holiness, consisting of righteous and joyful activities, or a shadowy <note>The author uses "shadowy" in the sense of a "foreshadowing" or a symbolic representation of a future reality</note> holiness, according to which everything belonging to that solemn Religion was holy, provided it satisfied the Laws of the worldly Sanctuary.

If this Commandment were grounded in the Nature of God and the relationship of the moral creation to Him, the sanctification of that day would have to be understood in the first sense; but in the case that it is shadowy, a double-meaning must necessarily take place here, as in all other exemplary Laws: namely, a literal holiness, and the observance of that which is foreshadowed by the letter.

The literal holiness is further described by abstaining from all kinds of work, etc. *Six days shalt thou,* etc. *but the seventh day then thou shalt not,* etc. Here, then, is prescribed a complete ceasing of all kinds of servile work, to which they were otherwise called by the necessity of this life, such as preparing food, lighting a fire in their dwellings, gathering wood, conducting trade, sowing, reaping, treading the winepress, etc. See Exodus 16, verses 23, 24; 35, verses 2, 3; Numbers 15, verses 32–36; Nehemiah 10, verse 32.

And this rest had to be strictly maintained throughout all Palestine by humans—*you, your Son, your Daughter,* etc.—and by cattle: not only because the irrational cattle, if used for labor on that day, would also provide work for humans, but because all of Canaan had to rest on that day. Even if the cattle could have worked without the help of humans, one would have transgressed the Commandment of the Lawgiver if the cattle had not had their share in this outward rest.

The question here is whether the Sanctification of this day consists solely in this rest—in the ceasing of work—or whether, besides the rest, this sanctification required spending the day with holy reflections in Religious exercise? Israel was always bound to Religious reflection and exercise by obligatory reason and the given Divine Laws; but that this Commandment in particular (regarding its literal sense) prescribes to them a specific Religious exercise does not appear at all, but rather the contrary. Nowhere does one see that the sanctification of that day lay in specific Religious exercise, or that anyone was punished because he had neglected Religion on that day; on the contrary, we read that Israel

...solemnly observed, and set apart for religious contemplation? Or, whether it was first instituted in the Wilderness, on the occasion of the raining of the Manna, the very first Sabbath being that day which followed the sixth day, on which the Manna rained double? From the opening of the Commandment itself, it follows that it has no relation to man in his state of original perfection <note>The author refers to "rect-geschapen mensch," the state of humanity before the Fall</note>; working could produce no unholiness in him, and resting could be no essential Holiness in him. And as far as religious contemplation is concerned—if one wishes to attribute the rest to that—the perfectly-created man found himself equally obliged and inclined to it every day and at all times. It is true, we read: *That the Lord God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it* <note>Genesis 2:3</note>, yet these words do not have the sense at all that God commanded that one should do no work specifically on that seventh day, and set it apart particularly for worship. I do not know how one could force that meaning onto these words, for then it must necessarily follow that God only ceased from bringing forth new works on that specific seventh day, and on that specific day, separately from other days, rested and delighted in His works. This is certainly not the case. It speaks for itself that the resting, the blessing, and the sanctifying are of the same extent. God, it says, rested on the seventh day, blessed it, and sanctified it: Since it is then certain that the rest is not limited to the seventh day, but extends to the other days, it is just as certain that one must not bind the blessing and the sanctifying to that one day alone. 

This, then, shall be the meaning: The seventh day was the first that beheld <term>Jehovah's</term> <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note> completed works; therefore, on that day, God made a beginning of ceasing to bring forth new creatures, and a beginning of delighting and resting in the completed works of His hands. Therefore He blessed that day, and sanctified it in that manner—yet not only that one, but all the following days of which it was the first, just as the nature of the matter itself brings this along. Now, I gladly admit that the perfectly-created man, after the example of his Creator, would also have found himself obliged and inclined to rest on that day and all following days, and to delight himself in a pure reflection and contemplation of God's works, to which he was equally obliged at all times; so that his rest, as little as the rest of God, was limited to the seventh day.

Now, if this Sabbath had not been the very first, then exactly seven days prior to it—and thus the fifteenth of that month—must have been a Sabbath again. His journey never proceeded, or he ceased the same, unless the Cloud gave the signal for it. How many things would one throw into confusion with such an answer, when the pure truth is so simple! If that rest, which God prescribed to Israel in the Fourth Commandment, did not take place in that manner previously, then that which—according to the letter—is the very content of that Commandment, did not take place previously. Now, we have indeed proven that the actual ceasing of work is that Sanctification <term>Heiliging: the act of setting something apart as holy</term> which the letter of the Law entails.

And even assuming that before the Giving of the Law they only ought to have rested insofar as the Divine Service was not disturbed, why then travel on such a day and thus set the entire multitude in motion? Indeed, by nothing could the rest necessary for the exercise of Divine Service be more disturbed. From what would one conclude that they traveled for exactly only half an hour? And even assuming it were so, when such a great Army <note>referring to the vast assembly of Israelites</note> makes a journey of only half an hour, the preparation for it and the making of such a movement involves such a commotion that not much of the Divine Service could take place on that day.

And if even the outward rest—though perhaps not maintained so strictly—was prescribed to the believers under the Promises and had to be religiously maintained, surely one ought not to transgress it at any hour of the day, even if it were only for half an hour? Surely one should not do such a coarse work as traveling, which sets everything in motion, by which not just the strict maintenance of the rest, but the rest itself is entirely taken away? And would the great Angel of the Covenant <note>original: "Bonds-Engel"; a theological term often referring to the pre-incarnate Christ guiding Israel</note> Himself—if 그날 had already been instituted in Paradise for the exercise of Divine Service and solemn rest—have transgressed that Commandment by giving Israel a Sign to travel, and that without cause?
