# The Literal and Spiritual Sabbath

<margin>A closer explanation of the Commandment:</margin>
IV. Now that we have discovered the true nature and origin of this Commandment, we shall best provide a concise explanation of it, as it first pertains to *Israel* according to the flesh, and then to the *Israel* of the *New Testament*, the *Church*, which first departed from the *Jewish* and later from the *Popish House of Bondage* <note>original: "Paapsche Dienst-Huis"; a common 17th-century Protestant reference to the Roman Catholic Church as a place of spiritual slavery similar to Egypt</note>.

Imagine, then, that the actual *Israel* is addressed thus: Remember what *God* did on the seventh day of the week after the first six-day Creation, and what He recently commanded you regarding the celebration of the seventh day—to spend it in a quiet rest—on the occasion of the *Manna* raining down doubly on the sixth day. Sanctify that day according to the letter by abstaining from all kinds of work. However, because this Law—though shadowy <note>The author uses "shadowy" in the sense of a "foreshadowing" or a type that points toward a future reality</note> like all the others—has the *Messiah* as its end for the justification of everyone who believes, you shall sanctify that day through a holy contemplation of that which is depicted by this shadowy rest: namely, the rest of the *Messiah* in the *Grave*, and the rest of the believers in Him, delighting and resting in the fully accomplished work of salvation. 

Thus, by the letter of this Commandment, *Israel* was bound to nothing other than rest, just as by the letter of those Laws prescribing Sacrifices, Washings, and Purifications of the flesh, they were only obligated to satisfy the outward Laws of the Sanctuary. But, just as they did not satisfy the objective of the Lawgiver if they did not look faithfully during the sacrifice to Him who would once offer Himself blameless to God through His eternal Spirit, so they also did not satisfy the spiritual sense of the fourth Commandment if they did not observe the true and spiritual rest to which they were called in a special way on that day. The literal rest *Israel* held in common with its Ox and Donkey; the spiritual rest was unique to those who knew the end of the Law.

This commandment, as far as its letter is concerned, is now just as much abolished as all the other commandments of the fleshly Religion. That outward rest, regarded as a religious work, and that specific seventh day of rest, now cease entirely. Only the spiritual sense remains: namely, a rest of the believers grounded on the rest of *Christ* in the grave; a release from all sinning as well as from all the burdensome labor of the Law; a joyful resting in that great salvation of the *New Covenant*. This is that rest which remained for the People of *God*, which the true *Shiloh* <note>A Messianic title from Genesis 49:10, translated here as "Giver of Rest"</note>, the Prince of Peace, has brought. # The Literal and Spiritual Sabbath

**Question:** Do we then, under the better Covenant <note>The New Testament/New Covenant</note>, have only nine commandments? For—besides the fact that there is no hidden mystery in the number ten, as if there strictly had to be ten commandments—we surely possess the essence of that commandment. Do we not have a Passover, Christ being our Passover sacrificed for us, even though we no longer have a literal Passover? Do we not have Circumcision, because we only have that Circumcision which is not performed by hands? Do we not have the fifth commandment in its entirety, because the Promise of the actual Canaan <note>The physical land of Israel</note> ceases, being now exchanged for the Magnificent Inheritance of the better Covenant?

This rest of the better Covenant was not known or observed by the fleshly Jews, for which reason the Angel of the Covenant <note>A reference to Christ in his pre-incarnate form or as the messenger of God's presence</note> also swore in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest. The Christian Church then, which had to go out from the Jewish house of bondage, is commanded by this commandment to celebrate the Spiritual rest (described above), and especially in the latter time (when the six days of difficult labor shall have ended) to look forward to that great Sabbath, Isaiah 58:13. For then the Church shall have rest from so many external combatants, internal offenses, and so many sinful defects that currently still disturb her rest.

This same thing should also be the practice of the Church having gone out from the Popish <note>Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church</note> house of bondage: namely, the restoration of that holy doctrine of rest and comfort, so greatly violated by those dismal inventions of lies—of Purgatory, the Sacrifice of the Mass, Auricular Confession, and the denial of the sealing of the Spirit—which doctrine is the sole foundation of all rest.

leave. Oh! He who has perceived and taken to heart such great and sublime things enclosed within this commandment, will soon lose sight of any trifling outward matters which he might consider—though wrongly—to flow from this commandment.

We shall therefore not occupy ourselves with a long-winded investigation into whether one is not obliged under the New Testament <note>original: "N. T."</note> to set aside a certain specific day for Divine Service, specifically by virtue of this fourth Commandment, and whether this day be Sunday, exchanged for the Jewish Sabbath by Christ and the Apostles? That one day has no essential Holiness above another is a matter that needs no proof; consequently, it can neither be grounded in natural equity, nor agree with the nature of the better Covenant, that one day should be better for the exercise of Divine Service than another; consequently, not even the first day of the week, which was instituted neither by Christ nor by the Apostles—indeed, of that there is neither shadow nor footprint. We do read that the Apostles came together on that day, but also on others; that the Apostle exhorts the Corinthians to lay something aside for the poor on the first day of the week; but what does this do to prove a solemn institution of that day? And even if Sunday were called the Lord's Day, and even if John had his visions upon it, what does that matter to the case? Shall we also have to mark with a red letter <note>A reference to "rubrics" or "red-letter days" in liturgical calendars marking feast days.</note> all the days and months upon which Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc., saw Divine visions, and make so many Holy days out of them? Indeed, these are reasons that do not require a long-winded refutation at all.

The ancient observance of that day in the Christian Church is also not a sufficient ground for its institution; for an arbitrary custom is not a Law, and Friday was also observed by the ancient Christians, as were other days, just as well as Sunday.

The observation of this day is then entirely free and arbitrary, and must be far removed from all kinds of superstition; and all days and specific times must be derived from the nature of Religion itself. The practice of Spiritual rest, and especially the public exercise of Divine Service, requires public places and times; just as no place is morally superior to another under the New Testament, so too is no time. Now, the celebration of the first day of the week being an ancient but free custom, one ought not to abolish it; for just as there is no Moral reason to prefer that day above others, there is also no reason to reject it above others.

And as far as the observation of Sunday is concerned, we are in agreement that set times are necessary for public religious exercise, and that no essential holiness resides in one day above another; that the first day of the week is among those days of religious exercise, sufficiently confirmed among us by ancient custom and civil laws; that therefore, since the Lord God in His good providence gives us occasion on that day for the public observation of religion above other days, one is singularly obligated to make holy use of that day, to do no work which might disturb either ourselves or others in the observation of religion. Certainly, that malicious heart could do nothing else / but cast up / gall and bitterness. For / even assuming / it had been contrary to the Divine command to use medicines <note>original: "genees-middelen"</note> upon the suffering on the Sabbath / would the Sabbath therefore also have been profaned by Jesus' healings / which were performed without any outward manual labor / or wearying work?

But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man who had the withered hand, rise up and stand in the midst, and he, having risen, stood upright, so that he could be seen by everyone.

Then Jesus said to them, I will ask you this, what is permitted, to do good on the Sabbath, or to do evil, to save a person, or to destroy, (*Mark* <note>original: "Marcus"</note>) to kill? To do good means to perform a work / which the Law of the love of God / or of one's neighbor commands / and counsels / and such from a pure principle / toward a holy purpose. To do evil, means to commit the opposite / or also to neglect any good work / for which one has the freedom / calling / and fitness. To save a person means to contribute everything / that is suited / to preserve that wondrous bond / placed between soul and body / in its entirety. To destroy a person, or to kill, means / to inflict such things upon him / which have death / or the miserable precursors of death / I mean diseases and discomforts, as their consequence / or also to kill a person means / to withdraw one's hand from one's neighbor / in a present danger / when one is powerful enough to assist him with help. ->**A Man Restored.**<-

Shadow-Laws <note>original: "Schaduw-Wetten"; refers to ceremonial or symbolic laws of the Old Testament</note> must yield to such Fundamental Laws <note>original: "Grond-Wetten"; refers to moral or natural laws</note> that are indelibly inscribed in the bosom of all mortals, when one is placed in such circumstances. Now, the Savior had a special charge to perform healings, to strengthen the weak hands; should He then let that opportunity to do good—to save a human being—slip by for the sake of an outward Shadow-Law, which was not even violated by His miraculous act of healing? In any case, such laws must always yield when they come into conflict with the Law of love for God or one's fellow man. Had the Savior let that opportunity escape, He did not know—according to His human nature—whether it would be given to Him again later, as His work during His journey on earth was so determined and limited.

It appears that the Jews answered this proposition with what is recorded by *Matthew*; they ask there: *Is it also lawful to heal on the Sabbath?* Even if it is not forbidden to do good on the *Sabbath*, is it nevertheless lawful to perform healings, and thus outward work, on the *Sabbath*? The Savior answered this objection of theirs with a closer and more pressing argument.

*What man shall there be among you, who has a sheep, and if that same sheep falls into a pit on a Sabbath, will he not lay hold of it and lift it out?* It is certain that this was permitted to the Jews in the time of the Savior; even the Jewish Laws define this case in exactly this way. See *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar famous for using Talmudic sources to explain the New Testament</note> regarding this passage, although modern-day Jews are superstitious enough to avoid such a thing.

*How much then is a man better than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do well on the Sabbath.* See a similar Holy artifice <note>original: "konst-greep"; here meaning a skillful or divine rhetorical maneuver</note> and the Savior's pressing manner of reasoning in the miracle of the bowed-down woman, *Luke XIII verse 15.*

At this, the enemies were silenced, and there was no counter-argument in their mouths.

*And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.* The Holy body of the Savior, not begotten from any sinful seed and animated in every way by a pure Spirit, could in no way be the subject of the slightest impure emotion; therefore, this anger here is not a sinful outburst, but a powerful disapproval and inward loathing of the Jews' malice, paired with an earnest sigh that *Jehovah* <note>The Hebrew name for God</note> God [would uphold] the holiness of His honor against their hand—

<margin>Proof for Jesus' Divinity</margin>
II. Certainly a standing proof of an Almighty power; it was a tangible proof of a Divine mission that the *Man of God* <note>Referring to the unnamed prophet in 1 Kings 13.</note>, sent to *Bethel* to prophesy against the *Altar*, restored the withered hand of *Jeroboam* through his prayers, 1 Kings 13, verses 4, 5, 6. What then shall one think of *Jesus*, who heals the withered hand of this man not through prayers, but through his own power and command?

And truly this miracle cannot be denied again; being performed in the *Synagogue*, and being the cause of that godless counsel of the *Pharisees* and *Herodians* against *Jesus*. And so *Jesus* performs here such a Miracle as the doctrine of expectations <note>The body of prophetic teachings regarding the coming Messiah.</note> concerning him entailed.

In *Isaiah* in the thirty-fifth Chapter, where we read that glorious Oracle <note>original: "God-spraake"</note>: the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped, the lame man shall leap as a deer, and the tongue of the dumb shall sing; there it is also cried out: strengthen the weak hands, verses 5, 6. We certainly hold it to be so, that we must not only understand here the literally deaf, blind, dumb, and lame—and consequently no physical healing—but a Spiritual healing; nevertheless, the doctrine of expectations entailed that the *Messiah*, whose name is *Wonderful*, would also perform such external healings, as sketches or instructional images <note>original: "Leerbeelden"</note> of higher and Spiritual matters; therefore those Oracles have a spiritual double-meaning, intending something Spiritual and something physical, just as the Savior himself sufficiently draws upon this passage in Matthew 11, verse 5, in his given answer to the *Baptist's* disciples sent to him, asserting that he did exactly such miracles as the Oracles, *Isaiah* 35 etc., had foretold of him; the Savior would therefore not only strengthen the weak hands—that is, bestow a holy readiness for work upon those given to him by the Father—but in the days of his wandering upon the earth perform something external, which could be a fitting depiction thereof; and then is this Oracle fulfilled in the present miraculous case.

# A Man Restored

<margin>The hidden things are traced out.</margin>
III. But if we peel back the bark and fix our eyes upon the secret—the hidden meaning that lies concealed beneath—we shall perceive how powerfully the *Savior* refuted the *Jews*, not only with words but also with deeds.

The *Sabbath*, on which this miracle was performed, and the formal dispute with the *Jews*, opens for us the secret chamber of mystery. The *Savior* performed this miracle on that day (as he did many others) to lead the *Jews* toward an understanding of the true Spiritual day of rest.

It is indeed true that the Lord *God* had commanded one to abstain from work on that day; however, that shadow-law <note>The author uses "shadow-law" to refer to Old Testament rituals that prefigured New Testament truths.</note> represented the true rest to be brought about by the *Savior*, which would consist of a Holy and restless <note>In this context, "restless" means unceasing or tireless activity in service to God.</note> activity.

The *Jews*, failing to understand this, were most strikingly sketched by this man whose right hand was withered; for as long as they clung only to those outward appearances, they could perform nothing of substance. The Spiritual sinews (the true power of holy movement and stirring) were entirely shrunken within them; the Spiritual life-juices had receded, rendering them unfit for Spiritual works. But the *Savior Jesus* would, on the true and antitypical <note>term: antitype (the New Testament reality that fulfills an Old Testament "type" or symbol)</note> rest day, restore that withered hand in many (I mean the remnant of grace), giving them a Spiritual readiness for action and work, strengthening the weak hands.

A. These would then stretch out and use the right hand:
a. To perform that which glorifies *Jehovah*, being pure of hand.
b. To make a new Covenant with *Jesus*, swearing to him by the raised right hand; see concerning this Covenant: *Jeremiah 31:31 etc. Hebrews 8:8.*
c. Giving the right hand to the *Savior* as a Heavenly Lover, entering into a marriage-Covenant. *Hosea 2:18.*
d. Also, the *Savior* would take hold of the right hand of such people (see that expression: *Isaiah 45:1*) to lead them, to lift them up, etc., and also to instruct them for Spiritual warfare. Always through his powerful influence of grace—like so many Heavenly life-juices flowing into them—and thus moving and stirring their right hand toward every holy work.

B. When the *Savior* would cause this new assembly to arise from the midst of the *Jews*—that is, by preserving them, making them alive, and not killing or destroying them (expressions which powerfully apply to the antitype)—the stubborn *Jews* were looked upon by the *Savior* with a face of anger. See *Deuteronomy 32.*

# The Centurion’s Servant Healed

To oppose the Work-Saints <note>original: "Werk-Heiligen"; a term for those who believe salvation is earned through good deeds rather than faith</note> who insist that there is by nature some worthiness or good disposition in man that obligates God to show him grace, or that works deserve an actual reward; otherwise, the expression of being "worthy," taken in a Scriptural sense, is quite appropriate. See Revelation 3, verse 4: *They shall walk with me in white clothing, for they are worthy.* However, in this passage, these Elders speak only of an outward dignity in this Centurion, considering that **Jesus**, in consideration of the same, might find Himself justly moved to honor him with an outward act of love.

These Elders also give the reason for this Centurion's worthiness: *For he loves our nation, and he has even built us the synagogue.* It appears that this Centurion, just like **Cornelius** in Acts 10, was a proselyte <note>A Gentile convert to Judaism</note> to the extent that he had an inward affection for the Jewish religion, although he had not yet submitted himself to all its ceremonies. This plea moves the Savior.

*And Jesus went with them, and when he was now not far from the house, the Centurion sent some friends to him, and said to him, Lord, do not take the trouble, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.* Truly a proof of the utmost high esteem for **Jesus** and a low estimation of himself; he sends to this all-worthy Prince of Heaven the most solemn delegation that he could. He continues: *Therefore I also did not consider myself worthy to come to you, but say it with a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this one, go, and he goes, and to another, come, and he comes, and to my servant, do this, and he does it.* A confession by which **Jesus** is recognized as the all-commanding God, at whose nod and command all of nature attends more readily than soldiers carry out the command of their Captain. With good reason, then, the Savior may say that the Jews, who were God’s "shadow-like" people <note>meaning they possessed the "shadow" or types of truth in the Old Testament, while Christ is the reality</note>, were put to shame by this confession.

*And Jesus, hearing this, marveled at him, and turning around said to the crowd that followed him, I say to you, I have not found such great faith even in Israel.* Very many among the best in **Israel** held **Jesus** to be a Prophet, a High-Worthy Heavenly Messenger, the **Messiah**, etc. But this man recognizes him as the All-Governing, All-Powerful God, who even while absent, by a single command of his will, can perform miracles; and truly, faith did not put this Centurion to shame.

And it happened on the following day, that he went to a city [called] Nais, Nain, or Naim, which means as much as "the beautiful," "lovely," or "pleasant," because of the delightfulness of its location. It was a village or small town near the borders of the tribe of Issachar, bordering the Samaritan territory to the North. <note>The author cites Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 20, Chapter 5: The Galileans are accustomed, when they travel up to Jerusalem for the celebration of the Feast, to take their journey through the land of the Samaritans, and then they take the road through the village of Nais; possibly the Savior also performed this miracle during his journey to Jerusalem. Yet this is uncertain; see the miracle in John 5.

And many of his disciples went with him, and a great multitude. And as he approached the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, who was the only-begotten son of his mother, and she was a widow. This oppressed and grieving woman was, by this most painful accident, robbed of the light of her eyes, the comfort of her fickle life, and the pillar of her widowhood. Certainly, this was a fitting encounter through which Jesus might exercise his Miraculous Love.

And a great multitude from the city was with her, to accompany the funeral procession.

And the Lord, seeing her, was moved with inward compassion for her, and said to her, "Do not weep." Because he wished to change and exchange her mourning into dancing, her grieving into rejoicing, and her painful heart-wound into the most sensible joy.

And he went up and touched the bier, he—who was shortly to become the conqueror of death—being not at all terrified by that danger of death.

Now the bearers stood still, and he said, "Young man, I say to you, arise."

And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. Truly a miracle which justly had this effect:

And fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: "A great Prophet has risen among us," and "God has visited his people."

# The Young Man of Nain Raised to Life

<margin>B.</margin> This revealed miracle will now provide us with an easier guide to follow the subsequent events more successfully—events that might otherwise have left us at a loss. For this *Widow*, whose only *Son* died and was raised by *Jesus*, could represent the Church under *Judaism*, *Paganism* (which persecuted her unto death), *Arianism* <note>A 4th-century theological movement that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, *Popery* <note>A historical, often polemical term for the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, and finally in the last days, when we look forward to a glorious resurrection from the dead. I say this instructional image is suited to represent not just one, but several historical states of the Church; for anyone practiced in the word of prophecy knows well enough that the Church often appears under this same symbolic image and similar modes of speech.

<margin>c.</margin> However, since the Holy Evangelist says that this miracle was performed the day after the previous one, we look specifically for what kind of death occurs after the Supreme Authorities had embraced the Christian *Doctrine of Faith*, and what kind of resurrection from that death took place. We then find ourselves imperceptibly brought to the times of the *Arians*, who denied the Divinity of the *Son*. They won over not only most of the overseers of the Church but also the civil authorities—not only the successors of the great *Constantine*, but *Constantine* himself, who favored *Arian* errors before his death and passed away essentially in that mindset. That death [of faith] penetrated so powerfully that not only the *Bishops* of the *East*, but also those of the *West*—even *Liberius*, the *Bishop* of *Rome*—had signed the *Arian Formula of Faith*. The whole world stood as if astonished to find that it had become *Arian*.

<margin>*</margin> Thus the Church was truly a *Widow*, abandoned not only by her churchmen but also by the authorities who should have been her nursing fathers and protectors, and who had previously so fully confessed *Christ’s* Divinity (as was prefigured by the confession of the *Centurion*). Indeed, not only did a spiritual deadness seize the Church, but also the bloodiest and most lethal conditions prevailed under those five *Arian* persecutions.

<margin>A.</margin> Thus they prepared the funeral procession of the Church—of the true Confessors—who lay dead in *Nain* (that is, in the "lovely inheritance" <note>The author derives "Nain" from the Hebrew word for pleasant or lovely.</note> of the Gentiles), in that Land which *Jehovah God* had granted to the Church. Indeed, this wicked heresy appeared in the lovely heritage of the Church and brought no small hindrance to winning the world and its fullness more and more for *Prince Messiah*.

IV. If one also wishes to show the common Truths in a brief Sketch:
A. Thus the Lord God knows how to make the Authorities <note>The "Overheden" or civil magistrates</note> who oppress His Church into its Nursing Fathers; but when one looks to them too much, He uses them again in a Holy manner to bring a deadness into and over the Church.
B. If one then again takes refuge in Him, with whom there are escapes from death, then He speedily ordains rescue.
C. In this present time, there is a deadness in the spiritual Nain—the Heritage, the elegant possession of the Church.
D. Oh! if only Jesus would come before the gate!
E. Comforted this Widow!
F. Raised many from that death!
G. Nevertheless, we hope against hope; this raised Young Man shall become the Heir of all things.
H. There shall also come a time once more when the Kings shall lay down all their dignity at the feet of Jesus.
I. That then the Elders of the people go only to Jesus.
K. The Heathen <note>Gentiles</note> yet to be converted shall shortly give evidence of a greater faith than has been seen in Israel—in the Christian Church—until now.

# The Sea and Winds Calmed.

While the Pharisees and Scribes <note>The religious leaders of Jesus' time, often portrayed as his primary legalistic opponents.</note> rejected God’s counsel, the Savior lamented the unbelief regarding himself and his Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>, verses 29–35. Thereupon he recounts the Meal at Simon’s house, and the incident of that Sinful Woman who anointed the Savior, verses 36–50. After that, the Lord travels from one City and Village to another, Chapter VIII. verses 1–3. Subsequently, the Holy Writer recounts the Parable-discourses that Jesus spoke, verses 4–18. Therefore, just before the Savior commanded his Disciples to cross over, he had opened his mouth in parables and spoken mysteries, teaching the people from the Ship as they stood upon the Shore. See Matthew XIII. verses 1–53. Mark IV. verses 1–35. Luke VIII. verses 4–9. Like a wise Teacher, he had wonderfully sketched the fates of the Church of the New Testament in parable-discourses, nevertheless applying himself most to depicting the state of the Church under the rising Anti-Christ, and its happy deliverance from that soul-slavery, since that change of state is one of the most decisive and weightiest paths that the Lord God has taken with his chosen Inheritance. The mouth of supreme wisdom has thus taught us that at a certain time the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches would, as it were, choke the good seed and make it unfruitful, just as if it were sown among the thorns. See Matthew XIII. verse 22. That Spiritual enemy would, at a determined time, while men were seized with a Spiritual slumber, sow weeds in the midst of the wheat. See verse 25. The Woman, whose name is wickedness, would hide the Spiritual leaven in the fine flour and gradually leaven the whole Mass, verse 33. In that time, the Kingdom of Heaven would be like a treasure hidden in the Field, verse 44. # The Sea and Winds Calmed

We receive the key to unlocking the spiritual meaning of the miracle we are now treating from **Jesus** himself, through those spiritual parables. For as soon as **Jesus** had presented His Heavenly Doctrine through allegories, He immediately—on the evening of that same day, see **Mark** verse 35—went out to seal and clarify the same upon the Sea through His deeds. He demonstrated, through an instructive masterpiece of a miracle, in what distress and dangers the Church would be entangled when that spiritual leaven <note>A reference to the Parable of the Leaven, symbolizing spreading influence</note> would permeate the mass of the Church, and that evil seed would shoot up in the Field. Oh! Then the Church would come even unto the gates of Hell; nevertheless, the gates of Hell would not overpower her. All the fury and cunning artistry of Hell and the world would shake the Church most piteously, yet not entirely destroy her. **Jesus Christ** is in the midst of His Church; He departs not from her with His Word and Spirit; this is required by the eternal Covenant which He has with her, confirmed in His own blood.

<margin>Literal sense opened.</margin>
I. But we first examine the literal event. *And on the same day* (namely, when He had spoken those parables), *when evening had come, He said to them* (His disciples), *Let us cross over to the other side.* To **Perea**, the **Trans-Jordanian region** <note>The land "across the Jordan"</note> situated directly opposite **Galilee**, of which we shall speak in the following miracle.

*And having left the multitude, they took Him along just as He was in the ship.* This ship must have been one of the heaviest vessels used to navigate the **Galilean Sea**, of sufficient capacity to contain **Jesus** and His retinue, the **Apostles** and **Disciples**.

*And there were also other little ships with Him.* Without doubt filled with people who, enticed by **Jesus'** teaching and miraculous deeds, followed the Savior.

*And behold, there arose a great turbulence in the sea.* **Mark** calls it a great storm. **Lucas** <note>Luke</note> a storm of wind or a whirlwind, which made everything shake and tremble; this ship, and the following little ships, now rising as if into the clouds, then again plunging down as if into the abyss, so that this small **Fleet** was in no small danger of perishing.

*So that the ship was covered by the waves.* **Mark** says, *the billows beat into the ship, so that it was now full; and they were in distress.* See **Luke**. This was certainly all the more terrifying because it was at night.

*And He was in the stern, sleeping on a pillow.* His body, exhausted throughout the entire day by teaching, was refreshing itself again through rest, and renewing His lost strength (for He had this in common with all men). Thus lay **Jesus**

# The Sea and Winds Calmed

->[Jesus] rested and slept, while the water-waves roared, and the raging storm-winds—as if broken loose from their bonds—whistled past with a snarling sound; the ship which carried the Savior ran the risk of sinking.<-

In these dangers, the disciples take refuge in him, with whom there is a way out even against death.

And they woke him up, and said to him, Master, do you not care that we are perishing? See **Mark**; **Luke** says: Master, Master, we are perishing. **Matthew**: Lord save us, we are perishing. In **Matthew**, they call him Lord <term>Kyrie (κύριε)</term> <note>original: "κύριε", meaning Lord or Sir</note>, who was mighty to save them; in **Mark** <term>Didaskale (διδάσκαλε)</term> <note>original: "διδάσκαλε", meaning Teacher</note> Schoolmaster; in **Luke** <term>Epistata (ἐπιστάτα)</term> <note>original: "ἐπιστάτα", meaning Master or Overseer</note> Protector, who could turn away their danger as their Guardian and Shield-Lord. It is certain that the disciples, calling out together in such urgent need, would have used different expressions—one using this, another that—or perhaps, repeating these prayers many times, they changed the titles they used. Meanwhile, they call out to him with those titles of honor by which they were accustomed to address him, and indeed in **Luke**: Master, Master, or Protector, Protector. This sudden doubling of language is a sign of a most distressed mind. Yet the most tender-loving Savior does not leave them long in that anxious worry, encouraging them first with words, and immediately after by deed.

And he said to them, why are you fearful, you of little faith? **Luke**: Where is your faith? How are you worried that such a ship shall go to the bottom, which carries the Son of Man, the true God-Man? If I could smother here with you in the waters, then at once the eternal decree of my Father—to redeem so many Elect through my death on the cross—would waver; at once it would be over with the honor of God and his truth in fulfilling the prophecies; at once it would be over with all the hope of the faithful expectants who died in faith in me, the coming Savior; at once it would be over with the restoration of the poor sinner, which I must bring about through death on the cross, and not by smothering in the sea-waters (the Oracles of God did not foretell such a death for me). Would Jehovah allow his honor and the salvation of the children of men to be overthrown at once? Oh! no. Why then are you of little faith and fearful while I am with you?

Then he stood up and rebuked the winds and the Sea, saying—as **Mark** relates—to the Sea: Peace, be still. This is again the word of an Almighty Commander, which the boisterous Sea and winds must obey.

# ->The Sea and Winds Calmed.<-

Those who travel the great waters (seeking to deliver the cargo of Gospel truths <note>original: "Evangeli-waarheden"</note> in all sorts of regions) see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. When he speaks, he raises a stormy wind that lifts the waves on high; they rise up to Heaven, they sink down into the abyss, their soul melts with anguish, they dance and stagger like a drunken man, and all their wisdom is swallowed up (so that they cry out in desperation, "we are perishing"). Yet, crying to the Lord in the distress they had, he led them out of their fear; he makes the storm winds stand still, so that their waves are silent; then they are glad because they are stilled, and because he has brought them to the haven of their desire. Verses 22—31. <note>The author is paraphrasing Psalm 107:23-30.</note> Nevertheless, let the sensible Reader consider whether these words, and also our explained miracle, refer only to the Church in danger under the Anti-Christianity <note>A common 17th/18th-century Protestant term for the Papacy.</note> and saved by the Reformation, or whether the miracle also refers to later times and dangers of the Protestant Church?

As a conclusion to this explained miracle, I shall transcribe the words of Cardinal Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Catholic historian who wrote the 'Annales Ecclesiastici'.</note>, who, depicting the miserable condition and the most abominable appearance of the Roman Church in the tenth century, finally burst out in this language: *Christ was then plainly sleeping in a deep slumber in the ship, when, with these strong winds blowing, the ship itself was covered with waves; and what was worse, there were none who by their cries would wake their sleeping Lord, while the disciples were all snoring.* <note>original Latin: "Dormiebat tunc planè alto sopore Christus in navi, cum hisce flantibus validis ventis navis ipsa fluctibus operiretur, & quod deterius erat, deerant qui Dominum suum dormientem clamoribus excitarent, discipulis stertentibus omnibus."</note> That is, Christ had at that time fallen into a deep sleep in the Ship which, by the blowing of strong winds, was covered with waves, and what was worst, there were none who by shouting woke the sleeping Lord, all the Disciples being asleep. 

But good Baronius! There were certainly enough, even in that time, who woke the Savior, even if those like you did not hear it. They were not in that Ship—I mean in the communion of the true Church—who themselves made up that Sea and those blowing winds by which the Ship was so dreadfully tossed. You miss the application entirely; the Roman Church was not that Ship which was so covered with waves; your Church was that Sea, that mud-pool of all godlessness, just as you yourself have depicted it. Those most wicked and filthy Popes <note>original: "Pauzen"</note> whom you have described were the whirlwinds that so shook the Spiritual Ship. The Ship is the true Believers who have kept their garments pure. Oh! Had you belonged to that Ship, the crying voice of the Disciples would have rung in your ears, even in your own time.

IV. Does anyone also desire the common Truths in a brief discourse?
<margin>Sketch of the common Truths</margin>
A. Just as the Church in general, so also every individual Believer experiences that the water-waves sometimes go over their head; this is the lot of true Teachers and true Pupils.
B. But Jesus is always with them; therefore they have the same ground of certain confidence that the entire Church possesses.
C. Therefore, in no oppression must one be of little faith; Jehovah can never forsake His own; if one only calls to Him, those tender and inseparable regards they have for Him ensure that He cannot abandon His own.
D. Therefore, let those weak in faith not take it amiss that Jesus, upon rising, does not immediately hear their voice, but instead rebukes them: *Why are you of little faith?* etc.
E. Oh! the sleeping Savior will awaken and presently command silence. Whether it be something external or internal that disturbs the heart and soul, He will command silence.

That this miracle—the treatment of which shall now occupy us—is suited to clarify the parables of the Savior spoken from the ship to the people (which we mentioned in the explanation of the previous miracle), and also to more fully establish the miracle performed upon the sea, will become apparent to us once we have exercised our attention regarding this rare case.

After the Savior had stilled the roaring waves and raging winds by his all-commanding word, the Holy Gospel-Writers relate to us:

And thus the Devil, immediately after the Reformation, did not yet need to move out of that Land entirely, or leave Popery behind. Indeed, we shall prove that the swine can be an example of such an unclean and soiled multitude, and that God’s Holy Word frequently portrays them under that symbol.

# Dangers in the Swine

<margin>Sketch of common truths.</margin>
IV. If one wishes to contemplate the common truths—those which hold true for all time—within this pictorial description, one finds here a most immediate representation of the most lamentable condition of unregenerate men, who:

A. Are so closely united with that unclean Spirit, so animated and governed by him, that they are called his house and vessels <note>See Matthew 12:29</note>. Just as believers are said to have the Spirit of Christ dwelling in them <note>See Romans 8:9</note>, so on the contrary the Devil dwells in all natural men: working powerfully within them <note>See Ephesians 2:2</note>, whose will and works they perform <note>See John 8:44</note>.

B. Indeed, all kinds of unclean impulses and lusts harbor within them, so that they lodge, as it were, a Legion of Devils; such possessed ones are found by the death-graves, in the Deserts, naked and bare, rushing headlong into all kinds of godlessness, restrained by no bonds of decency, being continually driven forward by their own unclean self-love.

C. Just as these possessed ones recoiled at the approach of Jesus, so do those spiritually possessed recoil at the proposal of the Doctrine of Christ, seeking to oppose it either through open combat or through fleshly <term>reasonings</term> <note>The original Dutch 'redenkavelingen' implies contentious or sophistical arguments used to avoid the truth</note>, always pretending that it is not yet time to listen to Jesus; and though they may confess Jesus with their mouths to be the Son of God and worship him, they deny him with their deeds.

D. Jesus alone is powerful enough to cast out that Satan; thus Holy Scripture testifies of this casting out of the Devil <note>See John 12:31 and 16:11; the original text cites verse 37 in error for chapter 12</note>. He who is thus delivered from spiritual possession sits at Jesus' feet, is clothed, and is in his right mind, whereas before he was but frantic; he wishes to be with Jesus immediately, yet at Jesus' command he serves His counsel in this life, proclaiming what great wonders Jesus has done for him.

E. But unhappy are those who, under the bright-shining light of the word of grace, still remain in their mud and filth, like swine—unclean animals that do not chew the cud <note>A reference to Kosher laws where 'chewing the cud' was a mark of a clean animal; spiritually interpreted here as meditating on the Word</note>, wallowing in the mire, and finally wallowing and plunging themselves into God's terrible judgments.

F. Unhappy also are those who, noticing God's finger and work, yet for the sake of outward interests, oppose that doctrine and life, or at the very least do not favor it.

This beloved daughter, the delight and hope of her parents—indeed, as the light of their eyes—was at her last extremity, struggling with death.

This drives the grieving father to *Jesus*, so that he might come and lay his hands on her, so that she might be saved and live; just as the man holds a firm hope, grounded in *Jesus’s* power, which had been so often proven in astonishing wonders, including the raising of the widow’s son at *Nain. Luke 7.* However, insofar as he believed that the Savior could not perform the healing of his daughter while absent—needing him to come and lay hands upon her—he did not yet have as great a faith as the Gentile Centurion, who entreated *Jesus* that he should only speak a word.

And he went with him (accompanied by the Disciples, see *Matthew*) and a great multitude followed him, and they thronged him, being so eager to hear his good words and see his works.

But it seems all the footsteps of this Savior must shine with miracles.

And a certain woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years. A sickness that rendered her unclean according to the Law <note>According to Levitical law, a discharge of blood made a woman ritually impure, preventing her from entering the Temple.</note> and barred her from the signs of the Covenant. It is remarkable that this woman had suffered the flow of blood for exactly as many years as comprised the lifespan of *Jairus’s* little daughter. Certainly, this long-standing ailment was irreparable by human medical art, since nature, accustomed to discharging itself through those opened paths, could not be changed; and so it proved.

She had suffered much from many physicians, and had spent all that she had on them, and found no benefit; one may see in *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar known for using Talmudic sources to explain the New Testament.</note> regarding this passage how many kinds of remedies the Jews prescribe in their *Talmud* <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing discussions on law, ethics, and custom.</note> against this ailment.

However, because of so many applied remedies, it had only grown worse for this woman. One can easily imagine that such a long-lasting flow of blood must cause dropsy <note>An old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> and other evil maladies.

She, hearing of *Jesus*, came behind him in the crowd and touched his garment (*Matthew* says the hem). For she said, "If I may but touch his clothes, I shall be made well." Not that she held the superstitious imagination that there was a...

# The Healing of the Woman with the Issue of Blood

Divine power resided in Jesus's garments; however, she wished to express her faith in that almighty Savior through such an outward sign, well knowing that He—who could "smell" the fear of the Lord <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:3, interpreting the Messiah's spiritual discernment as a sense of smell</note> (Isaiah 11:3)—knew the faithful deliberations of her heart. And certainly, this faith of hers did not put her to shame.

Immediately the fountain of her blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of the affliction. And immediately Jesus, recognizing the power that had gone out from Him, etc. This was not as if Jesus had not known beforehand what the woman’s intention was. He Himself, through His Divine providence, had led her to that place, or drawn her to Himself by His Spirit. He also knew well that He wished to exercise His healing power upon this woman; indeed, He must have had that intention before the healing was accomplished, and He could not be unaware of His own intent. For that power—if I may speak thus—did not escape the Savior without His feeling it; rather, this is a manner of speaking: "Jesus knowing that power," that is, knowing that He had truly exercised it. The woman intended to remain hidden, as if Jesus had not observed the incident so precisely, or at least would not wish to make it public; yet Jesus willed that it should be revealed before the people.

He turned around in the crowd, saying, "Who touched my clothes?" Not as if He did not know the one who had touched Him, but because He desired the personal confession of her to whom that power had gone out.

And His disciples said to Him, "You see that the crowd is thronging You, and You say, 'Who touched me?'" How can one tell You specifically who touched You? The entire pressed-together multitude squeezes You; they all touch You.

But Jesus looked around to see her who had done this, as a sign that He knew her well, but only sought to catch her eye.

The woman then, seeing that she was not hidden (Greek: *hoti ouk elathe* <note>original: "ὅτι οὐκ ἔλαθε" — meaning "that she did not escape notice"</note> says Luke), not that the woman thought she could hide from Jesus's all-seeing eye—for she recognized an omniscience in Jesus, otherwise how could she think He would accept the secret touching of the hems as a token of her faith?—but seeing that Jesus did not wish her to remain hidden, having possibly cast His eye upon her or indicated through some gesture that it was she, and thus revealed her to the people; seeing then that she had not remained hidden, she comes fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before Him, and told Him the whole truth.

# And the Daughter of Jairus Raised.

Noticing that Jesus desired a public confession from her, she acknowledged that she had touched Jesus, whereas all the others had denied doing so (see Luke). Just as the Savior desired a public expression of gratitude to reveal the miracle of this woman, so he also wished to pronounce a public testimony of his love for this believing woman, and to let all the people know how precious she was in his eyes.

**Daughter** (**be of good cheer**, see Luke) **your faith has saved you, go in peace**, a even greater benefit being proven to her soul than to her body.

In the meantime, the little daughter of Jairus died; for behold, while Jesus was still speaking, some came from the house of the Ruler of the Synagogue <note>The "Ruler of the Synagogue" was an official responsible for the building and the arrangements for services.</note>, saying: **your daughter is dead, why do you still trouble the Master.** They mean to say: as long as the soul was not separated from the body, there was still hope of recovery; but now that she has breathed her last breath, all hope is cut off; do not trouble the Master then in vain. It seems these people had not heard that Jesus had raised the dead youth at Nain <note>original: "Naïs"</note>; nor did they know that it was just as possible for the almighty Savior to command life as health by a single word. Therefore,

Jesus, having immediately heard the word that was spoken, said to the Ruler of the Synagogue, **do not fear, only believe.** Upon which comforting address of the Savior, the Ruler of the Synagogue resumed his plea, specifically that which Matthew records: **My daughter has just now died, come and lay your hand upon her, and she shall live.** Certainly, that wonderful healing of the woman with the flow of blood had strengthened him in that faith.

Meanwhile, Jesus hurried away, going to the house of the Ruler of the Synagogue, allowing no one to follow him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. These were to be the witnesses of the miracle, which three were also later dignified to be eyewitnesses of his glorious transfiguration <note>original: "gestalte-verwisseling"</note> on the Mountain.

Jesus, coming into the house of the Ruler of the Synagogue, saw the commotion (a milling multitude) and those who wept and wailed greatly (Luke says: and they all wept and made a great lamentation over her; and Matthew: he saw the flute-players <note>original: "Pypers"</note> and the milling crowd). But Jesus, having entered, said to them: "Why do you make this commotion? Why do you weep? The child is not dead, but she sleeps." It is true that death is often called a sleep in the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "H. Bladeren," literally "Holy Leaves"</note>; however, we believe that the Savior used this manner of speaking here because the soul of this little daughter—although separated from the body for a short while—nevertheless, by virtue of God's eternal ordinance, maintained its connection to the body and remained destined for the reunion that was soon to happen. The omniscient Jesus knew this, and therefore he calls that death a sleep with all right, as it would soon pass away. The Savior also used this expression to fulfill his hidden purpose which he had in this miracle, as we shall point out later. He also did not wish to deprive the mockers of the opportunity to laugh.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. Thus the Savior provides the opportunity for those who wished to mock him to give testimony of the true death of the little daughter; and thus they could not say later, when the miracle was spread abroad, that the little daughter had not died but had only been in a slumber; otherwise, they would have belied their own given declaration. Thus Jesus ensures that the death of the little daughter is acknowledged before he exercises his miracle-working power upon her.

On the contrary, when they—through those shadowy sacrifices—did not look upon the true sacrifice, they only became worse because of it, establishing a self-righteousness and thus overlooking the righteousness of God, which is from faith. Of those shepherds we read in Ezekiel, Chapter 34, verses 2, 3, 4: That those shepherds fed only themselves, eating the fat (that is, consuming the livelihood and goods of the professors <note>In this context, "professors" refers to those who profess the faith.</note>), not strengthening the weak, not healing the sick, not binding up the broken. But all those healers were useless.

**c.** Christ is that opened fountain for the house of David against sin and uncleanness—specifically the "uncleanness of separation," as the root word signifies—Zechariah 13, verse 1. This woman comes behind the Savior, touching the hem of His garment, saying, etc. The garment of the Savior is a symbol of His brought-forth righteousness, which becomes a robe and mantle of salvation to the believer. And the Holy History rightly says that she touched the *hem*. I would think here of the hems of the High Priest; from these hung the pomegranates and little bells. The pomegranates are an image of Jesus' death and the fruits of His death. The bells signify the sound of the Gospel, through which Jesus' death on the cross with all its fruits is proclaimed—that sound that goes out over the whole earth; Romans 10, verse 18. These High-Priestly hems (see Exodus 29, verses 24, 25), hems that filled the Temple (see Isaiah 6, verse 1), the believers touch in faith. However, this might seem to be sought too far afield and to have gone beyond the immediate context. Nevertheless, that reflection is not entirely to be rejected, since Jesus' garment here represents the same thing.

He interprets the hem of Christ's garment as a symbol of His righteousness and the priestly office.</summary>

# and the Daughter of Jairus raised.

<margin>d.</margin>
Thus, then, she embraced the perfect, brought-forth righteousness, and it delivers her from the spiritual flow of blood, when Jesus's righteousness excludes all those sacrifices of the Law and all those sheddings of blood. The handwriting of sins <note>A legal metaphor for the debt of sin owed to God</note> is broken by Him who entered the true Sanctuary, not through the blood of calves or goats, but through His own blood; those also who (though unknowingly) had made themselves guilty of Jesus's blood—being members of that body whose leaders had crucified the Lord of Glory—are cleansed of that blood-guilt by touching Jesus's spiritual garment and hems; that is, through a faithful acceptance of Jesus's Teaching and an embracing of the fruits of His death on the Cross.

<margin>e.</margin>
This woman intended to remain hidden, yet Jesus made her come forward to confess before the multitude that great power which had gone out from Him. In the same way, the Christian Church, which had thus touched Jesus in faith, could not remain hidden near the dwellings of the shepherds; she had to emerge from those secret places of the Jewish community into the public eye, to confess before all people the great benefit that Jesus had done for her.

<margin>f.</margin>
And so Jesus also openly declared His love for her, willing that everyone should praise her as blessed and as His favored companion; in His word and through His speaking deeds, He called out to her: *be of good cheer, go in peace, your faith has helped you.* Namely, that faith which regards the handwriting of sins as broken and that spiritual flow of blood as staunched, brings about true rest, applying to itself a complete forgiveness of sins.

See there how Jesus speaks the same through both Teaching and miracles; and although the disciples of the Baptist could not yet see this in Jesus's wonders, they nevertheless saw in general that Jesus sealed His Teaching with a miracle—leaving the investigation of that spiritual meaning to the Church.

# The Five Thousand Fed

<image-desc>A large ornamental historiated initial 'H' featuring intricate scrollwork and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Having presented the Miracle of the healed Woman with the flow of blood and the raised Daughter of Jairus, St. Luke relates that Jesus sent out the twelve with great power (Chapter IX, verses 1—5), who subsequently went through the villages proclaiming the Gospel and healing the sick (Verse 6). He notes that the report of Jesus caused distress at the Court of Herod (Verses 7—9), and that the returning Apostles gave an account of their activities (Verse 10). Following this, he relates that miraculous Feeding, and the other Gospel-Writers add yet another Miracle to it.

The miraculous feeding of five thousand Men in the Desert of Bethsaida, and the Savior’s amazing walking upon the buoyant Sea-waters, are two miracle-works so interwoven with one another, and so powerfully illuminating each other, that we are advised to explain them in one uninterrupted treatise. For this is how the matters are connected: Jesus, having satisfied that multitude in such an unexpected manner, ran the risk that they would have appointed him by force as a King over them. Therefore he withdrew, commanding his Disciples to go by ship and sail to the other side. Following this, they fell into danger of perishing, had Jesus not come to them toward the fourth watch of the night walking upon the Sea, entered into the Ship, and crossed over to the region of Gennesaret. There he performed many healings, and immediately after arriving at Capernaum, he became involved in a conversation with some of those whom he had fed in the Desert. He reproached them, saying they only followed him for the bread, and warned them that they should take care and work for the food that does not perish, but remains unto eternal life. From this discourse arose that carnal misconception of actually eating Jesus' flesh and actually drinking his blood, so that many of his followers, being offended by him, left him. However, he gave his wise Disciples the explanation that the words he spoke were Spirit and Life, and that the flesh profited nothing; whereupon these stayed with him, because they knew nowhere else to go where the words of life were to be found, except with Jesus alone. Indeed, the History of John provides us with such a tight connection of these linked events.

Jesus then, having heard of the cruelty of Herod committed against John the Baptist—which message he shall have received <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing the timeline of Jesus's withdrawal to the desert upon hearing of John's death.</note>

# and Jesus walking on the Sea.

after the return of the twelve. See *Matthew* / he departs to a deserted place, in order to also give his sent-out and returned Disciples some rest.

He departed to a deserted place of the City named *Bethsaida*. It would have been that *Bethsaida* / of which *Josephus* mentions in *Antiquities, Book XVIII, 3* <note>original: "Antiq. Lib. XVIII. 3." referring to Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian</note> / which City belonged to the territory of *Philip* the Tetrarch / who significantly renovated this place / and named it *Julias* / after *Julia* / the daughter of *Augustus* / according to the testimony of *Josephus* / at the aforementioned location. It lay by the Sea of *Tiberias* / but in the Trans-Jordan region / in lower *Gaulonitis* / near where the *Jordan* flows into the Sea / that is, on the Northern / or North-Eastern shore thereof. See *Josephus, On the Jewish War, II. 8. and III. 18.* Thus the Savior could sail there by ship from *Capernaum* / which lay in *Gennesaret* on the Western / or Northwestern shore of that Lake / and the Multitude could come to him by land / only crossing the *Jordan* / which had a bridge or ferry there. However, we read that *Bethsaida* is situated in *Galilee* by the Lake *Gennesaret* / *John XII. verse 21.* and therefore on the Western shore of the Lake. The question is therefore / whether this *Bethsaida* in *Galilee* is the same / as the *Bethsaida* of *Josephus* / which he places in the territory of *Philip* / and whether a part of *Gaulonitis* was also called *Galilee* / or whether there were two Cities of that Name, one in *Galilee* / and thus on the Western shore of Lake *Gennesaret* / the other in *Gaulonitis* and thus on the Eastern shore of the same? See on this *Cl. Relandus's Palestine, pages 653, 654, 655.* <note>Hadrian Reland (1676–1718) was a famous Dutch cartographer and orientalist who wrote "Palaestina ex monumentis veteribus illustrata."</note>

And the Multitudes, hearing that, followed him on foot out of the Cities. *Mark* says / that they had seen him sailing across, so that some saw it / others understood it from those who had seen it.

And *Jesus*, having gone out of the Ship, saw a great Multitude, whether *Jesus* had just stepped out of the Ship / or whether he was coming forth from his solitary place / in which he had been busy with his Father in fervent prayers / and thus meeting the multitude in this Wilderness.

And he was moved with inner compassion for them, because they (says *Mark*) were like Sheep that have no Shepherd, and he began to Teach them many things, says *Mark*. *Luke* / he having received them, spoke to them of the Kingdom of God, also healing those who had need of healing. Thus the Savior shows himself to be a good Shepherd / who feeds his Sheep with the true soul-nourishment of his Heavenly Doctrine / and heals their defects and weaknesses.

# The feeding of the five thousand,

When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, the place is desolate, and the hour has already passed; let the crowds go, so that they may go into the villages and buy food for themselves. The Jews had two evenings; see *Exodus 12, verse 6.* The first of which began at the third hour after noon <note>3:00 PM</note> and ended at the sixth <note>6:00 PM</note>; when the second evening took its beginning, lasting until the ninth hour <note>9:00 PM</note>; that we must understand the first, and not the second evening here, the entire history indicates to us sufficiently; those things which are recounted could not have happened within the limits of the actual evening <note>the second evening or nightfall</note>, for then there would also have been no time for the crowd to go into the hamlets and villages to buy food for themselves.

What gave the disciples cause for such a saying, *John* relates to us somewhat more circumstantially: Therefore when *Jesus* had lifted up his eyes, and heard that a great crowd had come to him, he said to *Philip*, from where shall we buy bread, so that these may eat. But he said this testing him, for he himself knew what he would do. *Philip* answered, two hundred pence <note>original: "penningen"</note> worth of bread is not enough for them, so that each one may get a little. The sum of two hundred pence, or *Denarii* <note>Roman silver coins</note>, amounts, as some calculate, to sixty-seven guilders and ten stivers *Dutch*; these are the words of the Lord van *Til* <note>Salomon van Til (1643–1713), a Dutch theologian</note>. "A *Denarius* was a *Roman* coin, containing in silver the weight of a quarter-ounce <note>original: "vierendeel loots"</note>; wherefore two hundred *Denarii* yielded a weight of three marks of silver and two ounces; if now the observations of *Brerewood* <note>Edward Brerewood (1565–1613), an English scholar of weights and measures</note> regarding the *Alloy* of the *Roman* coinage of that time can hold true, which says that their struck silver coin was mixed with only a forty-eighth part of foreign metal, then one finds the same sum compared with our currency to amount to sixty-seven guilders and ten stivers in modern value." Thus the disciples fear their purse would be entirely emptied, or would not sufficiently stretch to the feeding of such a multitude; moreover, fearing that *Jesus* might well send them out to buy bread, therefore, dreading the cost and effort, they advise the Savior that he should dismiss the multitude from him.

From where shall we (they say in *Matthew*) obtain so much bread in the desert, that we should satisfy such a great crowd, just as if he who is the bread of life were not also powerful enough to provide physical sustenance in a miraculous way.

**Jesus** took the five barley loaves and the two fish, and looking up toward **Heaven**, he blessed them; and when he had broken them, he gave the loaves to the **Disciples**, and the **Disciples** to the **Crowd**. His eye was turned upward toward **Heaven** to his **Father**, who now wished to glorify **Jesus** through a new miracle; he pronounces the blessing over the loaves, which had such a powerful effect as we shall soon see. Whether **Jesus** pronounced a set form of prayer—customary among the **Jews** in the blessing of bread—requires no investigation. The mouth of Heavenly wisdom, which itself had formed language and tongue, is bound to no specific words. He breaks the bread himself, like a good Father of the House, and reaches it to the guests through the hands of his students <note>original: "onderwijzelingen," referring to the disciples</note>, thus providing them the food not immediately, but mediately <note>meaning through intermediaries</note>.

> And they all ate and were satisfied, and they took up the leftover fragments, twelve full baskets.

Those who had eaten were about five thousand men, besides the women and children. The Savior, the great Master-Worker of nature, was as powerful in making the nutritional substances of the bread expand—and thus multiplying the food—as he is in gradually making bread come forth from the earth; here, only an accelerated movement was necessary. The leftover portion through this new Creation was greater than the original supply; there were twelve baskets. A basket, in **Greek** *kophinos* <note>original: κόφινος</note>, or a basket of woven wicker, was a piece of equipment with which the **Jews** often traveled. Whether these twelve baskets were those belonging to the twelve **Disciples** of **Jesus**, which they carried with them for their necessities, I do not know.

The people, seeing the sign that **Jesus** had performed, said: "This is truly that **Prophet** who was to come into the world," namely, that great **Prophet** par excellence, who was the primary subject of the doctrine of expectation—that great **Prophet** mentioned in **Deuteronomy 18:18.**

<margin>*The hidden meaning traced.*</margin>
III. But we primarily fix our attention on the Spiritual sense and meaning of these miracles; That through that miraculous feeding a Spiritual satisfaction is indicated is self-evident, and there is none among the Interpreters who has not remarked upon it.

# And Jesus Walking on the Sea

...followed for the sake of the bread—yes, and later argued with Jesus, having such fleshly thoughts about the spiritual food of the soul, just as they previously held regarding Jesus's Kingdom. I say, when these striking features float before my eyes, I find entirely different historical markers, and thus find myself gently yet powerfully drawn and fixed to a different era. And yet, who is so ignorant of the Divine Oracles <note>The scriptures or prophetic words</note> and the events of the Church, that they would need to ask for long what time and what people are being pointed out by the efforts of those men who wanted to make Jesus a worldly King? We shall also shortly point out the end of the exact period from Jesus's discourse—I mean from his dispute with the Jews. See John 6. We have only to climb from the bottom upwards to see how high the depictions in these miraculous events cause us to ascend.

When we had thus guided our thoughts, we designed for ourselves this sketch, which we modestly present, ready to exchange our own view for something better.

**A.** Jesus would once again, in and through His Church, withdraw Himself from the Jews, who are guilty of spiritual adultery and incest, and who kill those who rebuke them for it; being therein also examples of the Anti-Christian Church <note>Referring here to the perceived corruption in the Roman Church or institutional enemies of the Reformation</note>, which would fall into the same judgment of godlessness. The Savior would allure and lead His Church into the **Wilderness of the Gentiles**, where she would be fed. Here a great multitude would follow Him, whom we very fittingly understand under the image of the **five thousand**. Indeed, they would come from the East and West, North and South, to sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—that is, with their faithful descendants. See Matthew 8:11, Luke 13:29, exactly a group of five, etc. That the people follow the Savior on foot represents the rapid influx of so many faithful Confessors.

**B.** In this Wilderness, Jesus would graze His flock as the **only Shepherd**, gathering the lambs and His poor, carrying them in His bosom, and gently leading those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11), having abolished the Jewish shepherds (Ezekiel 34, Zechariah 11:8). He would teach them, laying bare to them the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, and indeed healing their defects and infirmities. # The Five Thousand Fed

namely during that most oppressive period under Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 AD) known for the last and most severe persecution of Christians.</note>, and afterwards under the Arians <note>Followers of Arianism, a theological belief that challenged the nature of the Trinity, leading to significant conflict in the early Church.</note> and other heretics, when the true food of souls became exceedingly scarce; we shall therefore take these two eras into consideration.

Under Diocletian, the teachers were banished and killed, God’s Word was committed to the fire, the opportunity for spiritual exercises was cut off, and indeed the profession of Christianity was in every way paired with the danger of death. The Church historian Eusebius tells us, *Book VIII, chapter 2*: "We have seen the houses of prayer thrown down from the top to the floor with their foundations, and the Divine and Holy Scriptures committed to the fire in the middle of the market; of the shepherds of the Church, some have shamefully fled, others ignominiously captured, and mocked by others." Truly, there was then such a lack,

D. That some imagined that no times of refreshment remained, that Jesus would not fulfill that soul-hunger in that wilderness, and that one should therefore let the confessors go their way without holding public gatherings. Such were those shepherds of whom Eusebius testified that they had shamefully hidden themselves, just as if Jesus were not powerful enough in this wilderness to provide for and fulfill the needs of His Church. They thought that all their spiritual treasures were by no means sufficient for this, just as Philip said: *two hundred pence will not be enough.*

E. However, the Savior shortly thereafter, when Constantine the first Christian Emperor was raised to the throne, made a remarkable change; the Church received all space, her churches were opened, new ones built, the pagan ones taken over, the Holy Scriptures explained without danger, indeed all spiritual and outward blessings pressed into the Church. *Psalm 107, verse 4, etc.*:

> Those who wandered in the desert, in a wilderness way... they were hungry and also thirsty and their soul was overwhelmed within them... he has satisfied the thirsty souls, and filled the hungry souls with good things.

F. After that miraculous feeding and the miracle that occurred upon the Sea, the Savior <note>Dutch: "Heiland"</note> had, as we have seen, returned to the Land of Gennesaret, in which region the sick were brought to him, who were healed merely by touching the hem of his garment. Now Jesus departs from Capernaum toward the borders of the Gentiles, intending shortly to show his Disciples in an illustrious miracle that the heart is purified by faith alone, and by no means by all those outward washings and purifications of the flesh; all those ceremonies shall be abolished when, the Gentiles being called to the Kingdom of God, the believers from among the Jews shall be saved in the same manner as they—namely, the converts from the Gentiles—whose hearts are purified through faith.

Tyre and Sidon were two cities situated on the Mediterranean Sea, bordering with their territory upon the Jewish land; they were the mother-cities of many Gentile nations. From them, various colonies had gone forth and settled throughout Africa and Europe, and from there the Greeks had brought over most of their sciences and forms of religion. The entire province standing under the dominion of these cities bore the name of Phoenicia, and because of the communion with the Syrians, Syro-Phoenicia.

# The Devil Cast Out of a Heathen Woman

Phoenicia, because the region of Tyre and Sidon (as we saw above) was called Syro-Phoenicia. The inhabitants of this region were remnants of the ancient Canaanites. See Judges 1, verses 31 and 32, where we read which inhabitants of Canaan were not driven out. Thus, a heathen woman <note>original: "Heidinne"; a non-Jewish woman, specifically a Syrophoenician</note> comes here to the Savior, the arrival of Jesus having become known to her. Mark relates that Jesus did not wish to be made known in that region, having therefore entered into a house; however, he could not remain hidden, as this woman—whose little daughter had an unclean spirit—having heard of him, came and fell down at his feet, praying him that he would cast the devil out of her daughter. See here, as soon as the Savior leaves Judaism, the heathens run after him and flow toward him. In Matthew, this woman says: *Lord, you Son of David, have mercy on me.* She had, without doubt, heard the rumor which was spread everywhere concerning the Savior throughout all Syria; those miraculous healings performed in Judea and Galilee had come to her ears. She had also certainly learned from her neighboring inhabitants of Palestine that a Messiah, who was to spring from David’s House, was expected, and that this Jesus showed himself in every way through wonders and deeds to be the one who was to come, who was expected.

However, the Spirit of Christ primarily illuminated this woman inwardly, awakened her, and led her to the Savior; this is sufficiently evident from her faithful reasoning with the Savior, which we shall consider in the sequel. Her cry is: *have mercy on me*, so that she presents herself to that merciful Savior as one truly miserable, suffering by the reflection of her beloved child, who was so piteously <note>original: "deerlijk"; miserably or lamentably</note> mistreated by an unclean spirit.

Yet the Savior answered her not a word, acting as if despising and disdaining her, and considering her unworthy of even the slightest attention or answer; meanwhile, the Savior’s bowels <note>A common 17th/18th-century idiom for the seat of deep emotion and compassion</note> rumbled within, being kindled by an inward compassion for this woman, who was driven to him by Jesus' Spirit and love. Yet Jesus behaved thus for wise and just reasons, which we shall see most vividly in the spiritual application. Meanwhile, the pressing desire of this woman was drawn out even more powerfully and kept going by the silence of Jesus, and her faith grew under this trial.

->...that lay only on this side of the Jordan in Galilee, extending toward Damascus and Caesarea Philippi, as the learned Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar known for using Talmudic evidence to explain the New Testament.</note> demonstrates at length regarding Mark. Thus, one might possibly understand that the Savior traveled from the plain in which Caesarea Philippi lay—formerly called Dan (Judges 18)—east of Sidon, that is, from the source of the Jordan, along the Transjordan region until reaching the Sea of Galilee. This entire region belonged to the borders of Decapolis <note><term>Decapolis</term>: A group of ten cities on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, largely Hellenistic in culture.</note> and lay under the jurisdiction of Philip. In this way, he escaped, as much as possible, the eye of Herod—the murderer of his Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>—and withdrew himself again from his enemies and the unbelievers among the multitude. At which part of the sea he arrived and stayed for several days cannot be determined other than from the place to which he subsequently departed. After the miracle of the seven loaves, performed at the place of his first arrival, he set sail for the borders of Magdala (Matthew 15:39). Mark says to the regions of Dalmanutha (8:10). There he remained a short while and crossed straight over the sea, as both Matthew and Mark state. But Mark adds that he landed at Bethsaida (8:22). Since Magdala was situated on the southern shore of the sea and Bethsaida on the northern, both in the Transjordan, it would seem most fitting that the Savior traveled through the borders of Decapolis until he arrived at the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, belonging to the territory of Philip. There he remained safely for several days with a great multitude and performed the great miracle with the seven loaves, etc.<-

And they brought to him one who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech. Deafness arises either from a slackening or breaking of the auditory nerves and instruments, or from a blockage or clogging of the ears or their small tubes, pipes, etc. Those who have been deaf from birth—or at least before they have learned to form language or produce an intelligible sound—are also mute, being unable to form words because they have never heard any. Therefore, such deaf persons are always mute, not necessarily because the nerves of the tongue are stiffened and the tongue is thus "bound," or because the tongue and speech organs are slackened or broken, but simply because they have never heard audible words. This patient of ours, however, was not entirely mute, but only spoke with difficulty, the organs of speech being hindered, from which it appears that he was not born deaf.
