# The Devil Cast Out of a Heathen Woman

The language of the Savior to the Disciples—*I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel* <note>Matthew 15:24</note>—makes a clear distinction in this passage between Jews and Gentiles. Likewise, the Savior’s answer to the Canaanite woman—*it is not meet to take the children's bread* (the Jews) *and to cast it to dogs* (the Gentiles)—and indeed the wise saying of this woman—*yet the dogs eat, etc.*—are so many strokes in this portrait that cause us to fix our eyes upon the conversion of the Gentiles.

<margin>a.</margin> The little daughter of this Canaanite woman is then a symbolic image of the unhappy Heathens, who were entirely inspired, ruled, and defiled by Satan, that unclean spirit. The cities of Tyre and Sidon, being mother-cities of the Heathens and the breeding and training grounds of idolatrous religion and doctrine (although in the Holy Scriptures they sometimes represent something else), favor this interpretation.

<margin>b.</margin> The mother of that little daughter, who becomes the moving cause of the healing, sketches for me here those Heathens who had become Jewish proselytes <note>original: "Jodengenooten," meaning Gentiles who adopted Jewish customs and beliefs</note>, who had thus already entered into the house where Jesus was and stayed there. Such people were the first-fruits of the converted Heathens; they were not so much converted indirectly through the Apostles, but, being visited and enlightened immediately by the Holy Spirit, they were not so much sought out as they were brought to meet the household messengers, just as this Canaanite woman met the Savior. See this clearly verified in the case of Cornelius, who, being a Heathen, was a Jewish proselyte. Acts 10.

<margin>c.</margin> These would recognize the Savior as the Son of David, follow after Him, and implore His merciful grace.

<margin>d.</margin> However, just as Jesus seemed not to concern Himself with this woman, even so strangely did the first believers conduct themselves toward the Heathens, behaving toward them entirely as if they wished to frighten them away and keep them from Jesus. Indeed, Peter had to be made ready by a Divine vision in order to go in to the Heathens with the Gospel Doctrine; see Acts 10:9, etc. How offended were the believers from among the Jews when they heard that Peter had gone in to men who were uncircumcised <note>original: "die de voorhuit hadden," literally "those who had the foreskin"</note>. Acts 11:3. Yet we must note this: that in the behavior of Jesus toward this woman there was nothing unjust, because at that time the "times of the Gentiles" had not yet come; whereas the conduct of the first believers toward the Heathens was thoughtless, because by then that middle wall of partition had been broken down in Jesus's death. Nevertheless, we see...

<margin>Sketch of the common truths.</margin>
### IV. Do you wish to understand the common truths in these miracles, and present them for the conviction of others?

A. See in this Canaanite Woman the characteristic image of one who begins to be moved by the soul-working Spirit of Jesus.

a. As soon as he hears of Jesus, he hurries to Him; nothing holds him back.
b. Enters the House where Jesus is.
c. Falls down before Him, worships Him.
d. And even if Jesus does not hear immediately, acts as a stranger, and seems to give no notice; he nevertheless does not stop.
e. Indeed, when He as it were goes away, he runs after Him.
f. Indeed, when He speaks harsh language, such a person nevertheless listens reverently.
g. When He presents the impurity, death, and guilt of damnation, he does not contradict Him, but says, "Yes," etc.
h. Nevertheless, not doubting His all-sufficient grace and cleansing power.
i. Demanding only the least grace, the least token of Jesus' love, being well able to see without envy that others receive more—

# And the Deaf and Speech-Impaired Healed

<margin>k.</margin> receive a different and more abundant grace, if they might only obtain the least—like scraps and crumbs. See how faith grows, love is kindled, and hope is lifted up under those circumstances which seemed to dampen and extinguish it.
<margin>l.</margin> And such people then become partakers of the most precious and abundant blessings.
<margin>m.</margin> Oh! Such people also run after the Savior for the conversion of others, just as this woman did.

These truths must be urged to give courage to God’s children, so that they follow Jesus tirelessly, pleading, indeed not ceasing at all until they obtain a blessing; according to these truths, one must also rebuke those less persistent, quickly ceasing efforts of God’s children—indeed, their sluggishness and laziness. One must show from this "painting" <note>The author uses "painting" or "picture" as a metaphor for the biblical narrative</note> that Jesus does not wish to reveal His favor to them, nor lead them to a closer enjoyment and experience of His goodness, except after such unceasing seeking; only then do they learn to rightly prize and value those goods.

But how clearly can the mouth-confessors <note>Those who profess faith with their lips but not their hearts</note>—if only they had eyes—see their lack of conformity to this image? Is the religious exercise of such people such a running after Jesus, such a persistence? Have they hurried after Jesus in this way, have they thrown themselves at His feet? Indeed, when He did not hear, went away, and did not deign to look at them, did they then cling to Him?

When He set their natural impurity before their eyes in His word, showing that they were dogs, how did they behave? Did they say, *Yes, Lord*, or the opposite? Have they considered that the utmost and unmerited grace was still being shown to them if they might only receive the first-fruits, the slightest glimpse of Jesus' love? Or do they think that the Lord God, by making His greatest and most precious blessings flow to them, would not be doing too much for them? This strives against true humility. He who wishes to win Jesus' favor, then, must ensure that the soul-disposition of this woman shines forth in him; only in this way is Jesus to be entreated, found, and enjoyed.

Here one must note the distinction between the outcome of this feeding and the previous one <note>The feeding of the five thousand described in Matthew 14.</note>; there the leftovers were gathered in hand-baskets <note>term: "korven" (cophinoi) — smaller wicker baskets typically carried by individuals.</note>: here in large baskets <note>term: "manden" (spyridas) — larger hampers or grain baskets capable of holding a human.</note>: then they kept twelve full hand-baskets: but now seven full large baskets: just as the hand-baskets were small wicker-weavings, so the large baskets were of a greater and wider capacity; the first sort the Jews commonly carried with them on their travels on their arm, but this second kind they seem to have taken with them because of the length of this journey, being of more extensive capacity, in order to carry a greater supply of provisions therein.

Those who had eaten were four thousand, without Women and Children, so that every loaf, distributed only among the Men, excluding the Women and Children, would have had to be divided into more than five hundred and seventy-five parts; had this food not been multiplied through the Savior’s creative power, it would have been impossible to still the hunger of this multitude.

# The feeding of the four thousand in the Wilderness,

One would be more successful in identifying the correct Church-era <note>Dutch: "Kerktijd," referring to a specific period in the history of the Christian Church</note> in which this feeding shall occur, if one had the right key to the secret meaning of the "days." Do they—besides signifying a year, which is clear from many Divine Oracles <note>Prophetic scriptures</note>—perhaps also constitute an entire Period (which for us is a time of three hundred and sixty years)? And could this be clearly demonstrated from the Doctrine of Types <note>The study of Old/New Testament events as "types" or foreshadowing of future spiritual realities</note>? Furthermore, does a day also sometimes amount to a thousand years, as we spoke of regarding the first miracle? These are matters which—along with other exemplary time-designations—we shall diligently investigate, if the Lord wills. Jesus says of this Multitude, *that they had now remained with him for three days*, it being then the third day. By this we could immediately be determined <note>In our chronological calculations</note>, were this work once composed from certain grounds indicated in God’s Word itself. However, since we cannot expand upon that now and within such a small space, we say only briefly: that if we were to presuppose here the same meaning of the days as in the first Miracle, we would find ourselves precisely within the time of that Wedding depicted back then. We are thus brought to that final satiation, or feeding of the Church. Jesus intended to teach through this subsequent Miracle that it would by no means remain at that first feeding—depicted by the satiation of the five thousand in Matthew Chapter 14 (when most did not partake of the inner grace)—but that a more excellent satiation would be miraculously provided toward the end times, after the Church had experienced a leaner enjoyment of the Goods of Salvation throughout all the times of the New Testament. We say this according to that supposition, until we receive further light upon this Miracle.

We shall not be wordy in explaining the symbols that present themselves in this Miracle-work, because we have already done so regarding the miracle of the five thousand who were fed.

A. The **Wilderness** then shall be the walking-place of the Church, which, from the beginning of the proclamation of the Gospel-Doctrine, speeds forward through this Wilderness toward Canaan <note>The Promised Land, symbolizing Heaven or the perfected state of the Church</note>.

B. In this Wilderness, Jesus has his **Mountain**, his people, his Spiritual Kingdom. Here he has enlightened the spiritually blind; given the maimed their full constitution—that is, a right apprehension and love of the truth, the truly essential parts of the state of grace; made the mute to speak and proclaim the virtues of Him who calls them out of darkness into his wonderful light; and made the lame to walk in the path of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of salvation.

# The Blind Man [Healed] First in Part

And having taken the hand of the blind man, he led him out beyond the Village, that is **Bethsaida** / just as **Bethlehem**, a City in **Luke 2:4**, is also called a Village in **John 7:42**. And he spat in his eyes (which he also did regarding the man born blind in **John 9** and the [deaf-mute] in **Mark 7**) and laid his hands upon him, and asked him if he saw anything. **Jesus** knew well / that he had restored his sight only in part / indeed, it was thus his Divine will / otherwise he could have restored his sight perfectly all at once; however, these actions are arranged / to fully demonstrate the spiritual counterpart <note>original: "tegenbeeld" - refers to the spiritual reality prefigured by the physical miracle</note>.

And he, looking up, said: I see men, etc. This blind man must have seen men before / before he became blind / for it is not probable / that he was born blind / so that he now easily knew / that those creatures / which he saw / were men. Yet he did not yet see clearly enough / his magnified vision did not yet show him things in their own form / in the proper quality / and magnitude; For he saw men walking as trees. Therefore, that great Physician <note>original: "Heel-Meester" - literally Healing-Master</note> laid his hands upon him a second time / for the complete restoration of his sight.

After that, he laid his hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up, and he was restored and saw everyone distantly and clearly. And he sent him to his house, saying: do not go into the Village, nor tell it to anyone in the Village. **Jesus** did not wish to become famous there / nor to honor those / who were in the Village / with that miracle / which is why he led the blind man outside the village. This sketches something in the spiritual counterpart.

<margin>
Proof for **Jesus'** Divinity.

# The blind man at first partially healed,
<note>original: "De blinde eerst ten deele"</note>
<margin>Q 4</margin>

What do we find here? At first glance, it suggests that the Reformation has its stages; yes, even those whose spiritual blindness was removed during the Church Reformation, whose eyes were illuminated, did not immediately possess the most vivid and clearest sight, but were gradually purified of those mists of ignorance and those scales of unknowing.

But this particular detail—that men appeared to him as large as trees—does this also have its significance? Who can doubt it, if they will attentively consider the following: that this sufferer saw men walking like trees was due to his magnifying vision, which did not show him objects in their correct proportions. Let us now remember that trees in the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "H. Bladeren," literally "Holy Leaves"</note> are symbols of high and prominent persons in the Church, who, driven by ambition <term>heersch-zugt: a lust for power or dominance</term>, raise their crowns too high from time to time, assuming for themselves an authority and dominion. Thus we read in Isaiah 2:11 &c.:
> *The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. For the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up...*

These are called all the high and exalted cedars of Lebanon, and all the oaks of Bashan. Of the Anti-Christ, the Psalmist says in Psalm 37:35:
> *I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green native tree;*

And what is more common in the Prophetic Writings than to call the Anti-Christ and those authority-exercising Churchmen "trees"? However, they would never have climbed to that height, never have become so prominent and formidable, had the magnifying ideas and the slavish imagination of a deluded multitude not come to their aid—those who imagined that in these men there was more than a human highness, a sovereign domain to rule even over the conscience. Truly, this authority of the Pope or of the Church has been the most harmful instrument for blindfolding people, even the practiced ones. Now, when the Church Reformation broke through and the light began to shine upon many, they were not yet so immediately enlightened that they could entirely discover the nothingness of such a presumed authority; those men still appeared to them as trees. When Luther's eye was illuminated to the extent that he discovered the wickedness of that spiritual commerce of Indulgences <note>original: "Aflaat-Briefjes"</note>, the Pope and those Churchmen nevertheless still appeared to him as prominent trees; indeed, he still appealed then to the Pope, then to a general and free Council <note>original: "Concilium"</note>, then to the High School of Paris <note>The Sorbonne</note> &c. still...

This object of deep compassion catches the Savior's eye, and at the same time, the sight of him falls upon the Disciples, who ask their Master whether this man or his parents might have sinned in some preeminent way, thus causing this man to be born blind. Whether the followers of the Savior were occupied with that delusion and prejudice—which was also present among the Jewish people and the teachers in Israel—that the sin of the parents (especially the neglect of the most solemn religious service, a <term>artifice|Dutch: konst-greep; referring here to a tactical interpretation used by religious leaders</term> by which they better kept the people to the observation of those difficult and costly ordinances) caused children to come into the world with outstanding defects; or perhaps, whether they may have thought that souls themselves, before they are united with the body, make themselves guilty of gross sins while they are still in the common dwelling-place of the Spirits <note>This refers to the Platonic or Rabbinic idea of the pre-existence of souls</note> which are ordained to a body, all being created at the same time and united with bodies at their determined time; and that those souls which preeminently transgressed against the Creator are paired with misshapen and defective bodies, thus bearing the public hallmark of their former wickedness?

Regarding that, we cannot say for certain; however, it is certain that they believed, according to whatever prejudice, that an outstanding sin clung to this man or his parents. Yet the Savior wished to make that prejudice disappear from the Disciples, saying: *neither this man nor his parents have sinned* (preeminently), *but that this man was born blind so that the works of God should be made manifest in him.* Indeed, Jesus had to have constant occasion to work the works of Him who had sent Him, as long as it was day, for a night would one day come when the hour and the power of darkness would be there to seize Jesus, to bind Him, to condemn Him, and to hang Him on the <term>gallows-wood|archaic term for the Cross</term>, yes, even to bury Him under the earth; in that night no one would be able to work. Therefore, as long as Jesus was still in the world, He had to show Himself to be the *Light of the World*. <meta>This page continues the theological and geographical analysis of Jesus healing the man born blind, specifically focusing on the physical actions taken by Jesus and the location of the Pool of Siloam.</meta>

# The eyes of the man born blind opened.

Jesus spat on the ground and made clay from that saliva, and spread that clay on the eyes of the blind man; an act of the Savior intended only to symbolize something that took place in the spiritual <note>original: "G." likely abbreviation for "Geestelijke" (Spiritual)</note> healing, and which could in no way contribute to removing natural blindness. On the contrary, it would seem to aggravate it—if it could be further aggravated—for whatever physicians may say about the soothing, opening, and healing power of saliva, anyone can easily understand that earth mixed with saliva could not have that natural effect. Jesus also spat in the eyes of the blind man in Mark 8, and likewise when he restored the deaf man who had an impediment in his speech in Mark 7.

To this act, Jesus added the command that the blind man should go away and wash himself in the Pool of Siloam, which is translated as *Sent* <note>original: "uitgezondenen"</note>. This was a river-pool from the Fountain of Gihon, or Siloah, which fountain was located outside the city by the Valley Gate, in the valley behind Mount Akra. From this fountain flowed two rivers, or one river streaming out in two directions; that part which ran along the south side of Jerusalem formed, after some windings, the Pool of Bethesda not very far from the Sheep Gate (see John 5), which was also possibly called the Upper Siloah. However, that river, or that part of the river, which ran from the fountain along the west of the city, formed a pool near the Fountain Gate, which was also used as a bathing place, bearing the name of the Lower Pond, or the Lower Pool. It is to this place, as some believe, that Jesus likely sent this man born blind, because this pool was the nearest and was also specifically known by the name of the Pool of Siloam, whereas the other river-pool was commonly called Bethesda. Thus, not only did the fountain bear the name Siloah, but also the river-pools flowing from it; having become a bathing place as if "sent out" from that sender (the fountain), adorned with walls and galleries. See Nehemiah 3, verse 15. The water of Siloah served the Jews for many purposes; it was suitable for bathing, as is evident from this passage and also from John chapter 5. From this fountain they drew water during the Feast of Tabernacles. Also the water which they mixed with the ashes of the burnt red heifer. The priests also drank from it when they had eaten too heartily of the sacrificial meat, from which it appears that it was a healthy water. See Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note> regarding this river and pools, and also read Mr. Reland <note>Adriaan Reland (1676–1718), a Dutch Orientalist and cartographer</note> regarding the Fountain and the Pool of Siloam, *Palestine* Volume II, pages 858 and 859.

# The eyes of the man born blind opened.

and you would have no sin; but now that you say, "we see," your sin remains. For if you were entirely blind—having no Divine revelation at all <note>original: "geenzins hebbende eene Goddelijke openbaaring"</note> in which the engravings of the **Messiah** are sketched out—you would not be so greatly to blame. But now you yourselves confess to being instructed in that Word, yet your sin remains because you do not recognize Him whom **Moses** and the **Prophets** so clearly point out. <margin>Proof for Jesus's Divinity.</margin>
II. Truly a miracle which could not have been fabricated out of a misguided zeal for the cause of **Jesus**. This man was well-known; he had sat by the road and begged for a long time. The neighbors, and even his own parents, declare that he was born blind and that he had now become sighted; no one could deny it. The **Jews**, who conducted the most diligent investigation into this matter, could not suspect this miraculous healing of any fraud, being forced into silence by the truth of the event.

Certainly, this miracle was an irrefutable proof of what **Jesus** asserted against the **Jews** in the previous chapter, and what he presented to this restored man: namely, that **Jesus** was from above, that the Father had sent him, that he was a Prophet, and not a sinner. Indeed, the **Lord God** would not perform such signs through wicked deceivers as the **Prophets** had foretold of the true **Messiah**. Now, the **Holy Men of God** <note>A reference to the biblical prophets.</note> had recorded this very miracle as a mark of the **Messiah** in Isaiah 35:5. Consequently, one who performs such wonders, and clothes them with Holy Doctrine and an elegant, blameless conduct, must be sent from **God** and is believable in the testimony he gave of himself: namely, that he was the **Christ**, the **Son of God**. It was therefore a willful blindness in the **Jews** that they did not know from where **Jesus** came, even though he had opened the eyes of the man born blind—it having been unheard of in all ages that anyone had opened the eyes of one born blind. Consequently, that divine prophecy in Isaiah 35:5 is fulfilled in no other than this **Jesus**, who must therefore be the glory and the ornament of **Jehovah** (cf. Isaiah 35:2).

<margin>Hidden meaning traced.</margin>
III. That through this blindness from birth, and its happy restoration, spiritual blindness and spiritual healing are signified, is taught to us by the **Savior** before, during, and after the miracle. John 8:12:
> I am the Light of the world; he who follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the Light of life.

# The eyes of the man born blind opened.

Amidst the miracle, he gives sufficient understanding that this blindness is a symbol of a **Spiritual night**, and the miraculous deed, which would immediately follow, a proof that he is the **Light of the world**. See verses 4 and 5. After the performed miracle, he said to the man born blind, who had been restored: *I am come into this world for judgment, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.* <note>original: "ik ben tot een oordeel in deze wereld, gekomen..." quoting John 9:39</note>

Let us observe whether we can, with equal success, point out from the preparation of this miracle and its circumstances what particular **Church-event** <note>The author likely refers to a prophetic or dispensational stage in the history of the Christian Church.</note> is sketched here. A certain Writer opines that in this man born blind (a sentiment which he shares with many) one can see the characteristic and life-like portrait of the blind **Gentiles** <note>original: "Heidenen," referring to non-Jewish nations.</note>, who, being born in the miserable ignorance of the Christ—who is a *Light to lighten the Gentiles* (See Luke Chapter II. v. 32)—receive opened eyes of understanding. He does not exactly prove this supposition from the composition of this miraculous history, but thinks that the appropriateness of the symbol gives him sufficient occasion for that conception. And certainly, when I considered this case somewhat more accurately, things emerged in this History that seemed in every way to favor this supposition. There may be a dispute concerning the time in which one ought to place this *Miracle*; whether one should join the account of *Lazarus’s* resurrection with the stay of the *Savior* across the *Jordan* / at the place where *John* first Baptized / see *Chapter X. verse 40.* *Jesus* having gone to *Judea* after that stay to perform this *Miracle*? Or whether this resurrection occurred shortly before the last *Passover* <note>original: "Pascha"</note> / and thus the departure to *Caesarea Philippi*—*See Mark VIII. verse 27. Matthew XVI. verse 13.*—and the subsequent journeys must be inserted in between? It *is* not easily feasible to make the correct determination / since difficulties arise on both sides. Let the well-meaning Reader preciousy weigh the reasons. For the latter position, these reasons seem to plead: **A.** The consequences of that Resurrection appear as though joined with the last *Passover. See Chapter XI. verses 47—57. and Chapter XII. verse 1.* The going up of the inhabitants of *Ephraim* and the *Wilderness* / and their deliberations / whether *Jesus* might indeed come to the *Feast* / seems to presuppose / that *Jesus* had not been there long before / and was indeed keeping himself hidden there / which is why the *Jewish Council* <note>The Sanhedrin</note> had given orders / that if anyone knew where he was / he should make it known, see *verses 55, 56. and 57.* **B.** Also, *Jesus* does not seem to have come from *Bethabara* for the resurrection of *Lazarus* / which is separated from *Judea* only by the width of the *Jordan*. Whereas the *Holy Writer* relates / that when *Jesus* received the news of *Lazarus’s* illness / he remained two more days in that place, *Chapter XI. verse 6.* After that / he says / let us go again to *Judea* / *verse 7.* Now / if since this saying of *Jesus* / and the death of *Lazarus* / the *Savior* spent four more days / before he came to *Bethany* / compare *verses 17, 39.* with *verses 6, 7.* he does not seem to have come this way from the nearby *Bethabara*. These reasons would win me over to that proposition. However, this difficulty hinders me: That the *Disciples* / when *Jesus* spoke of going to *Judea* / immediately interjected / The *Jews* have now (so recently) sought to stone you, and are you going there again, *verse 8.* Compare this with *Chapter VIII. verse 59. and Chapter X. verse 31.* The *Jews* then took up stones again, to stone him, which (however one might soften that difficulty) seems to indicate a simple sequence of these events. Also, against the raised difficulties, it may come into consideration / whether or not / *Chapter XI. verse 55.* begins a new narrative / and the *Passover* in *Chapter XII.* is connected therewith? Even if **Jesus** had been in that region shortly before; their deliberations and arguments concerning **Jesus** could still have occurred in that manner, even if **Jesus** had been among them some months prior. Nevertheless, let the **Reader** weigh this matter, which we leave undecided, since the spiritual contemplation of this Miracle does not depend entirely on that specific chronology. But *Jesus* held himself back because he wanted to give the greatest proof of love to this, his bosom friend. Meanwhile, his sisters, in this painful accident, know to turn to no one better than to *Jesus*, whose Heavenly Doctrine, powerful comforts, and rare deliverance they had many times seen proven.

# Lazarus Raised from the Dead

**A.** **Lazarus** <note>The name Lazarus is derived from the Hebrew *Eleazar*, meaning "God has helped"</note> signifies that the mighty God has helped; and this shall be made manifest when, through Him, there shall be a way of escape even against death itself.

**B.** He was the beloved friend of Jesus, and yet he became weak and died in the absence of the Savior. The favorites of Jesus—the faithful witnesses of truth—shall not only be spiritually ill but shall "give up the ghost" <note>referring to a spiritual or metaphorical death of the Church's testimony</note>; see **Revelation 11** <note>A reference to the "Two Witnesses" who are killed and then resurrected after three and a half days</note>. However, their death should properly only be called a "sleep," just as Jesus describes the death of Lazarus. 
And those who thus slept would certainly live again according to the words of the Disciples, since they were not dead in the most absolute sense—deprived of an internal principle of life—even though they were entirely dead in regard to the proclamation of truths (which then stood still). The Prophetic Scriptures also call this sleep a "death." See again **Revelation 11**. And this death forced its way into the Church while Jesus, with His Word and Spirit, had withdrawn Himself from the external assembly as if anew.

**C.** Yet this sickness, this death, was not unto a permanent death, but for the **glory of God**; the Church, under this great transformation, shall be placed not merely in her former state, but in a far more magnificent condition, so that this death shall provide the occasion for the most glorious work of all.

**D.** And therefore the Savior will not immediately take away that sickness when a spiritual **Mary** and **Martha** present the miserable state of the Church to Him through their supplications; that sickness shall proceed unto a death, and thus pave the way for a most glorious work of salvation <term>Heil-gewrocht: a divine masterpiece of saving grace</term>.

**E.** **Mary** signifies a "Sea of Bitterness" <note>A traditional etymology for the name Mary/Miriam</note>; Oh! how many bitter waters must the sisters and fellow believers drink in and out! (The Church now being viewed in another respect, perhaps with new Confessors of the Faith arriving from among the Jews or Gentiles). These shall yet make a preparation and prophecy for that spiritual burial; nevertheless, they shall secure the members of the body against total corruption through a spiritual anointing.

**F.** **Martha**, meaning "Mistress" or "Lady," signifies those who will recognize no foreign Lords over them; see **Isaiah 26:13**. Those who wish to stand in that liberty with which Jesus had endowed them.

Let us now also behold the preparation for that **Spiritual Awakening**.

This discourse of the Savior is clarified, further urged, and more powerfully impressed upon the minds of the Disciples by this rare vision. Indeed, the miracles and wondrous events recorded in the Gospel Books often serve for the more powerful confirmation of Jesus's immediately preceding, or soon following, doctrinal sermons; we shall attempt to demonstrate the truth of this by examining this illustrious case. 1. We shall clarify the literal sense. 2. We shall assert the truth of the history. 3. We shall show that Jesus in every way achieved his objective.

<margin>Literal sense opened.</margin>
I. And it came to pass about eight days after these words. Matthew and Mark say six days; six full days had flowed between the Savior's previous negotiation and this glorious appearance, excluding the day of the conversation and the day of the vision on the Mountain, which two days Luke also counts, and thus reckons eight days.

There is then no essential difference between the Gospel Writers; and it happened, that he took with him Peter and James and John; these three would shortly see him wrestling with fearful hellish agonies in his bloody garden of sorrow <note>A reference to Gethsemane</note>; therefore, to strengthen them against such a forthcoming sight, he makes them eye-witnesses of this his transformation of form <note>The Transfiguration</note>, a prelude to that glory which he would obtain through that suffering.

And climbed up the Mountain to pray. Whether this Mountain was Tabor—which does not seem probable to some—or another mountain range, requires no anxious investigation; had there been any secret in the proper name of the Mountain, the Holy Spirit would certainly have placed it in the pens of the accurate Gospel Writers. Whether it was a Mountain to which the Savior was often accustomed to withdraw, because Luke says with a finger-pointing, <note>original: "τὸ ὄρος"</note> *the* mountain, we also cannot determine.

Saint Peter, in the second Letter Chapter I. verse 18, calls that Mountain, because of this wonderful appearance, a Holy Mountain. Upon this Mountain the Savior had climbed to pray. Christ, considered as God, and consequently independent and in need of nothing, cannot be understood to pray; but as God-man, Mediator, the obedient Son, indeed the Servant of the Father, he could pray, and did pray in the days of his flesh, to the end that his human nature might be supported and adorned with the necessary gifts for the execution of the work of reconciliation.

# Jesus Glorified on the Mountain

The Prophets proclaim that Jesus must suffer, and thus enter into His Glory; Oh! rare spectacle, high-worthy company! What mortal eye, not enlightened by Jesus' Spirit, and not awakened from spiritual slumber—or kept awake by Him—can endure such a radiance?

*Peter now and those who were with him, were heavy with sleep, and being awakened they saw his glory and the two Men who stood by him.* From this we conclude that it was likely nighttime, when the Lord Jesus through His radiance, and the Heavenly beings through their glorious appearance, changed the night into day and the darkness into light. Whether the Disciples truly fell asleep and were awakened, or whether they remained awake despite being heavy with sleep, deserves investigation. And if they did fall asleep, when did sleep overcome them? Was it before they had seen Christ’s glory and those two Men, so that they did not see that glorious spectacle until they were awake—which the words *and being awakened they saw his glory* seem to imply? Or did sleep overtake them after Christ had been transformed in appearance before them, which the simple narrative seems to say? Read the account of Luke and compare it with the other Gospel-Writers. However, it is also not probable that the Disciples gave themselves over to sleep while this glorious spectacle still lasted, after they had beheld this glory of Jesus, this high-worthy and delightful company of the Heavenly beings, and had heard that conversation. Therefore, we propose either that they only saw this glorious transformation of Jesus after their awakening (and that it only then occurred), or rather, that although they were heavy with sleep, they nevertheless remained awake <note>original Latin: *pervigilantes*, meaning "staying awake throughout"</note>, if we give the word <term>διαγρηγορέω</term> <note>Greek: *diagrēgoreō*, to remain awake or to wake up thoroughly</note> that meaning, and consider that <gloss>through</gloss> <note>original Greek: *dia*</note> makes the meaning of <term>γρηγορέω</term> <note>Greek: *grēgoreō*, I watch or I am awake</note> more powerful. So that this most beautiful sight drove the sleep from their eyes, and they thus continued to behold that glorious phenomenon. How the Apostles knew exactly that these two Heavenly beings were Moses and Elijah (for Peter calls them by name, see the following verse) requires no anxious inquiry. They were either recognizable by some outward sign, or the Savior, in His conversation with Moses and Elijah, called them by name within earshot of these Disciples, or the Savior—when He caused His students to wake from sleep or kept the sleep from their eyes—simultaneously illuminated their eyes so that they recognized in these Heavenly beings the very features of Moses...

The Father at his Baptism (Matthew 3 verse 17) declared him as such once again. In this Son, the Father had a good pleasure, because he is the expressed Image of his substance <note>original: "zelfstandigheid," referring to the Greek 'hypostasis' or essential nature</note> and the radiance of his Glory; everything that is in the Father, all the power of his name, is to be seen in Jesus. And the Disciples hearing this (so Matthew relates) fell on their faces and became very afraid. This rare occurrence aroused wonder in them; this sudden sound coming from the "Excellent Glory" (2 Peter 1 verse 17) caused amazement—that intelligible language—and a childlike reverence and fear, especially in those who are conscious of many weaknesses. Compare Isaiah 6 verse 5 and Judges 13 verse 22.

And Jesus, coming to them, touched them and said, "Arise and do not be afraid." As they came down from the Mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: "Tell no one of this vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead." We shall trace the reason for this prohibition shortly.

# A. Some general truths.

a. That the Christ had to suffer; Moses and Elijah—and thus the Law and the testimony—speak of his departure <note>original: "uitgang," referring to the Greek 'exodos' or death</note> which he must fulfill at Jerusalem.

b. The Glories following upon Jesus' suffering; his appearance is changed, his face shines like the Sun, his clothes glisten. All symbols of an incomparable Glory.

c. They saw here also the neat accord and harmony between the Teaching of Christ and that of Moses and Elijah; however, they also notice at the same time that Moses and Elijah are but servants of this Lord of the House (Hebrews 3, verse 3). They discover so great a distinction between the Glory of Christ and that of Moses and Elijah—even though the latter came beautifully out of Heaven—that the glory of these was as no glory at all; or, to make the language of the great Apostle my own (2 Corinthians 3, verse 10), that "what was made glorious had no glory in this respect." <note>The author argues that Christ's glory so far outshines the Old Testament figures that their light seems to vanish by comparison.</note>

d. They learned from this vision that Moses and Elijah had to withdraw like shadows (indeed, those two went away) and that in Jesus, as in the body of those shadows, everything was fulfilled; Jesus remained alone on the Mountain after their departure. Therefore, those two Dispensations <note>term: "Huishoudingen" (Economies/Dispensations) refers to the different eras of God's dealings with humanity, i.e., the Old and New Testaments</note> could not remain paired; the tabernacles of Christ, Moses, and Elijah could not be pitched together on one Mountain; the old had to pass away, and all things become new.

e. Since Christ alone remained—Moses and Elijah having been carried away by a cloud—and they were exhorted by Divine command to hear that Son (alone), it appeared to them from this that no other name would henceforth be heard in the new Church-Heaven but the name of Jesus. Every name that would be named in this or the present Age could not prevail; Jehovah alone would be King, Judge, and Lawgiver.

f. This voice, being heard from a light-filled cloud, could bring to their minds that under the joyful Gospel-day all darkness would be cleared away and shine with a bright clarity. In olden times, the Lord dwelt in a dark cloud that covered the Tabernacle (see Exodus 40), but now he has clothed himself with light as with a garment (Psalm 104, verse 10). And the Heavenly voices now come from a light-filled cloud, brightened by Jesus' rays of grace.

glory. *Peter* represents those who, as living stones, are established upon the true rock *Jesus* through an unfeigned confession of faith. *James* <note>original: "Jacobus"</note> makes us think of the remnant according to the election of grace, who pursue others, indeed run ahead into the Kingdom of Heaven (I refer here to the name and the actions of *Jacob* <note>The author plays on the Hebrew etymology of Jacob, meaning "supplanter" or "one who follows at the heel."</note>). *John* brings to our minds by his name those who are favored and graced with super-heavenly blessings—all qualities which are found at all times, and specifically in those three, among the beholders of *Jesus’* glory.

<margin>a.</margin> The Disciples were weighed down with sleep, yet remained watchful—doubtless through *Jesus’* doing—in order to behold this glory. Likewise, believers are by nature exposed to a spiritual lethargy and sluggishness, and their blinking sight shimmers before these bright rays of light, unless they are awakened and made watchful by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who opens the eyes of the understanding to behold this glory. Also, a dark night has preceded each instance of the Savior’s glorification, the light having always shone out of the darkness.

<margin>b.</margin> But hear something rare: *Peter*, beholding this glory, wanted immediately to make booths <note>original: "hutten"; referring to the tabernacles or tents mentioned in Matthew 17:4</note> etc. This has at all times been the weakness of believers: that they were so filled, so taken up with the first principles of glory, that they imagined there was no greater radiance to be expected; wishing therefore to pitch their booths already, to linger by those first principles. Just as if they were not travelers who must not stand still, but must go from strength to strength. <margin>Psalm 84 verse 8.</margin> Thus St. *Paul* rebuked the *Corinthians*: <margin>1 Corinthians 4 verse 8.</margin> *Already you are filled, already you have become rich.* How weak and sluggish people also are after the Church Reformation <note>term: Kerk-hervorming (The Protestant Reformation)</note> to continue the work of a reformation, staying by those principles as if there were no greater light, holiness, and glory to be expected for the Church. And oh, if only against that latter time, when *Jesus* shall make a prelude to that final glory, one would not also want to pitch the tents and linger by that preliminary glory! But those who speak so, and shall speak so, know not what they say, not understanding the Scriptures, which promise not only a shining dawn, but a full midday radiance; to that extent, they deny the Promises.

<margin>c.</margin> Yet, just as *Peter* soon realized that he busied himself in vain with wanting to make booths when *Moses* and *Elijah* <note>original: "Elias"</note> were carried away by an airy cloud. So were the belie-

# Jesus Glorified on the Mountain. 313

The attentive observers also soon perceived that one must not rest in those first principles, but that the Church must continually go forward, leaving behind that which was past and reaching out to that which was ahead, thus becoming more and more "heavenized"—that is, being raised to a truly Spiritual and Heavenly state. We believe this is beautifully depicted by *Moses* and *Elijah*, who were taken away in a cloud out of the sight of the Disciples and, without doubt, toward Heaven.

The cloud is, in the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "H. Bladeren," literally "Holy Leaves"</note>, a symbol of covering, protection, and Divine indwelling (see *Exodus 40*); also of the Doctrine of Grace (see *Deuteronomy 32 verse 2*). Take all of this together: through the Divine protective overshadowing and indwelling nearness, and through the power of the Doctrine of Grace, the witnesses of truth—as if by a triumphant cloud-chariot, illuminated by the bright rays of Grace—have ascended to Heaven; see *Revelation 11 verse 12*, where the witnesses ascend to Heaven in a cloud. And this, in turn, would hold its truth across three periods of time.

<margin>d.</margin> From the midst of that airy cloud, the Heavenly voice is heard: "This is my Son," etc. This has at all times been the summary of the Doctrine of Grace: namely, that the Father took pleasure only in His sweet-smelling Sacrifice of the Cross, rejecting everything which man might devise as meritorious or acceptable to God outside of this Sacrifice of the Cross. This Son alone must be heard, with the rejection and denial of all human Teachings and Commandments; *Jehovah* <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note> alone is our Judge.

<margin>e.</margin> But when God’s Children rightly consider the content of this demand—"hear Him"—and with what thoughtfulness, reverence, love, and willing submission this Son must be heard, they are utterly embarrassed. They slip away in humble shame, falling on their faces with the Apostles out of a consciousness of their own sluggishness, weakness, and natural inability, finding in themselves no power, wisdom, or fitness to hear that Son as is becoming.

<margin>f.</margin> But the Savior, as a Spiritual Physician, touches them, saying: "Fear not, I am with you; with me is power, wisdom, etc., to lead you, to steer you, and to secure you against all calamities. Does my Father demand of you, in the Covenant, to hear me? Oh! my Covenant is a Covenant of Grace; I shall work the conditions of the same within you, being an all-sufficiency for you. Fear not then; do not remain lying down, but stand up, go forward, and hasten toward the end of your path of faith."

-># Jesus glorified on the Mountain.<-

g. Indeed, through this manifestation, such a **Glory** was depicted—comprising light—that it could not be proclaimed in all its particulars during the days of Jesus's flesh <note>original: "Jesus vleesch"; a reference to his mortal, human life on earth</note>, in the time of his humiliation. Such a narrative would have been improbable in that hour of darkness; furthermore, the Disciples themselves, at that time, did not have such enlightened ideas of all the particulars of Jesus's Glory that was to follow his suffering. Therefore, the account of this vision was more fittingly postponed until after Jesus's resurrection, when this vision was fulfilled, and consequently, the account of it began to be believable.

We can conclude from all this that St. Peter did not in vain make such a great point of this glorious manifestation, in 2 Peter Chapter 1, verses 16, 17.

<margin>Sketch of the common truths.</margin>
IV. Does one desire the common truths in a brief sketch? Let one behold here the happiness of the Believers; who were by nature also seated in a night, seized by a Spiritual slumber, regarding nothing as glorious or beautiful except that which is in the Creatures <note>referring to created, earthly things rather than the Creator</note>; only that which could adorn their vain eye, fill their ear, or stroke the outward senses was esteemed by them as something glorious or worthy. Christ, however much he shone as the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>original: "Zonne der geregtigheid"; a Messianic title from Malachi 4:2</note>, however properly presented in all his graceful beauties, was hidden from their eyes.

But God, who is rich in grace and mercy, has taken pity on them, calling out to them: *stand up, awake.* And then, with enlightened eyes of the soul, they beheld all that is desirable which is in Jesus. Oh! how quickly the Images of vanity vanished from their sight as soon as this radiance appeared before them! Now they see nothing glorious except precisely that which is in Jesus, or which leads them to him. And those eyes having once been opened by the grace of God, they remain open; however many things there may be that burden them and might seize them with drowsiness, that glorious radiance keeps sleep from the eyes of the understanding. They have approached that Sun of Righteousness, which serves for their illumination, for the working-in of a Heavenly glow of love—that fire of love becoming too powerful for them to resist—and also for a continual delight. For indeed, how pleasant it is to walk under this delightful sunlight toward **Spiritual fruitfulness**! This Sun coaxes the Spiritual sprouts of their good works forth from the earth; this Sun makes the fruits of their conversion ripe and fragrant. Oh! they never approach beneath this Sun without feeling a new quickening. Yes, under this light they become a light in

# Jesus Glorified on the Mountain

Those who never stand still in the work of conversion have the closer hope of being glorified with Jesus; thus they purify themselves, even as He is pure <note>Reference to 1 John 3:3: "And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure."</note>. They do not say with Peter, "let me linger here, let us build huts here" <note>A reference to the Apostle Peter's reaction during the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:4), suggesting a desire to remain in a state of spiritual ecstasy rather than continuing the earthly journey.</note>; Oh! They have received as yet only small beginnings, a tiny piece of the matter. How narrow is still:

8. Their **knowledge**; what adorable wonder-mysteries are still not perceived by them, what innumerable beauties are not yet fully known by them, which nevertheless—if viewed and looked through—would instill in them new wonder, reverence, high esteem, and love for God’s Holy Word.

9. Their **love for truths**, etc. How often can a straying <note>original: "af-hoerende," literally 'whoring away,' a common pietist metaphor for spiritual infidelity</note> love for the creatures <note>meaning created things or worldly attractions rather than the Creator</note> still creep into their bosom.

10. Their **experience** of God’s internal, comforting proximity.

11. Their **wakefulness and earnestness**, etc. How limited are all of these; and would they think that the richest and most tenderly loving Father could and would not give them more than those poor beginnings? Oh! With Him is an all-sufficient fullness; they simply continue onward like a traveler, never pitching their huts anywhere until they have arrived with God in Zion, etc.

To that end, they listen constantly to that Heavenly speech: *This is my beloved* <note>original: "deze is mijn geliefde," referring to the voice of God from the cloud: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him."</note>, etc. And whenever they become aware of their inability and unfitness to hear this Son properly with the required reverence, submission, and joyful willingness, they indeed acknowledge their nothingness, falling upon their faces with all humility. But on the other hand, they do not fear; Jesus is with them; in Him is power, wisdom, and all-sufficiency to fulfill every lack, to strengthen the hands, to guide the feet, and finally to bring them into the perfect glory—a glory of which the present is but a rough sketch, a glory whose complete description, as well as its enjoyment, is preserved for an eternity.

Matthew 10:1—8; Mark 6:7, 8; Luke 9:6; Luke 10:1—9. **Jesus**—for holy reasons—did not will that they should have or exercise this power at this specific moment, so that it would be clear that this power was not their own, it being granted to them by **Jesus**, whereas **Jesus** possessed that power as His own. Because His power depended on no one else, He could always make it effective as it pleased Him; thus, the unlimited power of this wonderful Master-Worker had to stand out above the borrowed power of His servants—not to mention (which we shall soon note) that this entire display was subordinate to the **Savior’s** spiritual purpose.

Now, the Lord God would not work such faith into them unless He had simultaneously determined to perform such a miracle upon their act of faith. The Savior <note>original: "Heiland"</note> only wishes to demonstrate that the power to perform miracles in the disciples was nothing other than believing that the Lord God had established a connection between their faithful will—which extended toward one thing or another—and the miraculous consequences; so that their ability to do wonders and their faith extended equally far. The Savior uses this example all the more gladly, and with all the more wisdom, because it would one day have its absolute truth in the spiritual sense. Indeed, when the Church (as we shall presently hear or see) should possess a faith that grows and overcomes all difficulties, raising its head above all other plants—that is, a faith like a mustard seed—then a figurative mountain would be moved.

**Nothing shall be impossible for you**, says the Savior; that is, you shall be able to perform everything that the Lord God has attached to your act of faith. The power to perform miracles is not an actual inherent strength in you, but only your faith, upon which (when it is awakened and directed toward this or that particular matter) the Lord God causes the miracles to follow. Understanding this, the disciples could soon surmise what the cause of their inability was: namely, their unbelief, just as the Savior had answered them: *because of your unbelief* etc., and now explained Himself more specifically.

It is indeed true that the *Romans* imposed a tax-penny on the Jews in *Judea* when *Judea* was made into a *Roman* Province, as we shall see further in *Matthew 22, verse 17.* However, it is not probable that the same would have been imposed on and demanded from the Jews in *Galilee*, as long as *Galilee* still stood and was ruled under its own King *Herod*, and not by the *Roman* Governor.

Because the tax-penny of the Sanctuary and that imposed by the *Romans* were distinct in all respects. # The Temple Tax for Jesus and Peter.

...as a stamp on one side, the image of the jar in which the Manna lay <note>The "golden pot" mentioned in Hebrews 9:4</note> with the inscription *Shekel of Israel*, or a censer from which a flame emerged; and on the other side, the blossoming rod of Aaron, or a palm branch with the inscription *Holy Jerusalem*. Against this, those who have knowledge of the matter testify that the Roman tax-coin was in value no more than a drachma—a little more than five Dutch stivers—and had as a stamp the image of the Emperor, Matthew 22 verse 21. They were also distinct in respect to the time when, the persons by whom, and the manner in which they were demanded. The first <note>The Temple tax</note> was collected in the month of Adar <note>roughly March</note> by the envoys of the Jewish Council, at that time without coercive power, from every Jewish head individually; thus they addressed Peter only in the form of a question, and received a didrachma <term>didrachma: a double-drachma or half-shekel</term> each for Jesus and Peter. But the other <note>the Roman tax</note> was collected in the month of Nisan <note>roughly April</note> by the Roman tax collectors, armed with public authority, and only for each house and family...

And this being so, how is it then conceivable that Roman or Pagan tax collectors, provided with coercive power and having neither knowledge of nor respect for Jesus, would have named Jesus as the Master of his disciples, and addressed Peter on his behalf, and that only in the form of a question: *Does your Master also pay the didrachmas?*

And principally because, in such a case—supposing the question here concerned the Roman tax—it cannot, in our opinion, be imagined what sense or consequence Christ’s reasoning would have had: namely, that He and His own, like Peter, being Sons—and that of the King and the Kingdom—and not strangers, were on that account free from the Roman and political taxes. For surely neither Jesus nor Peter were sons of an earthly and Pagan King, or of the Emperor, nor did they have the slightest worldly relation to any King or Emperor to be free from their taxes on that account. 

But if we take it in respect to God, the King of Kings, of whom Jesus was truly the own Son, and His followers through adoption in and through Him, then it follows well that they, as such, were indeed free from that tax imposed by God upon the Jews as a proof of their alienation due to sin—as a ransom to convince them that they still needed and awaited the true ransom of their souls—but certainly not that they were free from the political and Roman tax on that account; thus far Mr. Huisinga. See also Lightfoot, van Til, and Mr. Antonides on this passage, as well as what Mr. Burman has further noted regarding this in his *Harmony*. It appears then clearly,

that these <term>didrachmas</term><note>A Greek silver coin equivalent to two drachmas, or a half-shekel.</note> were the half-shekels of the Sanctuary, to be paid annually by every Israelite as a ransom for his soul for the benefit of the Temple.

Peter is then asked: *Does your Master not pay the didrachmas?* It seems that this polite question implies: "Does your Master also pay that customary Temple tax?" or, as others would have it, "Does he pay the didrachmas now, at this time, upon the first demand?" For whether Jesus was accustomed to paying the half-shekel annually or not, the collectors could well have known from the rolls.

And he said, *Yes*; because he was sufficiently aware of the Savior's custom. Thereupon Peter intended to go to Jesus to make known to him the demand for the didrachmas, but the omniscient Savior had no need of that announcement.

And when he had come into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: *What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take customs or taxes? From their sons or from strangers?* Jesus draws his parable from this. Kings are accustomed to exempting their closest blood relatives from taxes and burdens. Now, that King who had imposed this burden of paying the half-shekel upon Israel was the Father of Jesus; and the Disciples were Jesus's friends, indeed, sons of the Most High. Consequently, Jesus, as the Son of the King, and the Disciples, as his most secret bosom friends, could well have been free from that demand for tax.

Peter answered: *From strangers* (namely, the kings demand taxes) *and not from the sons.*

Jesus said to him, *Then the sons are free.* Jesus could well have withdrawn himself from the payment of that shadowy half-shekel, from that <term>exemplary ransom money</term><note>The author refers to the tax as "shadowy" or "exemplary" because it was a symbolic precursor to the actual spiritual ransom Christ would provide.</note>, because he would shortly provide the true ransom. He could also have exempted his Disciples—whom he released from many matters of the ceremonial Law—from that shadowy ransom, since they were his dearest confidants, who had to taste beforehand, now and then, something of that sweet freedom which the Savior would bring. Nevertheless, as long as that carnal Law held place, the Savior wished to fulfill it.

*But lest we give them offense, go to the sea, cast in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and having opened its mouth, you shall find a stater*—a type of coin amounting to a whole shekel, and therefore exactly valid to pay for Jesus and Peter—*take that and give it to them for me and you.*

# The Unclean Spirit Cast Out

Whether the miracle recounted by *Matthew* Chapter XII and by *Luke* Chapter XI is indeed one and the same case; and whether one ought not to posit distinct cases here, because the possessed man in *Luke* is only mute, while the one in *Matthew* is both mute and blind; also because *Luke* mentions nothing of the arrival of *Jesus'* Mother and Brothers, with which *Matthew* joins his narrative; also, because it seems that the miracle recounted by *Matthew* must have occurred much earlier than that in *Luke*. Nevertheless, when I read the histories in one and the other *Evangelist*, I read the same matters with the same words; and the fate of that man, out of whom the *Devil* was cast, who returns having taken seven other spirits with him, is the same in both *Gospel-Writers*. Therefore, I do not dare to distinguish these histories from one another. Regarding the raised difficulties, I say that one *Gospel-Writer* may well pass over a circumstance mentioned by the other, even if he describes the same history; and regarding the order of time, we do not yet have the necessary light as to which of the *Gospel-Writers* follows—or if they follow at all—the exact order of time; and I will not feign that these and similar histories are not somewhat questionable in that respect. But however it may be, we take the liberty to explain this miraculous deed as being the same in *Matthew* and *Luke*, and to give it this place.

# From the Mute and Blind.
<note>This header refers to the biblical account of Jesus healing a man who was both blind and mute, found in Matthew 12 and Luke 11.</note>

the Jews called them dung-houses <note>original: "drek-huizen"</note> because of the unclean idolatry and sacrificial services. But the Pharisees, having heard this, said, "This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons." Just as if Jesus, for the propagation of his teachings, had made a secret treaty with Hell and thus a shameful conspiracy with the unclean spirits. But Jesus, seeing their abominable deliberations and their equally wicked and foolish arguments, refutes them in a very concise manner, from the very nature of the matter—that is, from the character of his miracles. Certainly, those arguments derived from the matter itself are usually the most powerful.

> But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then shall his kingdom stand?"

Jesus did not merely perform miracles, but he allowed that at that same time the Devil also practiced his strange works; however, in such a way that he always had to yield to the commanding voice of Jesus. Thereby it became public that the Devil, with all his malice, wickedness, and power, could do nothing against him who is the Creator himself, and that he is consequently the greatest liar when he wishes to be served as a God, and indeed as something independent. If Jesus's miracles were directed toward making the Devil known as one powerless—and consequently as a creature, though he passed himself off as a God—and indeed as the greatest liar and seducer, would he then have had a secret alliance with Jesus to lend him a hand in the destruction of his own kingdom? The Savior adds another argument:

> "And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you."

<margin>Literal sense opened.</margin>
I. *And it came to pass, as he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath day, that they watched him. And, behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy.* <note>Luke 14:1-2</note> Without doubt, this Chief of the Pharisees—that is, a Pharisee who was a member of the Great Council <note>The Sanhedrin</note> or the Head of a Synagogue—must have invited the Savior on the Sabbath, and at the same time arranged for that man with dropsy to be present there. This was done with the malicious intent to test Jesus's miraculous power on this sufferer—whom they well knew to be truly afflicted with that plague and not a fraud—and to mock and expose the Savior if he could not effect the cure; or, if he did give proof of supernatural power, to brand him as a Sabbath-breaker. Dropsy <term>waterzucht: a historical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</term> is a disease that causes the whole body, or various parts of the body, to swell violently, making the limbs unable to perform their functions; it is also accompanied by heavy fevers. In our language, we call this disease *waterzucht* <note>water-longing/dropsy</note>, and the one burdened with it *waterzuchtig*, to express the longing and desire for moisture and drink that manifests in this condition. For it is evident that those with dropsy, although they are ill from a great excess of moisture and water and often swell from it until they nearly burst, can swallow down entire pots and jugs, and having poured them in, immediately a sigh...

### III. A peculiar symbol of Judaism, which was subject to a meager and unsatisfying administration of the Law, which is fittingly represented by water, in contrast to the more abundant and joyful Dispensation of the New Testament. However, we must view this administration of the Law here as being abused by Judaism, they being puffed up by a superstitious observation of those fleshly Commandments and Institutions, and therefore exalting themselves through a presumptuous pride above others, because the Lord God had given them that Shadowy Law. Yes, they were so foolish that they still wanted to cling to that Hill of the Law after the antitype of those shadows—the body itself—had been established; so that they felt, as it were, an unquenchable thirst for those waters, and yet could not be satisfied. For in that outward exercise of religion, if the Spirit did not look higher to the Image of the matter itself, there was no true soul-satisfaction or refreshment.

# The Man with Dropsy Healed

That we may rightly perceive the symbol, we learn from the parables of the Savior which He immediately allowed to follow the performed miracle, warning the invited guests that they should never choose the first place when they were called to a Wedding, because everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled. *See verses 7–11.* Jesus also gave this exhortation to the one who had invited Him: "When you give a dinner or a supper, do not call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your relatives, nor your rich neighbors, lest they also invite you back at some time... But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind." *Read the 12th, 13th, and 14th verses.* And that Jesus aimed at a Spiritual feast with all of this appears sufficiently from the fact that—on the occasion that one of those who sat at the table said, alluding to the parables of the Savior, "Blessed is he who eats bread in the Kingdom of God"—He concealed <note>or "veiled in allegory"</note> the Spiritual Supper and those invited to it through an artful Parable. *See verses 16–25.*

<margin>A.</margin> Thus then we understand this miracle: the Jews, puffed up by a vain delusion born from a precise and superstitious observation of the shadowy religion <note>The author uses "shadowy" to refer to Old Testament rituals which were seen as "shadows" of the coming Christ</note>, believed that they must have the seat of honor in the Kingdom of God, in the Kingdom of the Messiah, and that they, through their outward and fleshly privileges, were worthy and excellent above the Gentiles; indeed, deeming the Gentiles—who in their eyes, and truly also in deed, were blind, lame, and poor—unworthy to be invited along to that Spiritual Joy-feast.

<margin>B.</margin> But those who would be healed of that Spiritual dropsy <term>waterzucht: a condition of swelling; here used as a metaphor for pride and obsession with ritual</term> by Jesus's healing hands on the Spiritual Sabbath, would also simultaneously understand that Jesus not only wanted those poor and lame and blind to be invited, but that they would even obtain the preference; the converts from among the Jews must therefore cast off all delusion and pride, and with a humble and quiet spirit regard the Gentiles as their Brothers, happy partakers in the Inheritance of the Saints in light, whereas many of the Jews—indeed, the greatest part—were excluded because of their Spiritual dropsy, that is, that stubborn clinging to that Shadow-service and unbearable pride.

<margin>C.</margin> Just as the malicious Jews understood that to heal the man with dropsy was to violate the Sabbath, so truly was that Spiritual healing—the relief from those Shadow-Laws and the Delusion born from the observation of the same—a loosening from...

After the previous miracle and the aforementioned parables, the Historian <note>Referring to the Gospel writer, Luke.</note> records several more teachings on how a disciple of Jesus must forsake all things. This is illustrated through two parables: one of a man intending to build a tower, and a king who must march to meet a mightier foe (Verses 25–33), concluding that they must preserve the salt within them from becoming tasteless (Verses 34, 35). In Chapters XV and XVI, you have those glorious parables of the Prodigal Son, the Unjust Steward, and Lazarus and the Rich Man. In the XVII Chapter, he warns his disciples against offenses, and how one should behave toward another in forgiving sins to preserve unity (Verses 1–4). The Apostles' request for an increase of faith is answered with a demonstration of the power of faith, along with an exhortation to persevere in their service without slackening or boasting of any merit (Verses 5–10). Following this is the account of this Miracle.

<margin>The literal sense opened.</margin>
I. And it came to pass, as he traveled to Jerusalem (to there offer up his soul as a ransom for many) that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. The linguist Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar known for using Talmudic evidence to explain the New Testament.</note> has noted that the Syrian and Arabic translators have rendered it "between Samaria and Galilee," thus resolving the difficulty of how Jesus could continue his journey to Jerusalem by going through the middle of Samaria and Galilee; it must certainly refer to a specific border region.

# The Ten Lepers Cleansed

...having been [in the area] that was called the middle of Galilee and Samaria.

Whether this journey of Jesus to Jerusalem through the midst of Samaria is an entirely different trip than the one described in Luke Chapter 9, verses 51, 52, and 53—implying that Jesus, after that previous journey into Judea having arrived at Bethany near Jerusalem, went back down from Judea to Galilee and from there directed his journey to Jerusalem again between Galilee and Samaria—or whether it is the same journey (Luke wishing to bring us back to simultaneous events which he merely divided into certain categories by using the same heading), I will not investigate now. However, this must be carefully noted when constructing a <term>Gospel Harmony<note>A scholarly attempt to align the timelines of the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) into a single chronological narrative.</note></term>.

**And as he entered into a certain village, there met him ten men that were lepers.**

Regarding what the plague of leprosy is, we have given the necessary report in the [account of the] miracle of that one cleansed leper, to which we refer the reader back.

It is no wonder that the lepers met the Savior in a village, even though they were excluded from the community of the people according to the Law; this is only to be understood as a permanent residence among the people, which was not permitted to them. They also had to remain excluded only from the cities that were walled in the time of Joshua. See the aforementioned miracle work.

**They stood afar off**, because those who were occupied by this plague did not dare to approach close to other people, being required—in order to be avoided—to cry out, "Unclean, unclean!"

**They lifted up their voices, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.** By this, they confess the misery of their condition, the power of Jesus to deliver them, and his sovereign will in this matter, for which reason they implore his mercy. This impression, in the case of the nine, was not mixed with faith, as appears from what follows.

**And when Jesus saw them, he said unto them, Go show yourselves unto the priests.** Regarding this ceremony, see again the aforementioned miracle piece.

**And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed**, immediately experiencing the desired effect of the Savior's so favorable and irresistible will.

**And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, and fell down on his face at his feet**, acknowledging the Divine Power.

**And he was a Samaritan.** Whether this is said to distinguish him from the others—who perhaps were not Samaritans, which is likely why the Savior also said, "Were there not ten? And none are found to give glory to God except this stranger"—or whether this is noted simply because this man was a Samaritan, a foreigner, because it was something rare that even a Samaritan would honor the Savior with such reasonable religious devotion, it remains a wonder that the other nine did not follow this laudable example; this is not entirely clear. Nevertheless, that one was a Samaritan, a nationality we shall describe in somewhat more detail, as such will enrich and illuminate the spiritual meaning.

1. The Samaritans were possessed of a deadly hatred against the Jews, and the Jews likewise against the Samaritans, holding them under a solemn <term>Ban<note>A formal ecclesiastical excommunication or curse, known in Hebrew as 'Herem'.</note></term>.

2. They valued their own Temple over that of Jerusalem; 
> *Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you people say that Jerusalem is the place where one must worship,* 
says the Samaritan woman to the Savior. John 4:20. Therefore, the Samaritans falsified the words of Deuteronomy 27:4 in their copy; in the Hebrew text it stands: 
> *You shall set up these stones on Mount Ebal,* 
but in the Samaritan version, it says *on Mount Gerizim.* <note>The author highlights the ancient textual dispute between the Masoretic Text and the Samaritan Pentateuch regarding the location of the first altar.</note>

3. They did indeed have the Law of Moses among them and claimed to follow it strictly; they also believed that a Messiah would come: 
> *I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he has come, he will proclaim all things to us.* verse 25. 
Yet their religion and doctrine of the Messiah were mixed with much superstition and error, such that they differed little from idolaters; we learn this from the words of the Savior: 
> *You people worship what you do not know; we (Jews) worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.* verse 22.

4. They boasted wrongly of the Patriarchs, as if they were their true descendants: 
> *Are you greater than our father Jacob? Our fathers worshiped on this mountain.* 
John 4:12 and 20.

Hidden meaning explored.

III. The spiritual application of that plague and its restoration, as well as all the shadowy ceremonies <note>Refers to the "shadows" or types of the Old Testament law</note> to be observed regarding it under the Old Testament, you shall find in detail in the explanation of the aforementioned miracle. Therefore, we have only to note here what these ten cleansed lepers are a teaching-image <term>teaching-image: an allegory or type used for instruction</term> of, and this one Samaritan who returns to give God the glory.

A. That the plague of leprosy was a sign and prototype of spiritual death—the state of the Anti-Christian multitude—we believe we have sufficiently suggested for consideration in the said treatise. That entire Church-body is more than once described in the Oracles of God <note>The Holy Scriptures</note> by a ten-fold number; the whore has ten horns. Revelation 17:3. And those ten horns are explained to be ten kings, verse 12, that is, Kingdoms which give over their strength and power to the Beast. These ten Kingdoms were, in part, outwardly cleansed by the Gospel which was preached anew during the Church Reformation, and thus restored from spiritual leprosy according to outward appearance. That is to say, in those ten Kingdoms there have been some who (at least outwardly) turned themselves to reasonable worship, having a loathing for Popish Idolatry <note>A common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholic practices</note> and errors. At least this is certain: there was not one of those Kingdoms in which that restored Doctrine was not heard—in some more publicly, in others more secretly, in some with more, in others with less, or almost no consequence and fruit. However, if we now count the Lands or Kingdoms in which the reformed religion took hold, we shall find ourselves brought to a five-fold number. See Isaiah 19:18. And if among all those who are outward Professors of the restored Doctrine, we shall count only those who are inwardly cleansed and can give Jehovah the glory for their spiritual healing, we shall hardly have a tenth part remaining, and ask: where are the nine?

And do you wish to know what kind of people those restored professors of faith <note>original: "Geloofs-belijderen"; those who publicly declare their religious conviction</note> were before their spiritual healing, while they still moved within the community of that straying Church? They are very aptly sketched as:
$\alpha$. A Samaritan who adhered to a different Church than the one established by Jesus, wishing to serve God in a different manner than He had commanded.
$\beta$. Those who indeed possessed the Scriptures of Moses, of Christ, and the Apostles among them, yet had mixed the Holy Doctrine with many trifles and errors.
$\gamma$. And, whatever they claimed regarding the Savior, their fabrication of other Saviors and Intercessors <note>A critique of the veneration of saints in the Roman Catholic tradition</note> besides Jesus, and the total corruption of the Doctrine of Grace, meant they did not know what they worshipped.
$\delta$. And yet they boasted—though unjustly—of the ancient Teachers and Church Fathers, just as if those figures had been of the same mind as them in matters of religion.

And are you eager to see the inner soul-state of the truly reformed? They glorify God with a loud voice and fall on their faces at the feet of Jesus. Until He calls out to them: "Arise, your faith has saved you."

IV. Wherein the distinction lies between a true reformed person—one who is spiritually healed—and one who has only outwardly turned back from errors and idolatry, can be read in this Miracle; and such is evident in that heartfelt gratitude, namely, in:
A. Glorifying God.
B. With a loud voice, in proportion to the magnitude of the benefit received.
C. Casting oneself down at Jesus' feet.
D. And how happy are those who hear this voice: "Your faith has saved you!"
E. Many, indeed the most, show by their ungrateful behavior that they are not truly cleansed.
F. Would such people have become partakers of that benefit and not glorify God, nor cast themselves at Jesus' feet?
G. Let us now take count here; out of ten, there is not even one who returns, etc.
H. What reasons for gratitude do the Children of God have, then, that they are among those few!
