I. *Matthew* relates then / *And as they departed from Jericho, Mark* likewise / *as they departed from Jericho,* yet *Luke*: *And it came to pass, that as he was come nigh unto Jericho, or approached Jericho, a certain blind man sat &c.* It may be that *Jesus* / both upon entering / and exiting / *Jericho* / healed blind men / or that it is to be understood / that the Blind man already sat begging / when *Jesus* with his company came near *Jericho* / but the miracle first occurred / when the Savior went out of that City. # And the Faithless Fig Tree Withers

he alone could sufficiently serve as a teaching-image <note>Dutch: "Leer-beelde," an object lesson or symbolic representation</note> of that which *Jesus* wished to portray. Otherwise, it has sometimes come into my consideration whether these two healed blind men might represent the *Jews* and *Gentiles*, whose eyes are enlightened by the *Gospel* doctrine. But since the *Gospel-writers* *Mark* and *Luke* present us with only one, it seems to me that the *Holy Spirit* wishes to set forth only one as a teaching-image; and this is *Bartimaeus*, which means as much as the Son of *Timaeus*, just as the *Gospel-writer* gives that description of him. The linguist *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar</note> guesses that this name signifies as much as "a blind man," being *Timai* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: תמיא</note> the same as *Simai* <note>original: סמיא</note>, with the *S* changed into a *T* according to the custom of the *Chaldeans* <note>The author refers to the Aramaic language dialects</note>; and then *Bartimaeus* would mean as much as the Son of the Blind Man—a blind son of a blind father. We shall follow the history of this one alone for the reasons stated above.

He sat by the road and begged, and when he heard the passing multitude (*see Luke*), he asked what it was;

And after he was told that *Jesus* of *Nazareth* was passing by, he cried out with a great voice: Lord, you *Son of David*, have mercy on me. And although the crowd rebuked him, he cried out all the more: You *Son of David*, have mercy on me. And *Jesus*, standing 
still, commanded that he should be called. And they called the blind man, saying to him: Have good courage, rise up, he calls you. And having cast off his cloak (in order to run to *Jesus* with more speed), he rose up and came to *Jesus*. *Jesus* asked him what he wished that *Jesus* should do for him? He answered: *Rabbouni* <note>A title of respect for a teacher, more emphatic than "Rabbi"</note>, that I may receive my sight, or see again; so that possibly this man was not born blind. However, *anablepo* <note>original Greek: ἀναβλέπω</note> also means to look up, to look on high; nevertheless, it seems most natural here to require the meaning of "seeing again," and therefore this *Bartimaeus* can be a symbol of the enlightened *Jews*, and not of the *Gentiles*, who never had a spiritual sight.

And *Jesus*, being moved inwardly with compassion, touched his eyes (*see Matthew*) and said to him: Go your way (*see Mark*), your faith has saved you. And immediately he received his sight and followed *Jesus* on the road (*Luke*), glorifying God; and all the people, seeing it, gave praise to God.

# SKETCH OF THE MIRACLES THAT OCCURRED

### LUKE CHAPTER 23, verse 45
#### 45. And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the Temple was torn in the middle.

<image-desc>An ornate square drop cap 'T' decorated with detailed leaf patterns and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Between the last miracle discussed and that rare catch of fish <note>referring to the miraculous draught of lilies/fish in John 21</note> (John Chapter 21, verse 1, etc.), there are still to be read in the Gospel writers the miracles and wondrous events at the Passion and the Death of the Savior. However, these are so interwoven into the history of the Passion and the death of Jesus that—in order to treat them extensively and in the particulars of their spiritual significance—one would need to take into view those parts of Jesus's Passion and indeed (to proceed correctly) the entire history of the Savior's Passion, and to trace them in their secret meaning; something which ought to be a special work in itself. Nevertheless, so that nothing is lacking for a complete treatment of all the miracles, we shall make some general remarks on the secret sense of the miracles, presenting them in a brief sketch. Consider then:

<margin>
The multitude that captures Jesus, cast to the ground by Jesus's word, and Malchus's ear healed.
</margin>
A. In that great multitude consisting of the band of soldiers and the servants of the Chief Priests and Pharisees, armed with swords and clubs, arriving with torches and lanterns, led by Judas the feigned friend of Jesus, that wicked traitor; among which troop were also found some of the Chief Priests and Elders of the people, rushing at Jesus, yet cast down to the ground by his word, and getting up again; Jesus, who offered himself voluntarily and requested safe passage only for his weak disciples, being bound and led away; in which circumstance the disciples, and particularly Peter, behaved very imprudently and improperly, wishing to plead for his Master with the blade, hewing off the right ear of the High Priest's servant <note>The servant's name was Malchus</note>; and thereby making the cause of his Master suspicious. However, all of this gave Jesus the opportunity to bring light forth out of the darkness, by a serious rebuke disapproving of his disciple's deed, and glorifying himself through the miraculous healing of the severed ear, and in an emphatic manner defending his conduct and way of teaching—as being free from all rebellious principles—against the Chief Priests and Elders. # The Second Miraculous Catch of Fish

The Holy Writer <note>The Apostle John</note> notes that this was the third time that Jesus revealed himself to his disciples after he was raised from the dead. Through many certain signs, the risen Savior showed himself alive: to Mary Magdalene; to Peter; to James; to those travelers to Emmaus; twice to the eleven; and to more than five hundred brothers at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). John marks this one as the third. If one only considers the appearances that our writer has recounted, a difficulty arises. He has recounted the appearance to Mary Magdalene, and to the eleven twice—first in the absence of Thomas, and then in his presence—and thus this would be the fourth.

This difficulty is resolved when one either considers both appearances to the eleven as a single event (as the first was not "complete" until Thomas was also present), or when one counts the appearances only by the days on which they occurred. In that case, the appearance to Mary Magdalene and that to the eleven occurring on the evening of that same day would be just one revelation; eight days later the second; and this one the third.

<margin>Proof for Jesus' Resurrection.</margin>
II. In this appearance lies a certain proof for the truth of Jesus' resurrection. He appears to seven of his disciples and seals for them the truth—that he who was dead has become alive again—through two miracles. And while perhaps regarding the second miracle <note>The meal prepared on the shore</note> someone might have thought it possible that someone else had laid that fire, or brought that fish and bread (however improbable that was), the miracle of that extraordinary catch of fish was beyond and above all suspicion. They had spent the entire night fruitlessly; yet at Jesus' command, casting the net on the other side, they caught such a great multitude. Who can command such a work but the All-knowing and All-powerful Savior? It was right, therefore, that no one asked him, "Who are you?" From these miraculous events, they had to conclude for certain that it was the Lord.

<margin>Hidden meaning traced.</margin>
III. This miracle, no less than the previous ones that Jesus performed before his death and resurrection, shall be a "painting" of spiritual matters. If he gave his disciples instruction concerning the things of his Kingdom while dwelling with them for forty days after his resurrection, it was not inappropriate that he also depicted those same truths—which he presented in words—through the brush of miracles and teaching-pictures. No one will doubt that when he breathed on them in one of the previous appearances, saying "Receive the Holy Spirit," he made a prelude to that rich...

The torn net there represented to us the schism between the Eastern and Western Church, and especially that tear which the net of ensnared truths received through all those false doctrines in the Western Church under the rising Anti-Christ.

The net shall tear no more. There may remain offenses, brotherly disputes, etc., in the Protestant Church; a great decay may come into it, according to the prophecies; however, the Saving Doctrine shall no longer be corrupted in its fundamental principles within the visible Church; at least, I read nothing of that in the Oracles of God <note>original: "Godspraaken," referring to Holy Scripture</note>.

If Jesus held a midday meal with His disciples, after the Reformation a table was also prepared in the presence of our enemies, with a cup that was overflowing, after the Church had gone out from that valley of the shadow of death; Psalm 23, verses 4 and 5 <note>original: "Pf. XXIII. ÿ. 4, 5."</note>.

<margin>
Sketch of the common truths.
</margin>

IV. If you wish to consider some common truths more closely for reflection:
A. Jesus reveals Himself more closely:
   a. When the disciples are with one another;
   b. In Holy conversations;
   c. Also in a diligent observance of their outward calling;
   d. When they obey and follow Him without fleshly reasonings, then He performs wonders.
B. He prepares a table so unexpectedly and invites His own.
C. He prepares His own for Spiritual food by the fire of His love, and also that of trial.

## C. Of their QUALITIES, DISPOSITION Etc.

**FIVE WERE WISE.** five were stout-hearted / deliberate / prudent / as the root word <note>original: "grondwoord" - referring to the Greek 'phronimoi'</note> carries that force **Etc.** We shall not speak extensively here of the wisdom / and prudence of the Saints in general: We clarify the matters only under that relation and imagery as they appear here. The **WISE** then were

α. **Deliberate** / who had experienced / that the **Love** of earthly things can deliver no lasting pleasure **Etc.**
β. That the fulfillment of their desires was only to be found in the communion of that **Soul-Bridegroom**.
γ. Having therefore been advised / to learn to know that **Bridegroom** rightly from his **Word** / in his loveliness / **Glories** / and **Riches.**
δ. Also the manner / how to enter into a **Spiritual Marriage** with him / and to practice the purest love with him: For in the **Spiritual** sense the **Virgins** are not merely **Playmates** / but also the **Bride** herself.
ε. Just as they then became entirely resolved / to surrender their **Love** to that **Bridegroom**.
η. Therefore examining themselves in a quite serious and deliberate manner / whether he indeed possessed the highest of their **Love**.
ζ. And when they are convinced of that / they stoutly watch over everything / that can nourish that **Love** in them / or cause it to weaken / with that deliberate intent / to awaken the former in themselves in every way / and to extinguish the latter.
ι. Therefore they ingeniously watch their inclinations and affections / whether those are indeed the surrender of that pure **Love** / and consequently whether that **Love** increases or decreases in them?
κ. In every way one also perceives in them a stout-hearted dexterity / to observe all opportunities / with a **Spiritual** artifice / by which they can give evidence of that tenderest / and ruling **Love** / which they have holily sworn to this **Jesus**.
λ. Their prudence also consists in this / that they foresee the approaches of this **Bridegroom** to his **Church** or **Bride** from the word of the **Prophecies** / having a right understanding of the state of the **Church** / and so being able to judge / whether **Jesus** shall present himself to his betrothed people in the tokens of his favor / or the evidences of his righteous displeasure.

# Parabolic Discourse of the Wise and Foolish Virgins.

yet see here the distinction between the prudence of the Saints and the folly of the senseless.

☞ THE WISE TAKE OIL IN THEIR VESSELS; the Oil is the fuel for the flame. Consequently, in a Spiritual sense, it represents to us that which actually turns the knowledge of the Prophecies into a light and provides nourishment to it.

$\alpha$. It is indeed true that the Oil is a symbol of the truths expressed through earnest reflection and contemplation from those Spiritual Olive trees, the word of God. <note>The author refers to the "two olive trees" mentioned in the Bible as sources of divine truth.</note> See our explanation of Revelation XI and what we say in our Spiritual explanation regarding the Lamps and Oil in the Sanctuary in our *Diatribe* <note>original: "Diatribe"; likely referring to a formal scholarly discourse or treatise written by the author.</note>.

$\beta$. However, since the Oil here distinguishes the disposition of the foolish and wise Virgins—the lack of it being the reason why the foolish are shut out—it follows naturally that the Oil here signifies the known truths sanctified to the soul. For the foolish also had a knowledge of the Truths; without that, they could not be called Virgins, nor go out to meet the Bridegroom. Understand then this Oil:

a. Just as it has penetrated into the soul like a Spiritual wick <note>original: "lemmet"; the part of the lamp that absorbs the oil to produce light.</note>, and the soul is as if soaked through by the same. Thus, those truths must not only be known, but that knowledge of Jesus' Kingdom and all its preparation, drawn from the Divine Oracles <note>original: "Godspraaken"; refers to the prophetic words of Scripture.</note>, the very image of these matters, must be imprinted upon the heart. It is not enough that the glorious painting of that King, His excellent subjects, and His glorious and lovely governance, etc., are printed in the brain; those elegant features must penetrate into the heart and be vividly displayed there.

b. Truths thus known, thus imprinted on the heart, or thus penetrating the soul like an Oil, will ensure that the knowledge of Jesus' coming to His Church—to perform such glorious things in and through her—is accompanied by a ready self-surrender to serve Jesus in the execution of His counsel.

c. Then that knowledge shall also be directed, in times of oppression, to provide the consolation of the Scriptures.

d. It shall also possess a purifying power when the knowledge of the Church's defects, pointed out in the Divine Oracles, incites one to repair those defects. Without this Oil of the Spirit, the known word of the prophecies is no light; it is a Lamp whose wick only smokes or burns dimly without Oil, soon to be extinguished.

# The Parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins

### β. They fell asleep
**a.** Concerning the confused thoughts and activities, such as one has in sleep. They held confused thoughts regarding the Holy, merciful, wise, and mighty dealings of the Bridegroom <note>original: "Ec." - likely an abbreviation for "etcetera"</note>, as if His mercies were shut up by wrath, His goodness diminished, His power shortened, and His Holiness and wisdom darkened.
**b.** Concerning confused affections toward Him, being dissatisfied, sorrowful, fearful, and cooled in their love.
**c.** Indeed, just as one in sleep—in a dream—is now caressed by a vain joy, then tossed by a vain fear and sorrow, so it was with the sleeping Virgins; they rejoiced over matters that are no substance for essential joy, while fearing and grieving over things that ought not to have disturbed their joy and rest.

Thus these Virgins slept; however, this sleep is not the sleep of death. The principle of Spiritual life remained within them; therefore they pray:
<margin>*Psalm 13, verse 3* <note>The Dutch text cites verse 4, following the traditional numbering; in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 13:3: "Lighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death."</note></margin>
"Lest my eyes sleep in death." Nevertheless, as long as they sleep, they appear outwardly to accomplish as little for the Bridegroom as

### γ. The Foolish ones
who also slumber and sleep. Outwardly, there appears to be no distinction between them and the wise <note>original: "Ec."</note>; however:
**a.** The slumber of the foolish must be understood quite differently. Since they have never been sober and awake in a Spiritual manner, that Spiritual sleep which occasionally overtakes God’s sanctified children cannot seize them. Therefore, by their slumber and sleep, we understand a cessation of that outward activity and alertness which they previously practiced and displayed:
**a.** In reading God’s Word, investigating the truths, and tracing the ways of God in the Divine oracles <term>God-spraken: prophetic utterances or scriptures</term>.
**b.** In guarding themselves against the coarse temptations of lusts, and appearing then as if sober and moderate in their senses.
**c.** In defending the truth and suffering for it. In these things they are now sluggish, surrendered to their desires, shunning labor, seeking their pleasure and ease—yes, buried in the

# The Parabolic Discourse of the Wise and Foolish Virgins.

$\alpha$. Those who, having entered into the Inner Chambers, lamented the decay <note>The "decay" or "decline" refers to the perceived spiritual corruption of the church</note>.

$\beta$. Accusing and loathing themselves for their own lukewarmness and faithlessness.

$\gamma$. Sighing to the Lord with supplications and prayers—though not with that earnestness and boldness <term>vrijmoedigheid: a state of spiritual confidence or "boldness of speech" before God</term> as is proper—to the end that He would glorify His Bride, who is currently so unadorned.

$\delta$. Nourishing a quiet hope that Jehovah, against all expectation, would grant His final and most precious love to His Bride.

$\epsilon$. However, even if these did not sleep with the others, they nevertheless remained silent; for the fact that this voice was only first heard at midnight presupposes a prior silence. They were silent, then:

a. Out of fear of men, so as not to make themselves hated by them; for in those times, people could not endure a properly distinguished presentation of that Bridegroom—specifically, who alone is His Bride, and what constitutes the true practice of speaking <note>original: "spreek-oeffening"</note> in contrast to all kinds of deceitful appearances.

b. Out of despondency, seeing no fruit from their labor, and therefore giving up the work, just as if God were not powerful enough to make the dead living.

c. Out of a lack of boldness within themselves; they see so much deformity in their own bosom that they lose the desire to raise earnest rebukes and exhortations toward others.

d. Out of laziness and sluggishness, shrinking from the labor, and thus from a lack of heartfelt compassion and love for their fellow man.

$\zeta$. But the Lord God, in the closest and darkest part of that night, would so fill the heart and the mouth of such persons that they would not only speak, but shout.

$\alpha$. With boldness, as the awakened love and awe for Jesus shall banish the fear of men far away.

$\beta$. With earnestness and tirelessness, as the joyful hope of fruitfulness now shines upon them.

$\gamma$. With a renewed boldness; having received anew the assurance—upon a heartfelt confession of their crimes and manifold deviations—that with Jehovah there was much forgiveness to the end that He might be feared <note>A reference to Psalm 130:4</note>; so that, being cleansed once more from their sinful filth in the blood of the Lamb, they could teach transgressors the ways of God with undaunted speech.

# Parable-discourse of the Wise and Foolish Virgins.

a. This is a refutation of their proposition that a narrow measure of grace, when divided among so many, would be enough: Oh no, here is required:

α. The most urgent love of the Bride, since the Bridegroom wished to bestow his most precious love now.

β. The uttermost and most complete readiness to venture everything—with the sacrifice of oneself and all interests—to obtain those final and most ample treasures of salvation.

γ. The most untiring patience, since it would be crowned with the most glorious end.

δ. The most extensive desire, the widest opening of the mouth, since Jehovah wished to fill it now with all Heavenly delicacies, scarcely tasted in former times.

The wise, therefore, oppose that conception, as if a narrow measure would be enough for them and the foolish. *No, lest there possibly be too little for you and us.*

η. Thus the Lord Jesus, through his children, allows the foolish to be sweetly coaxed as long as the time of their visitation lasts; but if they then pay no heed to that great salvation, he afterwards changes that friendly enticement and invitation into a hard and rejecting answer, just as here the foolish received no other comfort than:

O. **GO TO THE SELLERS**. It is indeed true that the "buyers" <note>The author likely means "merchants" or "sellers" here in the context of the biblical metaphor</note> in the Holy leaves <note>The scriptures</note> are also symbols of Deceivers and false Teachers. See Hosea 12 regarding the Merchant in whose hand is a deceitful scale; yet Christ, in an opposite sense, also appears under that symbol in Revelation 3 and Isaiah 55. η. It is true, they slumber and sleep; yet in this, they appear to be equal to the wise.

ι. They also obey that voice according to the outward appearance: "Go out to meet the Bridegroom," setting out on the way once more alongside the wise.
κ. To that end, they also prepare their Lamps, diligently researching the word of prophecies, clarifying them, and presenting them to others in a demonstrative manner.
λ. By the light that has risen, they see their emptiness and their lack of the holy Oil <note>original: "g. Olie," referring to the Holy Spirit</note>, confessing the same with shame and embarrassment.
μ. Wishing, through the prayers, diligence, and labor of the Sanctified, to receive a share of the precious gifts of the Spirit, the holy Oil.
ν. They still run to the holy marketplaces <note>original: "g. koop-winkels"</note>, the places where they hope their deficiency shall be fulfilled.
ξ. After they have been informed of the Bridegroom’s coming, they betake themselves to the place where He had entered; and notwithstanding that the door is shut and the entrance sealed against them, they knock earnestly.
π. Praying to Jesus: "Lord, Lord, open to us."

# The Parable-Discourse of the Wise and Foolish Virgins. 435

Is that pure love for Jesus not sufficiently distinguished from all sham-love, and from a merely natural esteem and affection for Jesus? Is a faithful approach to Jesus—which belongs only to the sanctified children of God—not sufficiently sifted from the kind of encounter that belongs to the foolish, no matter how much they commend themselves through outward appearance? How is it possible, therefore, that such people still imagine that Jesus is their Bridegroom and they are His Bride; that they meet Christ in truth, driven by a holy desire for Christ and His fellowship? Is there then no distinction between that Bridegroom and that which a natural man <note>A person acting on human instinct rather than spiritual rebirth.</note> loves? Does the love of Jesus not differ from a sinful self-love, etc.? It is true, people currently excuse themselves by citing the flaws of God's children, arguing that such an essential difference does not manifest itself outwardly, etc. Yet one sees from this parable-discourse that the wise can also slumber and sleep, and yet remain fundamentally distinct from the foolish. But what will it be for them when the Lord—

<margin>† Who shall one day awaken, shall cause another Spirit and Life to be seen in those [the wise], to the shame of the others?</margin>

<margin>†† When the truths shall one day be presented in such a powerful manner that no coverings of shame shall remain, but their nakedness shall be made public in every way—not for their salutary conviction, but only for their shaming and torment.</margin>

<margin>††† What will it be when it finally comes to the test of whether one has Oil or not, and one then perceives the lack only too late?</margin>

If only one could learn to acknowledge one's lack in time! To cry out now with an inward embarrassment: "Our lamps are being extinguished; our imagined hope, joy, consolation, and boldness <term>vrymoedigheid: a state of spiritual confidence or assurance before God</term> fail us!" If only one made such a frank confession to God's children, desiring to be moved toward conversion through their supplications, diligence, and efforts—yet with the acknowledgment that Jehovah must actually do the work through His soul-transforming Spirit! Oh, one would not receive that reproachful answer: "Go instead," etc. <note>Referring to Matthew 25:9, where the wise tell the foolish to go to the sellers to buy oil.</note> For while the longsuffering of God still lasts, God's children would speak kindly to such people: "Oh, how we wish that everything about and within us were ready and prepared to share our Oil with you: do not despair, He still has the Spirit..."

### On the Mandatory Duties of a True
# SERVANT OF GOD’S CHURCH
->Sketched in a vivid depiction and poured forth in an Inaugural Oration in the Academy Church by the Highly Learned and Widely Renowned<-
## L O R D
# ANTONIUS DRIESSEN
->Doctor and Professor of Theology at Groningen.<-

*My Spirit, ignited by the fire of zeal,*
*Labors to pursue Your shadow,*
*As it shines upon the harness of the Clouds*
*O DRIESSEN, through the lessons You give:*
*Allow then that my lowly name*
*In the shadow of Your great fame*
*May also lift itself out of the dust,*
*While from Your preaching-work*
*I make a sketch of the true duties*
*For a Servant of God’s Church;*
*How lovely are the ornamental strokes*
*With which you go about painting a Preacher!*

---

*Observe the Servant according to the plan*
*Stripped of Worldly things*
*Where he sits in his Study* <note>original: "Boekvertrek" - literally a book-room or library</note>
*Enraptured in soul-contemplations,*
*Or for his People in true repentance*
*Falls at the feet of a wronged Deity:*
*From there follow him with wise steps*
*Where he speaks from God’s own Mouth*
*And having stepped upon the Temple-chair* <note>The "Temple-chair" refers to the pulpit.</note>
*Teaches us of His Covenant of Reconciliation,* <note>original: "Zoen-verbond" - a theological term for the promise of salvation through Christ.</note>
*Or else foretells, according to time and matters,*
*God’s favors or the blazing of His wrath.*

<column-break/>

*Furthermore, lead him down again from the Chair*
*And follow him in his life’s conduct,*
*While he, amidst the bustle of the People,*
*Interacts through daily walking,*
*A choice painting of an Interpreter*
*Who is Shepherd of Christ’s People!*
*Who shall henceforth behold Your image*
->boldly<-
*Unless his own image,*
*Tested against this, can stand the trial*
*Since it differs all too much?*
*Shame must immediately reveal itself*

a sanctified Teacher <note>original: "Leeraar," referring here to a minister or professor of theology</note>, who presents himself to God as one approved, as a laborer who does not need to be ashamed, who rightly divides the word of truth; and II. what the Apostle’s exhortation, or the duty of Teachers, entails in that regard, and how to apply oneself diligently to it.

### I. Let us then attend to the pure Disposition and holy activities of the Teachers

**A.** The first pure disposition or holy activity that the Apostle describes is to present oneself to God as approved. *Approved* <note>original Greek: "Δόκιμος" (dokimos)</note> means to be so constituted that, upon being examined, one receives approval and thus emerges as tested. To present oneself to God as approved means to conduct oneself before God—indeed, to present oneself before Him as Judge—as having that mindset which wins the approval of the Divine eye. This does not mean that nothing would be found in such a person that He, who is essential Holiness and purity itself, would not disapprove of; rather, it means that he possesses that sincerity, that truth in the inward parts, those essential qualities that make him pleasing in Jehovah’s eyes and able to withstand the test in the Divine Judgment. Let us describe this holy and elegant fundamental form, this disposition, piece by piece, so that we may complete the portrait of such a vigilant leader in Jehovah’s House and Sanctuary.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessary qualifications and internal convictions of a religious minister or teacher.</meta>

# of CITY and COUNTRY.

Such a Teacher <note>Dutch: *Leeraar*; referring here to a minister or preacher</note> must first know the truths, of which he shall be the Proclaimer, for himself—even to the point of conviction. He must be persuaded in his conscience that they have God as their Author, so that he himself first believes that which he preaches to others. He must be so convinced of the firmness, preciousness, and necessity of those truths, that he would dare to safely venture his own Soul’s salvation upon them, and be ready at all times to give up honor, goods, pleasure, yes, even life itself for them, if his Master calls him to do so. It must, therefore, not be enough for him that he was instructed in the foundations of that Doctrine by his Parents or Teachers, and that those tenets were thus imprinted in his memory; rather, he must see with his own eyes, by the light of his own conscience, bringing all the essential fundamental principles to the test, to see if they can stand the trial, and if he finds the stamp of a Divine origin placed upon them. This is so that he may proceed as surely in these matters as if he had seen those things with his eyes, heard them with his ears, and touched them with his hands <note>A reference to 1 John 1:1 regarding the physical witness of spiritual truth</note>. Thus, his faith should rest not upon men, nor upon the authority of any Church, whichever it may be, but upon the conviction of his own conscience, and thereby upon God, who is the Author of that light which shines upon the conscience <term>conscience: the internal moral and spiritual faculty of judgment</term>.

# of CITY and COUNTRY.

Observe his appearance, behold his gestures, and pay attention to his language and *modes of speech*.

a. Just as his *appearance* is far from all affectation and overbearing mastery, so it is nonetheless dignified, simple, and friendly.

b. Just as he seeks to avoid in his *gestures* or *movements* all that is offensive, which bores the eye of the listeners and breaks their attention; so he is also far from an overly sought-after elegance bound by the rules of art: something which I believe Christ and the Apostles <note>The author appeals to the simplicity of the New Testament figures as the ultimate model for ministry.</note> did not even think of in their preaching; although I also firmly maintain that they would have been far from all crude and ill-mannered displays and gestures. It is therefore useful that everyone tries to correct such defects through the rules of art <term>rules of art: formal rhetorical training</term>, provided that he never deviates from natural simplicity, which far surpasses an artificial affectation.

He shall also take heed of the disposition of his listeners, considering which expressions and manner of presentation are most accessible to them.

d. As for the *presentation of the matters themselves*, he does not do this with an indifferent or cold spirit, but with an awakened zeal for the salvation of his listeners, with compassion for the unconverted, and with a pure intent to lead the converted further into grace. And this holy fervor

**f. Do you wish to record the parts of his Oration?** <note>The "Oration" refers to the formal sermon or public discourse delivered by the minister.</note>

†. In his *Prayers*, he strives to place a language into the mouths of God’s Children that corresponds with their state of grace and its various degrees. ††.
